Build an ECS · part 2, components · 2.5

Typed access

ecs/src/2.components/2.5.typed_access/typed_access.rin

In the dojo: 4. a type-erased column, 8. index, not pointer, each on its own, to watch and to practise.

The world stores any component in any combination, as bytes. Game code should never see the bytes. This chapter adds the typed layer on top:

kayan_get<position>(w, e)          -> option<*position in level>: null if missing
kayan_has<velocity>(w, e)          -> b32
kayan_set<health>(w, e, value)     -> ok, dead, or missing

Each is a few lines that turn the type into an id, find the entity's table and row through its slot, and hand the row back as a T. The byte-level core underneath doesn't change at all. This is the split: a small unsafe core of byte fiddling below, checked generic procs on top, each written once.

Step 1: get

kayan_get: proc<T>(w: *kayan_world in level, e: kayan_entity) -> option<*T in level> = {
    if (!kayan_alive(w, e)) {
        return null;
    }
    slot: kayan_slot = vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots, cast(e.index, u64))*;
    t: *kayan_table in level = kayan_table_at(w, slot.table);
    if (!kayan_table_has(t, kayan_id_of<T>())) {
        return null;
    }
    rows: []T in level = kayan_slice<T>(t);
    return rows[cast(slot.row, u64)]&;
}

Handle, slot, table, row, typed view. It's the same path as 1.4's get_position, for any component. Two ways to get null: the handle is dead, or the entity has no T. The return type carries both facts the caller needs: option means test it first, and in level means that once tested, it's memory the program owns. The caller checks once and then has a real pointer.

Step 2: has and set

kayan_has: proc<T>(w: *kayan_world in level, e: kayan_entity) -> b32 = {
    return (kayan_signature(w, e) & kayan_mask_of<T>()) != 0;
}

kayan_has doesn't touch the row at all. An entity's components are its table's signature, one AND away.

kayan_set: proc<T>(w: *kayan_world in level, e: kayan_entity, value: T) -> kayan_status = {
    if (!kayan_alive(w, e)) {
        return kayan_status.dead;
    }
    p: option<*T in level> = kayan_get<T>(w, e);
    if (!p) {
        return kayan_status.missing;
    }
    p* = value;
    return kayan_status.ok;
}

kayan_set writes a component the entity already has. Giving it a component it doesn't have changes which table it belongs in, and that's 2.6. So the status gains a third value:

kayan_status: enum[must_use] = {
    ok,
    dead,
    missing,
}

Step 3: building things

With kayan_set, game code builds entities with small procs. Engines call these prefabs or archetype constructors:

spawn_drone: proc(r: region level, w: *kayan_world in level, x: f32, y: f32) -> kayan_entity = {
    e: kayan_entity = kayan_spawn(r, w, kayan_mask_of<position>() | kayan_mask_of<velocity>() | kayan_mask_of<health>());
    _ = kayan_set<position>(w, e, { .at = { .x = x, .y = y } });
    _ = kayan_set<velocity>(w, e, { .per_second = { .x = -1.0, .y = 0.0 } });
    _ = kayan_set<health>(w, e, { .points = 100.0, .max = 100.0 });
    return e;
}

The _ = says "I know this returns a status and I'm ignoring it on purpose". Here that's safe: the entity was just spawned with exactly these components.

Reading and changing is kayan_get, and a test:

        h: option<*health in level> = kayan_get<health>(w, a);
        if (h) {
            h*.points -= 25.0;
        }

Step 4: keep handles, borrow pointers

The pointer kayan_get returns points into a column. 2.2 showed what columns do when their table fills up: they move. So a pointer is good until the next structural change: a spawn, a despawn, or (from 2.6) an add or remove. The program proves it:

        kept: option<*health in level> = kayan_get<health>(w, a);
        for (i: u32 = 0; i < 8; i += 1) {
            _ = spawn_drone(level, w, 40.0 + cast(i, f32), 0.0);
        }
        if (kept) {
            kept*.points = 1.0;
        }
kept a pointer to 0:1's health, spawned 8 drones (the table grew), wrote 1 through it:
    0:1 at (20.00,  5.00), health 75
    the write went to the column's old block; the handle still finds the real one

The health is still 75. The write landed in the column's old block, which the region still owns, so nothing crashes and no sanitizer complains. It's just lost. Hence the rule every ECS has in some form:

Keep handles. Borrow pointers: get, use, forget.

It's worth being exact about what the checker did here, because this is the line between what regions give you and what they don't. It lets the program through, because in level asks for one thing: this pointer is memory in level, for as long as level is open. That's true. The old block is still there. What the pointer no longer is, is the component, and no amount of checking level can tell you that. That's what a handle is for: the handle goes through the slot, so it finds the row wherever it is now.

You can also ask for more. Write the pointer with no region, option<*health>, and it's no longer a claim about memory. It's a borrow from w, and the checker ends the borrow at the first call that may change w:

type error: 'kept' may be stale: 'w', which it was taken from, has been changed since; take it again

So a pointer you mean to use right away is best left without a region. Part 3's systems write their column slices exactly that way.

Run it

two drones and a bullet, built with kayan_set:
    0:1 at (20.00,  5.00), health 100
    1:1 at (30.00, -5.00), health 100
drone 0:1 is hit through kayan_get<health>:
    0:1 at (20.00,  5.00), health 75
the bullet has a velocity: yes; a health: no
kayan_get<health> on the bullet is null: yes
kayan_set<health> on the bullet: missing
despawned 1:1; kayan_set<health> on it now: dead
    1:1 is not a live drone
...
kayan_verify: 0 problems

Try

  1. Write spawn_turret and spawn_bullet-style procs for your own kinds of thing.
  2. Move the kept pointer's kayan_get to after the spawning loop. Now the write sticks. Why?
  3. Make kayan_set add the component when it's missing, instead of returning missing. What would it need from 2.6?
  4. Change kept to an option<*health> and compile. Why is the program refused now, when the pointer goes to exactly the same place?

This is the one123// place bytes become a type, so it takes nothing on trust. T must be the124// column's size, and plain data: any bytes are then a valid T, so reading the125// wrong type gives wrong numbers, never a bad pointer. The rows must fit, which126// the slice knows and no field can lie about, and the bytes must be aligned for127// T. After the column grows it is the129// old block, still readable, no longer the column: take the view again.130kayan_column_slice: proc<T>(c: *const kayan_column, count: u64) -> []T in level = {131    if (c*.size != sizeof(T)) {132        printfmt("kayan: a column of {}-byte rows read as a {}-byte type\n", c*.size, sizeof(T));133        exit(1);134    }135    if (!reflect_is_plain(T<>&)) {136        printfmt("kayan: a column holds plain data, and this {}-byte type is not\n", sizeof(T));137        exit(1);138    }139    if (count > c*.data.length / sizeof(T)) {140        printfmt("kayan: a view of {} rows on a column with room for {}\n", count, c*.data.length / sizeof(T));141        exit(1);142    }143    unsafe {144        if (cast(c*.data.data, usize) % alignof(T) != 0) {145            printfmt("kayan: a column's bytes are not aligned to {}\n", alignof(T));146            exit(1);147        }148        raw: ^T = cast(c*.data.data, ^T);149        return cast(raw[0..count], []T in level);150    }151}152 153// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------154// The table155// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------156 157// `columns[id]` is in use when the signature has bit `id`; the others stay158// zeroed. info*.name : "?";210}211 212kayan_table_has: proc(t: *kayan_table in level, id: u32) -> b32 = {213    return (t*.signature & kayan_bit(id)) != 0;214}215 216// A table for a signature: one empty column per component in it, sized from217// the registry. Every component in the signature must be registered.218kayan_table_init: proc(w: *kayan_world in level, t: *kayan_table in level, signature: u64) -> void = {219    t*.signature = signature;220    for (id: u32 = 0; id < 64; id += 1) {221        if ((signature & kayan_bit(id)) != 0) {222            info: option<*const reflect in permanent> = id < w*.component_count ? w*.infos[id] : null;223            if (!info) {224                printfmt("kayan: signature {} uses component {}, which was never registered\n", signature, id);225                exit(1);226            } else {227                kayan_column_init(t*.columns[id]&, info);228            }229        }230    }231}232 233// Double the room in `entities` and in every column at once.234kayan_table_grow: proc(r: region level, w: *kayan_world in level, t: *kayan_table in level) -> void = {235    capacity: u64 = t*.capacity == 0 ? 4 : t*.capacity * 2;236    entities: []kayan_entity in level = new_slice<kayan_entity>(r, capacity);237    for (row: u64 = 0; row < t*.count; row += 1) {238        entities[row] = t*.entities[row];239    }240    t*.entities = entities;241    for (id: u32 = 0; id < w*.component_count; id += 1) {242        if (kayan_table_has(t, id)) {243            kayan_column_grow(r, t*.columns[id]&, t*.count, capacity);244        }245    }246    t*.capacity = capacity;247}248 249// A new row at the end, owned by `e`, with every component zeroed.250kayan_table_add_row: proc(r: region level, w: *kayan_world in level, t: *kayan_table in level, e: kayan_entity) -> u64 = {251    if (t*.count == t*.capacity) {252        kayan_table_grow(r, w, t);253    }254    row: u64 = t*.count;255    t*.count += 1;256    t*.entities[row] = e;257    for (id: u32 = 0; signature);303    if (found) {304        return found*;305    }306    index: u32 = cast(w*.tables*.length, u32);307    t: *kayan_table in level = new<kayan_table>(r);308    kayan_table_init(w, t, signature);309    _ = vec<*kayan_table in level>push(w*.tables, t);310    _ = hashmap<u64, u32>set(w*.by_signature, signature, index);311    return index;312}313 314// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------315// The world316// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------317 318kayan_world_make: proc(r: region level) -> *kayan_world in level = {319    return new<kayan_world>(r, {320        .tables = vec<*kayan_table in level>make(r, 8),321        .by_signature = hashmap<u64, u32>make(r),322 y } });485    _ = kayan_set<velocity>(w, e, { .per_second = { .x = -1.0, .y = 0.0 } });486    _ = kayan_set<health>(w, e, { .points = 100.0, .max = 100.0 });487    return e;488}489 490spawn_bullet: Build an ECS · part 2, components · 2.6

Adding and removing components

ecs/src/2.components/2.6.add_remove/add_remove.rin

In the dojo: 2. swap-remove and the back-reference, 10. memoized edges, each on its own, to watch and to practise.

A drone catches fire: it gains a burning component. The fire goes out: it loses it. Changing what an entity is, while the game runs, is the thing the C kayan couldn't do, because its archetypes were structs fixed at compile time. In an archetype ECS a table holds exactly one combination, so a drone that gains a component no longer belongs in its table. It moves:

  1. find the table for its signature plus (or minus) the component;
  2. add a row there, and copy every component the two tables share;
  3. swap-remove its old row, fixing whoever moves into the hole;
  4. point its slot at the new table and row.

Its handle doesn't change. Everything else about it is where it was, one table over.

Step 1: the move

kayan_move: proc(r: region level, w: *kayan_world in level, e: kayan_entity, to_index: u32) -> void = {
    slot: kayan_slot = vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots, cast(e.index, u64))*;
    from_index: u32 = slot.table;
    if (from_index == to_index) {
        return;
    }
    from: *kayan_table in level = kayan_table_at(w, from_index);
    to: *kayan_table in level = kayan_table_at(w, to_index);
    from_row: u64 = cast(slot.row, u64);
    to_row: u64 = kayan_table_add_row(r, w, to, e);
    for (id: u32 = 0; id < w*.component_count; id += 1) {
        if (kayan_table_has(from, id) && kayan_table_has(to, id)) {
            kayan_column_copy_row_from(to*.columns[id]&, to_row, from*.columns[id]&, from_row);
        }
    }
    kayan_table_remove_row(w, from, from_row);
    // The slot is written after the calls that were handed the world.
    moved: *kayan_slot = vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots, cast(e.index, u64));
    moved*.table = to_index;
    moved*.row = cast(to_row, u32);
}

Every piece is something you've already built: kayan_table_add_row (2.3), a byte copy per shared column (2.2), kayan_table_remove_row with its slot fix (1.4). Components only the new table has start zeroed (add_row zeroes them). Components only the old table has disappear with the old row.

The pointers follow 2.4's rules, and they make this proc easy to read. from and to are held across everything, because tables don't move. The slot is copied out at the top, and the one pointer into it that writes is taken at the bottom, after the calls.

The new copy goes between two columns, so it's a new small proc, the same bounds-checked byte loop as kayan_column_copy_row:

kayan_column_copy_row_from: proc(dst: *kayan_column, to: u64, src: *const kayan_column, from: u64) -> void = {
    for (i: u64 = 0; i < dst*.size; i += 1) {
        dst*.data[to * dst*.size + i] = src*.data[from * src*.size + i];
    }
}

A move changes where an entity's data lives, and that's the thing type erasure makes risky, yet nothing here is unsafe. The two trusted procs are still the column's own, from 2.2.

A move costs one row copy in and one row copy out. That's cheap, but not free, and it's why components that flip on and off every frame are sometimes better as a field (a bool on_fire inside health) than as a component.

Step 2: add and remove, typed

kayan_add: proc<T>(r: region level, w: *kayan_world in level, e: kayan_entity, value: T) -> kayan_status = {
    if (!kayan_alive(w, e)) {
        return kayan_status.dead;
    }
    if (!kayan_has<T>(w, e)) {
        from: u32 = vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots, cast(e.index, u64))*.table;
        kayan_move(r, w, e, kayan_table_with(r, w, from, kayan_id_of<T>()));
    }
    return kayan_set<T>(w, e, value);
}

If the entity already has a T, adding is just setting. Otherwise it moves to the table with T, then sets it. kayan_remove<T> is the mirror image: missing if it has no T, otherwise a move to the table without T.

Step 3: the archetype graph

Which table is "the table with T"? Its signature is the old one plus T's bit, so it could be looked up in by_signature every time. But a game toggling components does that constantly, always between the same few tables. So each table remembers its neighbours:

kayan_table: struct = {
    signature: u64;
    count: u64;
    capacity: u64;
    entities: []kayan_entity in level;
    columns: [64]kayan_column;
    add_edges: [64]u32;
    remove_edges: [64]u32;
}

add_edges[id] is where this table's entities go when they gain component id. remove_edges[id] is where they go when they lose it. Each is stored as index + 1, so the zero a new table starts with means "not known yet", with no initialization pass.

kayan_table_with: proc(r: region level, w: *kayan_world in level, from: u32, id: u32) -> u32 = {
    edge: u32 = kayan_table_at(w, from)*.add_edges[id];
    if (edge != 0) {
        w*.edge_hits += 1;
        return edge - 1;
    }
    w*.lookups += 1;
    to: u32 = kayan_table_for(r, w, kayan_table_at(w, from)*.signature | kayan_bit(id));
    kayan_table_at(w, from)*.add_edges[id] = to + 1;
    kayan_table_at(w, to)*.remove_edges[id] = from + 1;
    return to;
}

The first move from {position velocity health} with burning looks the table up (and makes it). It then writes the answer on both tables: an add edge one way and a remove edge back. After that, catching fire and putting it out both follow edges. The tables and their edges form a graph, the archetype graph, and flecs is built around it.

Run it

4 drones:
    table 0 {position velocity health}: 0:1 1:1 2:1 3:1
frame 1
    0:1 catches fire: ok
    2:1 catches fire: ok
    table 0 {position velocity health}: 3:1 1:1
    table 1 {position velocity health burning}: 0:1 2:1
frame 2
    0:1 is put out: ok
    1:1 catches fire: ok
    2:1 catches fire: ok
...
frame 3
    1:1 is put out: ok
    2:1 is put out: ok
    3:1 is put out: missing
    3:1 catches fire: ok
...
2:1 moved tables twice and kept its data: at (30.00, 0.00), health 100
moves that looked up a table by signature: 1; that followed an edge: 6
kayan_verify: 0 problems

Watch row order shuffle as entities move: 3:1 jumps to row 0 of table 0 when 0:1 leaves. Order is never promised, and swap-remove is why. And one lookup for seven moves: that's the graph working.

Try

  1. Add a stunned component and a second edge: stun a burning drone. How many tables exist now, and which edges were written?
  2. Print every table's known edges after frame 3.
  3. Make kayan_add<burning> on a drone that's already burning add to the rate instead of replacing it. Where does that logic belong: in kayan or in the game?

In an archetype ECS a table holds exactly one combination, so a5// drone that gains a component no longer belongs in its table. It moves:6//7//   1. find the table for its signature plus (or minus) the component;8//   2. add a row there, and copy every component the two tables share;9//   3. swap-remove its old row, fixing whoever moved into the hole;10//   4. point its slot at the new table and row.11//12// Its handle does not change. Everything else about it is where it was, one13// table over.14//15// Step 1 is a hashmap lookup by signature, and a game toggling components16// does it constantly, always between the same few tables. So each table17// remembers its neighbours: "add burning: table 2", "remove burning: table 1".18// These edges make the tables a graph, the archetype graph, and after the19// first move between two tables every later one follows an edge instead of20// looking anything up.21//22// As in 2.4 and 2.5: the world and its tables live in the23// `level` region, the two trusted procs are the column's, and the row copy24// between tables is a bounds-checked byte loop.25 26import "std/print.rin"27import "std/memops.rin"28import "std/vec.rin"29import "std/hashmap.rin"30import "std/slice.rin"31 32level: region;33 34vec2: struct = {35    x: f32;36    y: f32;37}38 39position: struct = { at: vec2; }40velocity: struct = { per_second: vec2; }41health: struct = { points: f32; max: f32; }42damage: struct = { amount: f32; }43lifetime: struct = { seconds: f32; }44turret: struct = { cooldown: f32; timer: f32; }45burning: struct = { per_second: f32; }46 47component: enum = {48    position,49    velocity,50    health,51    damage,52    lifetime,53    turret,54    burning,55}56 57component_of: proc<position>() -> component = { return component.position; }58component_of: proc<velocity>() -> component = { return component.velocity; }59component_of: proc<health>() -> component = { return component.health; }60component_of: proc<damage>() -> component = { return component.damage; }61component_of: proc<lifetime>() -> component = { return component.lifetime; }62component_of: proc<turret>() -> component = { return component.turret; }63component_of: proc<burning>() -> component = { return component.burning; }64 65// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------66// Entities (Part 1)67// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------68 69kayan_entity: struct = {70    index: u32;71    generation: u32;72}73 74// `missing`: the entity is alive but has no such component.75kayan_status: enum[must_use] = {76    ok,77    dead,78    missing,79}80 81// Where an entity lives: which table, and which row of it.82kayan_slot: struct = {83    generation: u32;84    table: u32;85    row: u32;86}87 88// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------89// Columns (2.2)90// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------91 92kayan_column: struct = {93    data: []u8 in level;94    size: u64;95    align: u64;96}97 98kayan_column_init: proc(c: *kayan_column, info: *const reflect) -> void = {99    c*.size = info*.size;100    c*.align = info*.align;101}102 103kayan_column_grow: proc(r: region level, c: *kayan_column, count: u64, capacity: u64) -> void = {104    unsafe {105        raw: ^u8 = cast(memops_arena_push_zero(r, c*.size * capacity, c*.align), ^u8);106        bytes: []u8 in level = cast(raw[0..c*.size * capacity], []u8 in level);107        // Slicing checks both ends: a count past either block stops the program.108        kept: u64 = c*.size * count;109        slice<u8>copy(bytes[0..kept], c*.data[0..kept]);110        c*.data = bytes;111    }112}113 114kayan_column_copy_row: proc(c: *kayan_column, to: u64, from: u64) -> void = {115    for (i: u64 = 0; i < c*.size; i += 1) {116        c*.data[to * c*.size + i] = c*.data[from * c*.size + i];117    }118}119 120// Row `from` of one column over row `to` of another: the same component in121// two tables, as a move between tables copies it.122kayan_column_copy_row_from: proc(dst: *kayan_column, to: u64, src: *const kayan_column, from: u64) -> void = {123    for (i: u64 = 0; i < dst*.size; i += 1) {124        dst*.data[to * dst*.size + i] = src*.data[from * src*.size + i];125    }126}127 128kayan_column_zero_row: proc(c: *kayan_column, row: u64) -> void = {129    for (i: u64 = 0; i < c*.size; i += 1) {130        c*.data[row * c*.size + i] = 0;131    }132}133 134// The typed view: the column's first `count` rows as `[]T`. This is the one135// place bytes become a type, so it takes nothing on trust. T must be the136// column's size, and plain data: any bytes are then a valid T, so reading the137// wrong type gives wrong numbers, never a bad pointer. The rows must fit, which138// the slice knows and no field can lie about, and the bytes must be aligned for139// T. The view is `[]T in level`: the bytes are in the region, so the view is140// good memory for as long as the region is. After the column grows it is the141// old block, still readable, no longer the column: take the view again.142kayan_column_slice: proc<T>(c: *const kayan_column, count: u64) -> []T in level = {143    if (c*.size != sizeof(T)) {144        printfmt("kayan: a column of {}-byte rows read as a {}-byte type\n", c*.size, sizeof(T));145        exit(1);146    }147    if (!reflect_is_plain(T<>&)) {148        printfmt("kayan: a column holds plain data, and this {}-byte type is not\n", sizeof(T));149        exit(1);150    }151    if (count > c*.data.length / sizeof(T)) {152        printfmt("kayan: a view of {} rows on a column with room for {}\n", count, c*.data.length / sizeof(T));153        exit(1);154    }155    unsafe {156        if (cast(c*.data.data, usize) % alignof(T) != 0) {157            printfmt("kayan: a column's bytes are not aligned to {}\n", alignof(T));158            exit(1);159        }160        raw: ^T = cast(c*.data.data, ^T);161        return cast(raw[0..count], []T in level);162    }163}164 165// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------166// The table167// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------168 169// `columns[id]` is in use when the signature has bit `id`; the others stay170// zeroed. Count and capacity are the table's, shared by its columns and by171// `entities`, so they can never disagree.172//173// The edges: `add_edges[id]` is the table this one's entities move to when174// they gain component `id`, and `remove_edges[id]` when they lose it. Each is175// the table's index plus one, so 0, which a new table starts with, means "not176// known yet".177kayan_table: struct = {178    signature: u64;179    count: u64;180    capacity: u64;181    entities: []kayan_entity in level;182    columns: [64]kayan_column;183    add_edges: [64]u32;184    remove_edges: [64]u32;185}186 187// The world: the registry, the slots and free list, and every table, with a188// map from signature to table index so finding one is a lookup, not a search.189// Tables are referred to by index in the slots, and by pointer everywhere190// else: a table is made once in the region and never moves.191kayan_world: struct = {192    infos: [64]option<*const reflect in permanent>;193    component_count: u32;194    tables: *vec<*kayan_table in level> in level;195    by_signature: *hashmap<u64, u32> in level;196    slots: *vec<kayan_slot> in level;197    free: *vec<u32> in level;198    live: u64;199    // How table moves found their destination, for this chapter's output.200    lookups: u64;201    edge_hits: u64;202}203 204kayan_bit: proc(id: u32) -> u64 = {205    return 1'u64 shl cast(id, u64);206}207 208kayan_id_of: proc<T>() -> u32 = {209    return cast(component_of<T>(), u32);210}211 212kayan_mask_of: proc<T>() -> u64 = {213    return kayan_bit(kayan_id_of<T>());214}215 216kayan_register: proc(w: *kayan_world in level, id: u32, info: *const reflect in permanent) -> void = {217    if (id >= 64) {218        printfmt("kayan: component id {} is past the 64 a signature can hold\n", id);219        exit(1);220    }221    w*.infos[id] = info;222    if (id + 1 > w*.component_count) {223        w*.component_count = id + 1;224    }225}226 227// A component's name, for printing: a registered id's, or "?" for a slot228// nobody filled.229kayan_name: proc(w: *kayan_world in level, id: u32) -> ^const char = {230    info: option<*const reflect in permanent> = w*.infos[id];231    return info ? info*.name : "?";232}233 234kayan_table_has: proc(t: *kayan_table in level, id: u32) -> b32 = {235    return (t*.signature & kayan_bit(id)) != 0;236}237 238// A table for a signature: one empty column per component in it, sized from239// the registry. Every component in the signature must be registered.240kayan_table_init: proc(w: *kayan_world in level, t: *kayan_table in level, signature: u64) -> void = {241    t*.signature = signature;242    for (id: u32 = 0; id < 64; id += 1) {243        if ((signature & kayan_bit(id)) != 0) {244            info: option<*const reflect in permanent> = id < w*.component_count ? w*.infos[id] : null;245            if (!info) {246                printfmt("kayan: signature {} uses component {}, which was never registered\n", signature, id);247                exit(1);248            } else {249                kayan_column_init(t*.columns[id]&, info);250            }251        }252    }253}254 255// Double the room in `entities` and in every column at once.256kayan_table_grow: proc(r: region level, w: *kayan_world in level, t: *kayan_table in level) -> void = {257    capacity: u64 = t*.capacity == 0 ? 4 : t*.capacity * 2;258    entities: []kayan_entity in level = new_slice<kayan_entity>(r, capacity);259    for (row: u64 = 0; row < t*.count; row += 1) {260        entities[row] = t*.entities[row];261    }262    t*.entities = entities;263    for (id: u32 = 0; id < w*.component_count; id += 1) {264        if (kayan_table_has(t, id)) {265            kayan_column_grow(r, t*.columns[id]&, t*.count, capacity);266        }267    }268    t*.capacity = capacity;269}270 271// A new row at the end, owned by `e`, with every component zeroed.272kayan_table_add_row: proc(r: region level, w: *kayan_world in level, t: *kayan_table in level, e: kayan_entity) -> u64 = {273    if (t*.count == t*.capacity) {274        kayan_table_grow(r, w, t);275    }276    row: u64 = t*.count;277    t*.count += 1;278    t*.entities[row] = e;279    for (id: u32 = 0; id < w*.component_count; id += 1) {280        if (kayan_table_has(t, id)) {281            kayan_column_zero_row(t*.columns[id]&, row);282        }283    }284    return row;285}286 287// 1.4's swap-remove, for every column: the last row is copied over `row`, and288// the slot of the entity that owned the last row is told where it went.289kayan_table_remove_row: proc(w: *kayan_world in level, t: *kayan_table in level, row: u64) -> void = {290    last: u64 = t*.count - 1;291    if (row != last) {292        for (id: u32 = 0; id < w*.component_count; id += 1) {293            if (kayan_table_has(t, id)) {294                kayan_column_copy_row(t*.columns[id]&, row, last);295            }296        }297        moved: kayan_entity = t*.entities[last];298        t*.entities[row] = moved;299        vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots, cast(moved.index, u64))*.row = cast(row, u32);300    }301    t*.count = last;302}303 304// The typed view of one of the table's columns: T's rows, all of them in use.305// Asking for a component the table does not have is a bug, so it stops.306kayan_slice: proc<T>(t: *kayan_table in level) -> []T in level = {307    id: u32 = kayan_id_of<T>();308    if (!kayan_table_has(t, id)) {309        printfmt("kayan: the table has no column for component {}\n", id);310        exit(1);311    }312    return kayan_column_slice<T>(t*.columns[id]&, t*.count);313}314 315// The table at an index: a pointer into the region, good for as long as the316// level is. The vec of pointers may grow, but what it points at does not move.317kayan_table_at: proc(w: *kayan_world in level, index: u32) -> *kayan_table in level = {318    return vec<*kayan_table in level>at(w*.tables, cast(index, u64))*;319}320 321// The table for a signature: found if it exists, made if it does not. This is322// where archetypes come from.323kayan_table_for: proc(r: region level, w: *kayan_world in level, signature: u64) -> u32 = {324    found: option<*u32> = hashmap<u64, u32>get(w*.by_signature, signature);325    if (found) {326        return found*;327    }328    index: u32 = cast(w*.tables*.length, u32);329    t: *kayan_table in level = new<kayan_table>(r);330    kayan_table_init(w, t, signature);331    _ = vec<*kayan_table in level>push(w*.tables, t);332    _ = hashmap<u64, u32>set(w*.by_signature, signature, index);333    return index;334}335 336// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------337// The world338// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------339 340kayan_world_make: proc(r: region level) -> *kayan_world in level = {341    return new<kayan_world>(r, {342        .tables = vec<*kayan_table in level>make(r, 8),343        .by_signature = hashmap<u64, u32>make(r),344        .slots = vec<kayan_slot>make(r, 8),345        .free = vec<u32>make(r, 8),346    });347}348 349kayan_alive: proc(w: *kayan_world in level, e: kayan_entity) -> b32 = {350    if (cast(e.index, u64) >= w*.slots*.length) {351        return false;352    }353    return vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots, cast(e.index, u64))*.generation == e.generation;354}355 356// A new entity with the components in `signature`, all zeroed, in the table357// for that signature.358kayan_spawn: proc(r: region level, w: *kayan_world in level, signature: u64) -> kayan_entity = {359    e: kayan_entity = {};360    if (!vec<u32>is_empty(w*.free)) {361        e.index = vec<u32>pop(w*.free);362    } else {363        e.index = cast(w*.slots*.length, u32);364        _ = vec<kayan_slot>push(w*.slots, { .generation = 1 });365    }366    e.generation = vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots, cast(e.index, u64))*.generation;367    table_index: u32 = kayan_table_for(r, w, signature);368    t: *kayan_table in level = kayan_table_at(w, table_index);369    row: u64 = kayan_table_add_row(r, w, t, e);370    // Both calls were handed the world, so the pointer into the slots is371    // taken after them.372    slot: *kayan_slot = vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots, cast(e.index, u64));373    slot*.table = table_index;374    slot*.row = cast(row, u32);375    w*.live += 1;376    return e;377}378 379kayan_despawn: proc(w: *kayan_world in level, e: kayan_entity) -> kayan_status = {380    if (!kayan_alive(w, e)) {381        return kayan_status.dead;382    }383    slot: kayan_slot = vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots, cast(e.index, u64))*;384    kayan_table_remove_row(w, kayan_table_at(w, slot.table), cast(slot.row, u64));385    vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots, cast(e.index, u64))*.generation += 1;386    _ = vec<u32>push(w*.free, e.index);387    w*.live -= 1;388    return kayan_status.ok;389}390 391// The components a live entity has: its table's signature. 0 for a dead one.392kayan_signature: proc(w: *kayan_world in level, e: kayan_entity) -> u64 = {393    if (!kayan_alive(w, e)) {394        return 0;395    }396    return kayan_table_at(w, vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots, cast(e.index, u64))*.table)*.signature;397}398 399// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------400// Moving between tables401// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------402 403// The table an entity of table `from` moves to when it gains component `id`.404// The first time, it is found by signature, which can make the table; the405// answer is written on both tables, as from's add edge and the destination's406// remove edge, so neither direction is looked up again.407kayan_table_with: proc(r: region level, w: *kayan_world in level, from: u32, id: u32) -> u32 = {408    edge: u32 = kayan_table_at(w, from)*.add_edges[id];409    if (edge != 0) {410        w*.edge_hits += 1;411        return edge - 1;412    }413    w*.lookups += 1;414    to: u32 = kayan_table_for(r, w, kayan_table_at(w, from)*.signature | kayan_bit(id));415    kayan_table_at(w, from)*.add_edges[id] = to + 1;416    kayan_table_at(w, to)*.remove_edges[id] = from + 1;417    return to;418}419 420// The same for losing component `id`.421kayan_table_without: proc(r: region level, w: *kayan_world in level, from: u32, id: u32) -> u32 = {422    edge: u32 = kayan_table_at(w, from)*.remove_edges[id];423    if (edge != 0) {424        w*.edge_hits += 1;425        return edge - 1;426    }427    w*.lookups += 1;428    to: u32 = kayan_table_for(r, w, kayan_table_at(w, from)*.signature & ~kayan_bit(id));429    kayan_table_at(w, from)*.remove_edges[id] = to + 1;430    kayan_table_at(w, to)*.add_edges[id] = from + 1;431    return to;432}433 434// Move a live entity to table `to_index`. Components both tables have are435// copied, byte for byte; components only the new table has start zeroed;436// components only the old table has are dropped with its old row.437kayan_move: proc(r: region level, w: *kayan_world in level, e: kayan_entity, to_index: u32) -> void = {438    slot: kayan_slot = vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots, cast(e.index, u64))*;439    from_index: u32 = slot.table;440    if (from_index == to_index) {441        return;442    }443    from: *kayan_table in level = kayan_table_at(w, from_index);444    to: *kayan_table in level = kayan_table_at(w, to_index);445    from_row: u64 = cast(slot.row, u64);446    to_row: u64 = kayan_table_add_row(r, w, to, e);447    for (id: u32 = 0; id < w*.component_count; id += 1) {448        if (kayan_table_has(from, id) && kayan_table_has(to, id)) {449            kayan_column_copy_row_from(to*.columns[id]&, to_row, from*.columns[id]&, from_row);450        }451    }452    kayan_table_remove_row(w, from, from_row);453    // The slot is written after the calls that were handed the world.454    moved: *kayan_slot = vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots, cast(e.index, u64));455    moved*.table = to_index;456    moved*.row = cast(to_row, u32);457}458 459// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------460// The typed layer461// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------462 463// e's T, or null if e is dead or has no T. Handle, slot, table, row, typed464// view: the same path as 1.4's get_position, for any component. The pointer is465// good until the next structural change, so use it now and keep the handle.466kayan_get: proc<T>(w: *kayan_world in level, e: kayan_entity) -> option<*T in level> = {467    if (!kayan_alive(w, e)) {468        return null;469    }470    slot: kayan_slot = vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots, cast(e.index, u64))*;471    t: *kayan_table in level = kayan_table_at(w, slot.table);472    if (!kayan_table_has(t, kayan_id_of<T>())) {473        return null;474    }475    rows: []T in level = kayan_slice<T>(t);476    return rows[cast(slot.row, u64)]&;477}478 479kayan_has: proc<T>(w: *kayan_world in level, e: kayan_entity) -> b32 = {480    return (kayan_signature(w, e) & kayan_mask_of<T>()) != 0;481}482 483// Write e's T. It must already have one: giving an entity a component it does484// not have changes its table, which is 2.6.485kayan_set: proc<T>(w: *kayan_world in level, e: kayan_entity, value: T) -> kayan_status = {486    if (!kayan_alive(w, e)) {487        return kayan_status.dead;488    }489    p: option<*T in level> = kayan_get<T>(w, e);490    if (!p) {491        return kayan_status.missing;492    }493    p* = value;494    return kayan_status.ok;495}496 497// Give e a T. If it already has one, this is kayan_set; if not, it moves to498// the table with T and then sets it.499kayan_add: proc<T>(r: region level, w: *kayan_world in level, e: kayan_entity, value: T) -> kayan_status = {500    if (!kayan_alive(w, e)) {501        return kayan_status.dead;502    }503    if (!kayan_has<T>(w, e)) {504        from: u32 = vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots, cast(e.index, u64))*.table;505        kayan_move(r, w, e, kayan_table_with(r, w, from, kayan_id_of<T>()));506    }507    return kayan_set<T>(w, e, value);508}509 510// Take e's T away, moving it to the table without T.511kayan_remove: proc<T>(r: region level, w: *kayan_world in level, e: kayan_entity) -> kayan_status = {512    if (!kayan_alive(w, e)) {513        return kayan_status.dead;514    }515    if (!kayan_has<T>(w, e)) {516        return kayan_status.missing;517    }518    from: u32 = vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots, cast(e.index, u64))*.table;519    kayan_move(r, w, e, kayan_table_without(r, w, from, kayan_id_of<T>()));520    return kayan_status.ok;521}522 523// The invariant, over every table: each row belongs to a live entity whose524// slot points back at that table and row, and the rows of all tables add up to525// the live count.526kayan_verify: proc(w: *kayan_world in level) -> u64 = {527    problems: u64 = 0;528    rows: u64 = 0;529    for (ti: u64 = 0; ti < w*.tables*.length; ti += 1) {530        t: *kayan_table in level = kayan_table_at(w, cast(ti, u32));531        for (row: u64 = 0; row < t*.count; row += 1) {532            e: kayan_entity = t*.entities[row];533            if (!kayan_alive(w, e)) {534                printfmt("kayan_verify: table {} row {} holds dead entity {}:{}\n", ti, row, e.index, e.generation);535                problems += 1;536                continue;537            }538            slot: kayan_slot = vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots, cast(e.index, u64))*;539            if (cast(slot.table, u64) != ti || cast(slot.row, u64) != row) {540                printfmt("kayan_verify: {}:{} is in table {} row {}, its slot says table {} row {}\n",541                    e.index, e.generation, ti, row, slot.table, slot.row);542                problems += 1;543            }544        }545        rows += t*.count;546    }547    if (rows != w*.live) {548        printfmt("kayan_verify: {} rows in tables, {} live entities\n", rows, w*.live);549        problems += 1;550    }551    return problems;552}553 554kayan_print_signature: proc(w: *kayan_world in level, signature: u64) -> void = {555    printfmt("{");556    first: b32 = true;557    for (id: u32 = 0; id < w*.component_count; id += 1) {558        if ((signature & kayan_bit(id)) != 0) {559            if (!first) {560                printfmt(" ");561            }562            printfmt("{}", kayan_name(w, id));563            first = false;564        }565    }566    printfmt("}");567}568 569kayan_print_tables: proc(w: *kayan_world in level) -> void = {570    for (ti: u64 = 0; ti < w*.tables*.length; ti += 1) {571        t: *kayan_table in level = kayan_table_at(w, cast(ti, u32));572        printfmt("    table {} ", cast(ti, u32));573        kayan_print_signature(w, t*.signature);574        printfmt(":");575        for (row: u64 = 0; row < t*.count; row += 1) {576            e: kayan_entity = t*.entities[row];577            printfmt(" {}:{}", e.index, e.generation);578        }579        printfmt("\n");580    }581}582 583// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------584// The program585// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------586 587spawn_drone: proc(r: region level, w: *kayan_world in level, x: f32, y: f32) -> kayan_entity = {588    e: kayan_entity = kayan_spawn(r, w, kayan_mask_of<position>() | kayan_mask_of<velocity>() | kayan_mask_of<health>());589    _ = kayan_set<position>(w, e, { .at = { .x = x, .y = y } });590    _ = kayan_set<velocity>(w, e, { .per_second = { .x = -1.0, .y = 0.0 } });591    _ = kayan_set<health>(w, e, { .points = 100.0, .max = 100.0 });592    return e;593}594 595ignite: proc(r: region level, w: *kayan_world in level, e: kayan_entity) -> void = {596    printfmt("    {}:{} catches fire: {}\n", e.index, e.generation,597        kayan_add<burning>(r, w, e, { .per_second = 10.0 }));598}599 600put_out: proc(r: region level, w: *kayan_world in level, e: kayan_entity) -> void = {601    printfmt("    {}:{} is put out: {}\n", e.index, e.generation, kayan_remove<burning>(r, w, e));602}603 604main: proc() -> i32 = {605    level: region = {606        w: *kayan_world in level = kayan_world_make(level);607        kayan_register(w, kayan_id_of<position>(), position<>&);608        kayan_register(w, kayan_id_of<velocity>(), velocity<>&);609        kayan_register(w, kayan_id_of<health>(), health<>&);610        kayan_register(w, kayan_id_of<damage>(), damage<>&);611        kayan_register(w, kayan_id_of<lifetime>(), lifetime<>&);612        kayan_register(w, kayan_id_of<turret>(), turret<>&);613        kayan_register(w, kayan_id_of<burning>(), burning<>&);614 615        d: [4]kayan_entity = {};616        for (i: u32 = 0; Build an ECS · part 2, components · 2.7

Inspecting the world

ecs/src/2.components/2.7.inspecting/inspecting.rin

In the dojo: 11. a reflection walk, on its own, to watch and to practise.

The world can store, copy and move any component, but it can't show you one. When something goes wrong at frame 3,000, you want to see an entity: every component it has, every field, with names. In C that means writing a printer per component and keeping each in step with its struct. In rin, the compiler already wrote down everything a printer needs. Each component's reflect record lists its fields with their names, types and byte offsets. The world registered those records back in 2.1 to learn component sizes. Here they pay off a second time.

kayan_inspect(w, e)       every component of e, field by field
kayan_print_layout(w)     every table, its columns, and their memory

Neither names a single component type. Add a component tomorrow and both print it.

Step 1: a component as bytes

Tools work from reflect records, not types, so they need the byte view:

kayan_get_bytes: proc(w: *kayan_world in level, e: kayan_entity, id: u32) -> []u8 in level = {
    none: []u8 in level = {};
    if (!kayan_alive(w, e) || id >= w*.component_count) {
        return none;
    }
    slot: kayan_slot = vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots, cast(e.index, u64))*;
    t: *kayan_table in level = kayan_table_at(w, slot.table);
    if (!kayan_table_has(t, id)) {
        return none;
    }
    c: *kayan_column in level = t*.columns[id]&;
    row: u64 = cast(slot.row, u64);
    return c*.data[row * c*.size..(row + 1) * c*.size];
}

It's kayan_get<T>'s path, stopping one step early: the row's bytes as a slice, sized by the column. Game code uses the typed layer; tools use this.

Step 2: walking fields

kayan_print_fields: proc(type: *const reflect, base: []const u8, depth: u32) -> void = {
    for (i: u64 = 0; i < type*.count; i += 1) {
        f: option<*const reflect_field> = reflect_field_at(type, i);
        if (!f) {
            continue;
        }
        if (reflect_field_has_attr(f, "hidden")) {
            continue;
        }
        at: []const u8 = base[f*.offset..f*.offset + f*.size];
        kayan_indent(depth);
        printfmt("{}:", f*.name);
        info: option<*const reflect> = f*.info;
        if (info != null && info*.kind == reflect_kind_struct) {
            printfmt("\n");
            kayan_print_fields(info, at, depth + 1);
        } else {
            printfmt(" ");
            kayan_print_builtin(f*.type, at);
            printfmt("\n");
        }
    }
}

For each field the record says, cut its bytes out of the component by offset and size. A struct field (at: vec2 inside position) has a record of its own, so the printer recurses into it. A builtin field (f32, u32) is printed by its type's name.

reflect_field_at is how checked code walks a record: it says when i is past the end, as a null, so there's no raw array to index. And because each field's bytes are cut with a bounds-checked slice, a record that disagreed with the data would stop the program instead of printing garbage.

That leaves the last step, turning bytes into a value, and it's the inspector's one trusted proc:

kayan_print_builtin: proc(type_name: ^const char, at: []const u8) -> void = {
    if (at.length < 4) {
        printfmt("<{} bytes>", at.length);
        return;
    }
    unsafe {
        if (strcmp(type_name, "f32") == 0) {
            f: f32 = 0.0;
            memcpy(f&, at.data, 4);
            printfmt("{:.2}", cast(f, f64));
        } else if (strcmp(type_name, "u32") == 0) {
            u: u32 = 0;
            memcpy(u&, at.data, 4);
            printfmt("{}", u);
        } else if (strcmp(type_name, "i32") == 0) {
            i: i32 = 0;
            memcpy(i&, at.data, 4);
            printfmt("{}", i);
        } else {
            printfmt("<{}>", type_name);
        }
    }
}

This is unsafe for the same reason as the column's typed view in 2.2: bytes read as a type the checker can't know. And it believes as little. at carries its own length, so that's tested before the block. It copies into a local rather than casting the address, so a field at any offset is fine, aligned or not. And f32, u32 and i32 are plain numbers, so any four bytes are a valid one: a record that disagreed with the data would print a wrong number and nothing worse. Everything else in the inspector is checked.

Step 3: hiding bookkeeping

Fields can carry tags with @:

turret: struct = { cooldown: f32; timer: f32 @ "hidden"; }

The inspector skips anything tagged "hidden". The component decides what a tool shows; the tool doesn't need to know the component.

Step 4: an entity, and the layout

kayan_inspect walks the entity's signature and prints each component with kayan_print_fields. kayan_print_layout walks every table and prints each column's row size and bytes used out of bytes allocated, which shows where memory goes.

Run it

0:1 {position turret}
    position
        at:
            x: 0.00
            y: 0.00
    turret
        cooldown: 0.50
...
2:1 {position velocity health burning}
...
    health
        points: 60.00
        max: 100.00
    burning
        per_second: 10.00
...
1:1 (dead)
table 1 {position velocity health}: 0 rows, room for 4
    position   8 bytes a row,    0 of   32 bytes in use
    velocity   8 bytes a row,    0 of   32 bytes in use
    health     8 bytes a row,    0 of   32 bytes in use

The turret's timer isn't printed. Table 1 is empty but keeps its capacity: drone 1:1 was its only remaining row after 2:1 caught fire and moved out, and then 1:1 was despawned. Tables never shrink in this course. A real engine might trim empty ones between levels.

Part 2 in one picture

handle 2:1 ──> slots[2] { generation 1, table 2, row 0 }
                                         │
table 2 {position velocity health burning}
  entities  [ 2:1 ]
  position  [ (30, -5) ]     velocity [ (-1, 0) ]     health [ 60/100 ]     burning [ 10 ]
  add_edges / remove_edges ──> neighbouring tables in the archetype graph

The storage half of the ECS is done: identity (Part 1), and any component, in any combination, changing at run time (Part 2). Part 3 is the behaviour: queries to find tables, and systems to run over them.

And here's how it stayed safe. Everything lives in level and ends with it, so nothing can be freed early. Things that may be missing are options, so nothing reads a null. Tables never move, so a table pointer is always good. A column can move, but its old block stays in the region, so a stale pointer is a wrong answer and never a bad address, and handles are the cure for wrong answers. In kayan, the only code the checker takes on trust is the three unsafe { } blocks where bytes meet types, and those check what they're handed instead of believing it.

Try

  1. Add a field to health and run it. Nothing in the inspector changes.
  2. Tag health.max as hidden.
  3. Write kayan_set_f32_by_name(w, e, "health", "points", 10.0) with the reflect records: find the component by name, the field by name, check it's an f32, write it. That's the core of an editor or a console. The search is all checked code. The last step, putting an f32 into bytes, is kayan_print_builtin in reverse, so give it a small unsafe { } of its own: test the slice's length first, then memcpy from a local.

>= w*.slots*.length) {350        return false;351    }352    return vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots, cast(e.index, u64))*.generation == e.generation;353}354 355// A new entity with the components in `signature`, all zeroed, in the table356// for that signature.357kayan_spawn: proc(r: region level, w: *kayan_world in level, signature: u64) -> kayan_entity = {358    e: kayan_entity = {};359    if Build an ECS · part 3, systems · 3.1

Queries

ecs/src/3.systems/3.1.queries/queries.rin

In the dojo: 6. bitsets, 12. a watermark, each on its own, to watch and to practise.

Part 2 finished the storage. Everything from here on is behaviour, and in an ECS behaviour lives in systems: code that runs over every entity with some set of components. "Every entity with a position and a velocity" isn't in one place. It's spread over every table whose signature has both bits. So a system's first job is finding those tables, and the thing that finds them is a query:

all {position velocity}, none {}   ->   tables 1, 2, 3

A query matches tables, not entities. A game has a handful of tables and rarely makes new ones, so the matching is done once and kept. Each frame, a system walks the kept list, and inside each table streams the columns.

First: the storage, ready for systems

Part 3 is about to call kayan from deep inside a frame, and that changes a few things about the storage. Open this chapter's file beside 2.7's and you'll see them, so here they are. The design is the same. What moved is who holds what.

The world remembers its region. In Part 2, every proc that could allocate took r: region level, and that was fine with main at the top of every call. A system won't have level to hand, so the world keeps it, the way a vec keeps its own:

kayan_heap: struct = {
    arena: ^memops_arena;
}

kayan_spawn(w, signature) no longer takes a region. kayan_heap_make sets this up once, inside kayan_world_make, and nothing above the byte core hands an arena around.

Procs that only read say so. kayan_alive, kayan_get, kayan_verify and the printers take *const kayan_world.

Column slices are checked, and the caller says how long it wants one. This is the proc every system lives on, and there's no unsafe in it:

kayan_slice: proc<T>(t: *const kayan_table) -> []T in level = {
    id: u32 = kayan_id_of<T>();
    c: option<*kayan_column in level> = t*.columns[id];
    if (!c) {
        printfmt("kayan: the table has no column for component {}\n", id);
        exit(1);
    }
    return kayan_column_slice<T>(c, t*.count);
}

The result is in level, because that's the truth about the memory. What a caller does with it is up to the local it goes in. Write ps: []position, with no region, and it's the kind of borrow 2.5 ended on: keep it across a call that may change the world it came from, and the checker refuses.

type error: 'keep' may be stale: 'w', which it was taken from, has been changed since; take it again

Nothing in the core believes the table. 2.2's rule matters more here, because now there's a lot of code above the core. rin has no private fields, so any proc holding a table can write t*.count, and kayan_slice passes that field straight down. It's safe anyway. The view measures count against the column's slice, and stops the program if it doesn't fit. A row's bytes are the same story:

kayan_column_bytes: proc(c: *kayan_column, row: u64) -> []u8 in level = {
    return c*.data[row * c*.size..(row + 1) * c*.size];
}

That needs no unsafe, and it doesn't ask its caller to keep the row in range. data is a slice, so a wrong row, or a wrong size, is a bounds failure wherever it came from. Every proc above it, however it got its numbers, inherits that. This is the design: checked code can have every kind of bug, and the worst it can do to a column is stop the program or get a wrong number.

**The unsafe { } blocks are six**, each a few lines with an honest signature, and every other proc in the file is checked:

  • kayan_heap_make: keeping the region's arena where the core can reach it;
  • kayan_column_make, kayan_table_new: a column and a table allocated from that arena;
  • kayan_column_grow, kayan_column_slice: 2.2's core;
  • kayan_print_builtin: 2.7's bytes read as a value.

One thing in these blocks is still a field believed on its word: the heap's arena pointer has no bound for anyone to check. rin seals a struct holding a raw pointer to the file that declares it, so nothing importing this file can write that field. Inside the file it's on the author: only kayan_heap_make writes it. That's the same line Rust draws at a module, and it's what unsafe code owes.

Tables are still allocated one by one and never move. A column still does, and 3.3 is about that.

Step 1: the query

kayan_query: struct = {
    all: u64;
    none: u64;
    tables: *vec<u32> in level;
    checked: u64;
}
  • all: a table must have every one of these components.
  • none: and none of these. "Drones that aren't burning" is all {health}, none {burning}.
  • tables: the matching tables, by index. An index is what a slot holds too: plain data, a few bytes, with no region to name. kayan_query_table turns one into a pointer when a walk needs it.
  • checked: how many of the world's tables the query has looked at.

The list of tables lives in the world's region, so a query is told which region it's made in. Making one costs nothing: it matches when first updated.

kayan_query_init: proc(r: region level, all: u64, none: u64) -> kayan_query = {
    return { .all = all, .none = none, .tables = vec<u32>make(r, 4) };
}

Matching is two ANDs on the signature:

kayan_matches: proc(signature: u64, all: u64, none: u64) -> b32 = {
    return (signature & all) == all && (signature & none) == 0;
}

Step 2: keeping it up to date

Tables are only ever added, always at the end of w.tables, and never removed. So a query that has checked the first checked tables only needs to look at the ones after that:

kayan_query_update: proc(w: *const kayan_world, q: *kayan_query) -> void = {
    for (ti: u64 = q*.checked; ti < w*.tables*.length; ti += 1) {
        if (kayan_matches(kayan_table_at(w, cast(ti, u32))*.signature, q*.all, q*.none)) {
            _ = vec<u32>push(q*.tables, cast(ti, u32));
        }
    }
    q*.checked = w*.tables*.length;
}

The first update checks every table. After that, a frame with no new tables costs one comparison. A new table is checked once, by each query, the next time each is updated. flecs does the same thing in reverse: when a table is made, it tells the queries.

Step 3: walking a query

This is the shape of every system:

        kayan_query_update(w, movers&);
        for (i: u64 = 0; i < movers.tables*.length; i += 1) {
            t: *kayan_table in level = kayan_query_table(w, movers&, i);
            ps: []position = kayan_slice<position>(t);
            vs: []velocity = kayan_slice<velocity>(t);
            for (row: u64 = 0; row < t*.count; row += 1) {
                ps[row].at.x += vs[row].per_second.x * 0.5;
                ps[row].at.y += vs[row].per_second.y * 0.5;
            }
        }

Two loops. The outer one is over tables, a few iterations. The inner one is over rows: two dense arrays, read and written in order. That's lesson 1's move_soa. The query's job is to hand you the arrays; what you do with them is the same data-oriented loop as always.

The drones and the bullet are in different tables, and the loop doesn't care. The turret isn't matched (no velocity), and the loop never sees it, not even to skip it.

The pointers fit the loop. t names level and can be kept. ps and vs are borrows, taken fresh for each table and gone at the end of its turn, which is exactly as long as a slice into a column should live.

Run it

movers: all {position velocity}, none {}; tables: 2, entities: 4
    table 1 {position velocity health}: 1:1 2:1 3:1
    table 2 {position velocity damage lifetime}: 4:1
targets: all {position health}, none {burning}; tables: 1, entities: 3
    table 1 {position velocity health}: 1:1 2:1 3:1
on_fire: all {health burning}, none {}; tables: 0, entities: 0

Then drone 2:1 catches fire, which makes table 3, after the queries were made:

2:1 catches fire, and the world makes table 3 for it
the queries have checked 3 tables; updating them checks the new one only
movers: all {position velocity}, none {}; tables: 3, entities: 4
    table 1 {position velocity health}: 1:1 3:1
    table 2 {position velocity damage lifetime}: 4:1
    table 3 {position velocity health burning}: 2:1
targets: all {position health}, none {burning}; tables: 1, entities: 2
    table 1 {position velocity health}: 1:1 3:1
on_fire: all {health burning}, none {}; tables: 1, entities: 1
    table 3 {position velocity health burning}: 2:1

movers picked up the new table, targets refused it (none {burning}), and on_fire got its first. Nobody re-scanned the old tables.

Last, the bullet is despawned. Its table is now empty, and stays in movers. Walking an empty table costs one look at count.

Why this is fast

A query's cost doesn't depend on how many entities there are. It depends on how many tables match, and that number is small and stable. 10,000 drones in one table is one table to visit. That's the payoff of grouping entities by signature back in 2.4: the "which entities have X and Y?" question gets answered per table, once, instead of per entity, every frame.

The flip side is archetype fragmentation (2.4's Try): if every entity had a unique signature, every query would match thousands of one-row tables.

Try

  1. Write a query for "everything with a position that isn't a turret" and print it.
  2. Make 100 drones and walk movers. How many times does the outer loop run?
  3. Add any: u64 to the query: at least one of these components. Where in kayan_matches does it go?
  4. After the walk, keep a []position from kayan_slice, call spawn_drone, and write through the slice. Read the error. Then write the local's type as []position in level and compile again. What did you just promise, and what did you give up?
  5. Write kayan_table_at(w, 1)*.count = 100000; and then take a kayan_slice of that table. rin check has no objection, since count is only a field. Run it. What stops the program, and what did it measure count against?

Components both tables have are481// copied, byte for byte; components only the new table has start zeroed;482// components only the old table has are dropped with its old row.483kayan_move: proc(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity, to_index: u32) -> void = {484    slot: *kayan_slot = vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots, cast(e.index, u64));485    from_index: u32 = slot*.table;486    if (from_index == to_index) {487        return;488    }489    from_row: u64 = cast(slot*.row, u64);490    from: *kayan_table in level = kayan_table_at(w, from_index);491    to: *kayan_table in level = kayan_table_at(w, to_index);492    to_row: u64 = kayan_table_add_row(w, to, e);493    for (id: u32 = 0; id < w*.component_count; id += 1) {494        fc: option<*kayan_column in level> = from*.columns[id];495        tc: option<*kayan_column in level> = to*.columns[id];496        if (fc && tc) {497            dst: []u8 = kayan_column_bytes(tc, to_row);498            src: []u8 = kayan_column_bytes(fc, from_row);499            for (i: u64 = 0; i < dst.length; i += 1) {500                dst[i] = src[i];501            }502        }503    }504    kayan_table_remove_row(w, from, from_row);505    slot = vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots, cast(e.index, u64));506    slot*.table = to_index;507    slot*.row = cast(to_row, u32);508}509 510// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------511// The byte layer, for tools512// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------513 514// e's component `id` as its bytes: an empty slice if e is dead or has no such515// component. The typed layer is for game code, which knows its types; this is516// for tools that work from reflect records instead.517kayan_get_bytes: proc(w: *const kayan_world, e: kayan_entity, id: u32) -> []u8 in level = {518    none: []u8 in level = {};519    if (!kayan_alive(w, e) || id >= w*.component_count) {520        return none;521    }522    slot: *kayan_slot = vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots, cast(e.index, u64));523    table: u32 = slot*.table;524    row: u32 = slot*.row;525    t: *kayan_table in level = kayan_table_at(w, table);526    c: option<*kayan_column in level> = t*.columns[id];527    if (!c) {528        return none;529    }530    return kayan_column_bytes(c, cast(row, u64));531}532 533// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------534// The typed layer535// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------536 537// e's T, or null if e is dead or has no T. Handle, slot, table, row, typed538// view: the same path as 1.4's get_position, for any component. `option<*T>` says the539// null is possible, so the caller tests before it reads. The pointer is good540// until the next structural change, so use it now and keep the handle.541kayan_get: proc<T>(w: *const kayan_world, e: kayan_entity) -> option<*T in level> = {542    if (!kayan_alive(w, e)) {543        return null;544    }545    slot: *kayan_slot = vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots, cast(e.index, u64));546    table: u32 = slot*.table;547    row: u32 = slot*.row;548    t: *kayan_table in level = kayan_table_at(w, table);549    if (!kayan_table_has(t, kayan_id_of<T>())) {550        return null;551    }552    rows: []T in level = kayan_slice<T>(t);553    return rows[cast(row, u64)]&;554}555 556kayan_has: proc<T>(w: *const kayan_world, e: kayan_entity) -> b32 = {557    return (kayan_signature(w, e) & kayan_mask_of<T>()) != 0;558}559 560// Write e's T. It must already have one: giving an entity a component it does561// not have changes its table, which is 2.6.562kayan_set: proc<T>(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity, value: T) -> kayan_status = {563    if (!kayan_alive(w, e)) {564        return kayan_status.dead;565    }566    p: option<*T> = kayan_get<T>(w, e);567    if (!p) {568        return kayan_status.missing;569    }570    p* = value;571    return kayan_status.ok;572}573 574// Give e a T. If it already has one, this is kayan_set; if not, it moves to575// the table with T and then sets it.576kayan_add: proc<T>(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity, value: T) -> kayan_status = {577    if (!kayan_alive(w, e)) {578        return kayan_status.dead;579    }580    if (!kayan_has<T>(w, e)) {581        from: u32 = vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots, cast(e.index, u64))*.table;582        kayan_move(w, e, kayan_table_with(w, from, kayan_id_of<T>()));583    }584    return kayan_set<T>(w, e, value);585}586 587// Take e's T away, moving it to the table without T.588kayan_remove: proc<T>(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity) -> kayan_status = {589    if (!kayan_alive(w, e)) {590        return kayan_status.dead;591    }592    if (!kayan_has<T>(w, e)) {593        return kayan_status.missing;594    }595    from: u32 = vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots, cast(e.index, u64))*.table;596    kayan_move(w, e, kayan_table_without(w, from, kayan_id_of<T>()));597    return kayan_status.ok;598}599 600// The invariant, over every table: each row belongs to a live entity whose601// slot points back at that table and row, and the rows of all tables add up to602// the live count.603kayan_verify: proc(w: *const kayan_world) -> u64 = {604    problems: u64 = 0;605    rows: u64 = 0;606    for (ti: u64 = 0; ti < w*.tables*.length; ti += 1) {607        t: *kayan_table in level = kayan_table_at(w, cast(ti, u32));608        for (row: u64 = 0; row < t*.count; row += 1) {609            // Taken row by row: kayan_alive takes the world, and the checker610            // does not know that it leaves the rows where they are.611            es: []kayan_entity = kayan_entities(t);612            e: kayan_entity = es[row];613            if (!kayan_alive(w, e)) {614                printfmt("kayan_verify: table {} row {} holds dead entity {}:{}\n", ti, row, e.index, e.generation);615                problems += 1;616                continue;617            }618            slot: *kayan_slot = vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots, cast(e.index, u64));619            if (cast(slot*.table, u64) != ti || cast(slot*.row, u64) != row) {620                printfmt("kayan_verify: {}:{} is in table {} row {}, its slot says table {} row {}\n",621                    e.index, e.generation, ti, row, slot*.table, slot*.row);622                problems += 1;623            }624        }625        rows += t*.count;626    }627    if (rows != w*.live) {628        printfmt("kayan_verify: {} rows in tables, {} live entities\n", rows, w*.live);629        problems += 1;630    }631    return problems;632}633 634kayan_print_signature: proc(w: *const kayan_world, signature: u64) -> void = {635    printfmt("{");636    first: b32 = true;637    for (id: u32 = 0; ti < cast(w*.tables*.length, u32); ti += 1) {664        kayan_print_table(w, ti);665    }666}667 668// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------669// The inspector: reflect records, no component types670// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------671 672kayan_indent: proc(depth: u32) -> void = {673    for (i: u32 = 0; i < depth; i += 1) {674        printfmt("    ");675    }676}677 678// One value of a builtin type, read from its bytes by its type's name. The679// bytes may sit at any address, so the read is a copy into a local: this is the680// inspector's one unsafe block.681kayan_print_builtin: proc(type_name: ^const char, at: []const u8) -> void = {682    if (at.length < 4) {683        printfmt("<{} bytes>", at.length);684        return;685    }686    unsafe {687        if (reflect_cstr_equal(type_name, "f32")) {688            f: f32 = 0.0;689            memcpy(f&, at.data, 4);690            printfmt("{:.2}", cast(f, f64));691        } else if (reflect_cstr_equal(type_name, "u32")) {692            u: u32 = 0;693            memcpy(u&, at.data, 4);694            printfmt("{}", u);695        } else if (reflect_cstr_equal(type_name, "i32")) {696            i: i32 = 0;697            memcpy(i&, at.data, 4);698            printfmt("{}", i);699        } else {700            printfmt("<{}>", type_name);701        }702    }703}704 705// Every field of a struct whose bytes are `base`, nested structs indented706// under their field. A field's bytes are cut from `base` by its offset and707// size, both from the reflect record.708kayan_print_fields: proc(type: *const reflect, base: []const u8, depth: u32) -> void = {709    for (i: u64 = 0; i < type*.count; i += 1) {710        f: option<*const reflect_field> = reflect_field_at(type, i);711        if (!f) {712            continue;713        }714        if (reflect_field_has_attr(f, "hidden")) {715            continue;716        }717        at: []const u8 = base[f*.offset..f*.offset + f*.size];718        kayan_indent(depth);719        printfmt("{}:", f*.name);720        info: option<*const reflect> = reflect_field_info(f);721        if (info && info*.kind == reflect_kind_struct) {722            printfmt("\n");723            kayan_print_fields(info, at, depth + 1);724        } else {725            printfmt(" ");726            kayan_print_builtin(f*.type, at);727            printfmt("\n");728        }729    }730}731 732kayan_inspect: proc(w: *const kayan_world, e: kayan_entity) -> void = {733    if (!kayan_alive(w, e)) {734        printfmt("{}:{} (dead)\n", e.index, e.generation);735        return;736    }737    printfmt("{}:{} ", e.index, e.generation);738    signature: u64 = kayan_signature(w, e);739    kayan_print_signature(w, signature);740    printfmt("\n");741    for (id: u32 = 0; id < w*.component_count; id += 1) {742        if ((signature & kayan_bit(id)) != 0) {743            info: *const reflect in permanent = kayan_info(w, id);744            printfmt("    {}\n", info*.name);745            bytes: []u8 = kayan_get_bytes(w, e, id);746            kayan_print_fields(info, bytes, 2);747        }748    }749}750 751// Every table: rows in use out of room, and per column its row size and its752// bytes in use out of bytes allocated. i < q*.tables*.length; i += 1) {867        t: *kayan_table in level = kayan_query_table(w, q, i);868        ps: []position = kayan_slice<position>(t);869        es: []kayan_entity = kayan_entities(t);870        for (row: u64 = 0; row < t*.count; row += 1) {871            e: kayan_entity = es[row];872            p: position = ps[row];873            printfmt("    {}:{} at ({:5.2}, {:5.2})\n", e.index, e.generation, cast(p.at.x, f64), cast(p.at.y, f64));874        }875    }876}877 878main: proc() -> i32 = {879    level: region = {880        w: *kayan_world in level = kayan_world_make(level);881        kayan_register(w, kayan_id_of<position>(), position<>&);882        kayan_register(w, kayan_id_of<velocity>(), velocity<>&);883        kayan_register(w, kayan_id_of<health>(), health<>&);884        kayan_register(w, kayan_id_of<damage>(), damage<>&);885        kayan_register(w, kayan_id_of<lifetime>(), lifetime<>&);886        kayan_register(w, kayan_id_of<turret>(), turret<>&);887        kayan_register(w, kayan_id_of<burning>(), burning<>&);888 889        _ = spawn_turret(w, 0.0, 0.0);890        _ = spawn_drone(w, 20.0, 5.0);891        b: kayan_entity = spawn_drone(w, 30.0, -5.0);892        _ = spawn_drone(w, 40.0, 0.0);893        shot: kayan_entity = spawn_bullet(w, 1.0, 0.0);894        printfmt("{} entities in {} tables:\n", w*.live, w*.tables*.length);895        kayan_print_tables(w);896 897        // Three queries. Build an ECS · part 3, systems · 3.2

Systems

ecs/src/3.systems/3.2.systems/systems.rin

In the dojo: 13. a dispatch table, on its own, to watch and to practise.

3.1's movement loop had the shape of every system: bring a query up to date, then for each of its tables take the columns as slices and loop over the rows. This chapter names that shape and splits it in two:

  • the kernel: a plain loop over plain slices. It knows nothing about tables, entities or worlds. This is lessons 1 to 7: noalias, streaming, vectorization.
  • the system: a query, plus a small proc kayan calls on each table the query matches. It takes the table's columns and calls the kernel.

A frame runs the systems in order, each over all of its tables. The order is the schedule, and it's written down once, as data.

Step 1: the kernels

integrate: proc[unsafe](ps: noalias []position, vs: []const velocity, dt: f32) -> void = {
    for (i: u64 = 0; i < ps.length; i += 1) {
        ps[i].at.x += vs[i].per_second.x * dt;
        ps[i].at.y += vs[i].per_second.y * dt;
    }
}

That's the whole thing, and it's the code you'd want to write if there were no ECS at all. Kernels are where you profile, read assembly and reach for SIMD (the lessons). Everything else in this course exists to hand them the right slices. burn and age look the same.

Why proc[unsafe], on a loop this innocent? Because of one word. noalias tells the C optimiser these slices don't overlap, and that's a promise the checker has no way to keep. It wants you to mark that plainly:

type error: noalias is a promise to the C optimiser that the checker cannot keep: it belongs on a 'proc[unsafe]'

The body is as ordinary as it looks, bounds checks included, and overlap is still tested on the way in unless you turn the checks off. All that [unsafe] means here is that the performance promise is yours to keep.

Step 2: what a system gets

kayan_iter: struct = {
    world: *kayan_world in level;
    table: *kayan_table in level;
    dt: f32;
}

kayan_system_proc: alias = *proc(it: *kayan_iter) -> void;

One struct instead of three parameters. It's the same idea as flecs' ecs_iter_t, and it has two practical reasons. Adding to it later (3.3 adds two fields) changes no system's signature. And a system that uses only the table still uses its one parameter. rin compiles to C with -Wextra -Werror, and an unused parameter is an error there. Both pointers name their region, so the struct can be made anywhere level is open.

The system itself is the adapter:

move_system: proc(it: *kayan_iter) -> void = {
    unsafe { integrate(kayan_slice<position>(it*.table), kayan_slice<velocity>(it*.table), it*.dt); }
}

Columns out, kernel in. No loop here: the kernel has it.

This is where you keep the kernel's promise, so it's where the unsafe { } goes. It's easy to keep: a position column and a velocity column are different allocations, so they can't overlap. It's the only line in the system, and it says what you're vouching for.

Step 3: a system is data

A system is a name, a proc, a query, and the counts of the work it's done. Only the first two never change, and that turns out to be the seam the checker needs, so a system comes in two halves.

The code:

kayan_system: struct = {
    name: ^const char;
    run: kayan_system_proc;
}

kayan_system_make: proc(r: region level, name: ^const char, run: kayan_system_proc) -> *kayan_system in level = {
    unsafe {
        s: *kayan_system in level = cast(memops_arena_push_zero(r, sizeof(kayan_system), alignof(kayan_system)), *kayan_system in level);
        s*.name = name;
        s*.run = run;
        return s;
    }
}

A C string and a proc pointer are both pointers without a region, so the checker can't place them. It won't let new make a struct holding them, and it says what it wants instead:

type error: a value made by new holds 'kayan_system' by value, and it carries a pointer whose region the checker cannot see; safe code keeps such a value through a pointer into a region, '*kayan_system in R', made by a proc of its own; if a field of it is stored from two regions, write its region on the field

So a small trusted proc makes it, once, and everyone else holds a pointer. Nothing is lost, because nothing here changes either field after that.

The data:

kayan_scheduled: struct = {
    system: *kayan_system in level;
    query: kayan_query;
    tables: u64;
    rows: u64;
}

Everything that changes as the frames go is here, as plain checked data. tables and rows count the work, for the output. The schedule is a list of these:

        systems: *vec<*kayan_scheduled in level> in level = vec<*kayan_scheduled in level>make(level, 3);
        kayan_schedule_add(level, systems, "burn", kayan_mask_of<health>() | kayan_mask_of<burning>(), 0, burn_system);
        kayan_schedule_add(level, systems, "age", kayan_mask_of<lifetime>(), 0, age_system);
        kayan_schedule_add(level, systems, "move", kayan_mask_of<position>() | kayan_mask_of<velocity>(), 0, move_system);

It's a vec of pointers for the same reason as w.tables in 2.4. Each entry is its own allocation, so a pointer to one is a pointer into level, which never goes stale.

Step 4: a frame

kayan_progress: proc(w: *kayan_world in level, systems: *const vec<*kayan_scheduled in level>, dt: f32) -> void = {
    for (s: u64 = 0; s < systems*.length; s += 1) {
        sys: *kayan_scheduled in level = kayan_scheduled_at(systems, s);
        kayan_query_update(w, sys*.query&);
        for (i: u64 = 0; i < sys*.query.tables*.length; i += 1) {
            it: kayan_iter = { .world = w, .table = kayan_query_table(w, sys*.query&, i), .dt = dt };
            if (it.table*.count > 0) {
                sys*.tables += 1;
                sys*.rows += it.table*.count;
                sys*.system*.run(it&);
            }
        }
    }
}

kayan_progress is flecs' name for the same thing. For each system in order, for each of its tables, one call. The game loop becomes:

        for (frame: u32 = 1; frame <= 8; frame += 1) {
            kayan_progress(w, systems, dt);

Order is data flow

Systems run one after another, never interleaved, and each sees everything the earlier ones wrote this frame. So the order is a statement about data: a system that reads what another writes runs after it. Move before collide means bullets hit where they are now, not where they were. Damage before death means a drone dies in the frame its health hits zero, not the next. 3.4's schedule has nine systems, and each position in it is one of these decisions.

Bigger engines go further. Each system declares what it reads and writes, and the scheduler uses that to run systems that don't conflict at the same time, on other threads. Underneath, the order is still a list like this one.

Run it

the schedule, run in this order every frame:
burn: all {health burning}, none {}; tables: 1, entities: 1
    table 2 {position velocity health burning}: 2:1
age: all {lifetime}, none {}; tables: 1, entities: 3
    table 3 {position velocity damage lifetime}: 4:1 5:1 6:1
move: all {position velocity}, none {}; tables: 3, entities: 6
    table 1 {position velocity health}: 1:1 3:1
    table 2 {position velocity health burning}: 2:1
    table 3 {position velocity damage lifetime}: 4:1 5:1 6:1
...
after frame 8, 2.00 seconds:
    0:1 at ( 0.00,  0.00)
    1:1 at (18.00,  4.00)  health 100
    3:1 at (26.00, -4.00)  health 100
    2:1 at (22.00,  0.00)  health 84, burning
    4:1 at (17.00,  0.00)  lifetime -1.50
    5:1 at (17.00,  4.00)  lifetime -1.00
    6:1 at (17.00, -4.00)  lifetime -0.50

8 frames, one call per table per frame:
    burn called  8 times, over  8 rows
    age  called  8 times, over 24 rows
    move called 24 times, over 48 rows
3 bullets are out of time and still in the world

move made 24 calls in 8 frames, three tables a frame, and each call is one tight loop. Call overhead is per table, never per entity.

And the last line is the cliffhanger. Each bullet's lifetime ran out, and nothing removed it, because a system in this chapter changes values, never structure. Despawning from inside a system looks like a one-line fix. It isn't, and 3.3 shows why.

Try

  1. Swap burn and move in the schedule. Does anything change? Now think of a pair where it would.
  2. Add a heal system for drones that aren't burning (all {health}, none {burning}).
  3. Build in Release and find integrate in the assembly. Is it vectorized? (Lesson 1 shows how to look.)
  4. Take noalias and [unsafe] off age, and the unsafe { } off its system. Now the whole system is checked. What did the optimiser lose? For a kernel with one slice, was there anything to lose?
