(edge != 0) {500        return edge - 1;501    }502    to: u32 = kayan_table_for(w, kayan_table_at(w, from)*.signature & ~kayan_bit(id));503    kayan_table_at(w, from)*.remove_edges[id] = to + 1;504    kayan_table_at(w, to)*.add_edges[id] = from + 1;505    return to;506}507 508// Move a live entity to table `to_index`. Components both tables have are509// copied, byte for byte; components only the new table has start zeroed;510// components only the old table has are dropped with its old row.511kayan_move: proc(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity, to_index: u32) -> void = {512    slot: *kayan_slot = vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots, cast(e.index, u64));513    from_index: u32 = slot*.table;514    if (from_index == to_index) {515        return;516    }517    from_row: u64 = cast(slot*.row, u64);518    from: *kayan_table in level = kayan_table_at(w, from_index);519    to: *kayan_table in level = kayan_table_at(w, to_index);520    to_row: u64 = kayan_table_add_row(w, to, e);521    for (id: u32 = 0; id < w*.component_count; id += 1) {522        fc: option<*kayan_column in level> = from*.columns[id];523        tc: option<*kayan_column in level> = to*.columns[id];524        if (fc && tc) {525            dst: []u8 = kayan_column_bytes(tc, to_row);526            src: []u8 = kayan_column_bytes(fc, from_row);527            for (i: u64 = 0; i < dst.length; i += 1) {528                dst[i] = src[i];529            }530        }531    }532    kayan_table_remove_row(w, from, from_row);533    slot = vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots, cast(e.index, u64));534    slot*.table = to_index;535    slot*.row = cast(to_row, u32);536}537 538// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------539// The byte layer, for tools and for commands540// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------541 542// Give e component `id`, with `value` for its bytes: 2.6's add, by id instead543// of by type, because a command holds its value as bytes. The copy is a loop544// over two slices the checker has sized.545kayan_add_id: proc(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity, id: u32, value: []const u8) -> kayan_status = {546    if (!kayan_alive(w, e)) {547        return kayan_status.dead;548    }549    from: u32 = vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots, cast(e.index, u64))*.table;550    if (!kayan_table_has(kayan_table_at(w, from), id)) {551        kayan_move(w, e, kayan_table_with(w, from, id));552    }553    bytes: []u8 = kayan_get_bytes(w, e, id);554    if (value.length != bytes.length) {555        printfmt("kayan: a {}-byte value for a component of {} bytes\n", value.length, bytes.length);556        exit(1);557    }558    for (i: u64 = 0; i < bytes.length; i += 1) {559        bytes[i] = value[i];560    }561    return kayan_status.ok;562}563 564kayan_remove_id: proc(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity, id: u32) -> kayan_status = {565    if (!kayan_alive(w, e)) {566        return kayan_status.dead;567    }568    from: u32 = vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots, cast(e.index, u64))*.table;569    if (!kayan_table_has(kayan_table_at(w, from), id)) {570        return kayan_status.missing;571    }572    kayan_move(w, e, kayan_table_without(w, from, id));573    return kayan_status.ok;574}575 576// e's component `id` as its bytes: an empty slice if e is dead or has no such577// component. The typed layer is for game code, which knows its types; this is578// for tools that work from reflect records instead.579kayan_get_bytes: proc(w: *const kayan_world, e: kayan_entity, id: u32) -> []u8 in level = {580    none: []u8 in level = {};581    if (!kayan_alive(w, e) || id >= w*.component_count) {582        return none;583    }584    slot: *kayan_slot = vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots, cast(e.index, u64));585    table: u32 = slot*.table;586    row: u32 = slot*.row;587    t: *kayan_table in level = kayan_table_at(w, table);588    c: option<*kayan_column in level> = t*.columns[id];589    if (!c) {590        return none;591    }592    return kayan_column_bytes(c, cast(row, u64));593}594 595// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------596// The typed layer597// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------598 599// e's T, or null if e is dead or has no T. Handle, slot, table, row, typed600// view: the same path as 1.4's get_position, for any component. `option<*T>` says the601// null is possible, so the caller tests before it reads. The pointer is good602// until the next structural change, so use it now and keep the handle.603kayan_get: proc<T>(w: *const kayan_world, e: kayan_entity) -> option<*T in level> = {604    if (!kayan_alive(w, e)) {605        return null;606    }607    slot: *kayan_slot = vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots, cast(e.index, u64));608    table: u32 = slot*.table;609    row: u32 = slot*.row;610    t: *kayan_table in level = kayan_table_at(w, table);611    if (!kayan_table_has(t, kayan_id_of<T>())) {612        return null;613    }614    rows: []T in level = kayan_slice<T>(t);615    return rows[cast(row, u64)]&;616}617 618kayan_has: proc<T>(w: *const kayan_world, e: kayan_entity) -> b32 = {619    return (kayan_signature(w, e) & kayan_mask_of<T>()) != 0;620}621 622// Write e's T. It must already have one: giving an entity a component it does623// not have changes its table, which is 2.6.624kayan_set: proc<T>(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity, value: T) -> kayan_status = {625    if (!kayan_alive(w, e)) {626        return kayan_status.dead;627    }628    p: option<*T> = kayan_get<T>(w, e);629    if (!p) {630        return kayan_status.missing;631    }632    p* = value;633    return kayan_status.ok;634}635 636// Give e a T. If it already has one, this is kayan_set; if not, it moves to637// the table with T and then sets it.638kayan_add: proc<T>(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity, value: T) -> kayan_status = {639    if (!kayan_alive(w, e)) {640        return kayan_status.dead;641    }642    if (!kayan_has<T>(w, e)) {643        from: u32 = vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots, cast(e.index, u64))*.table;644        kayan_move(w, e, kayan_table_with(w, from, kayan_id_of<T>()));645    }646    return kayan_set<T>(w, e, value);647}648 649// Take e's T away: the byte proc, with the type turned into an id.650kayan_remove: proc<T>(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity) -> kayan_status = {651    return kayan_remove_id(w, e, kayan_id_of<T>());652}653 654// The invariant, over every table: each row belongs to a live entity whose655// slot points back at that table and row, and the rows of all tables add up to656// the live count.657kayan_verify: proc(w: *const kayan_world) -> u64 = {658    problems: u64 = 0;659    rows: u64 = 0;660    for (ti: u64 = 0; ti < w*.tables*.length; ti += 1) {661        t: *kayan_table in level = kayan_table_at(w, cast(ti, u32));662        for (row: u64 = 0; row < t*.count; row += 1) {663            // Taken row by row: kayan_alive takes the world, and the checker664            // does not know that it leaves the rows where they are.665            es: []kayan_entity = kayan_entities(t);666            e: kayan_entity = es[row];667            if (!kayan_alive(w, e)) {668                printfmt("kayan_verify: table {} row {} holds dead entity {}:{}\n", ti, row, e.index, e.generation);669                problems += 1;670                continue;671            }672            slot: *kayan_slot = vec<kayan_slot>at(w*.slots, cast(e.index, u64));673            if (cast(slot*.table, u64) != ti || cast(slot*.row, u64) != row) {674                printfmt("kayan_verify: {}:{} is in table {} row {}, its slot says table {} row {}\n",675                    e.index, e.generation, ti, row, slot*.table, slot*.row);676                problems += 1;677            }678        }679        rows += t*.count;680    }681    if (rows != w*.live) {682        printfmt("kayan_verify: {} rows in tables, {} live entities\n", rows, w*.live);683        problems += 1;684    }685    return problems;686}687 688kayan_print_signature: proc(w: *const kayan_world, signature: u64) -> void = {689    printfmt("{");690    first: b32 = true;691    for (id: u32 = 0; id < w*.component_count; id += 1) {692        if ((signature & kayan_bit(id)) != 0) {693            if (!first) {694                printfmt(" ");695            }696            printfmt("{}", kayan_info(w, id)*.name);697            first = false;698        }699    }700    printfmt("}");701}702 703kayan_print_table: proc(w: *const kayan_world, ti: u32) -> void = {704    t: *kayan_table in level = kayan_table_at(w, ti);705    printfmt("    table {} ", ti);706    kayan_print_signature(w, t*.signature);707    printfmt(":");708    es: []kayan_entity = kayan_entities(t);709    for (row: u64 = 0; row < es.length; row += 1) {710        e: kayan_entity = es[row];711        printfmt(" {}:{}", e.index, e.generation);712    }713    printfmt("\n");714}715 716kayan_print_tables: proc(w: *const kayan_world) -> void = {717    for (ti: u32 = 0; ti < cast(w*.tables*.length, u32); ti += 1) {718        kayan_print_table(w, ti);719    }720}721 722// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------723// The inspector: reflect records, no component types724// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------725 726kayan_indent: proc(depth: u32) -> void = {727    for (i: u32 = 0; i < depth; i += 1) {728        printfmt("    ");729    }730}731 732// One value of a builtin type, read from its bytes by its type's name. The733// bytes may sit at any address, so the read is a copy into a local: this is the734// inspector's one unsafe block.735kayan_print_builtin: proc(type_name: ^const char, at: []const u8) -> void = {736    if (at.length < 4) {737        printfmt("<{} bytes>", at.length);738        return;739    }740    unsafe {741        if (reflect_cstr_equal(type_name, "f32")) {742            f: f32 = 0.0;743            memcpy(f&, at.data, 4);744            printfmt("{:.2}", cast(f, f64));745        } else if (reflect_cstr_equal(type_name, "u32")) {746            u: u32 = 0;747            memcpy(u&, at.data, 4);748            printfmt("{}", u);749        } else if (reflect_cstr_equal(type_name, "i32")) {750            i: i32 = 0;751            memcpy(i&, at.data, 4);752            printfmt("{}", i);753        } else {754            printfmt("<{}>", type_name);755        }756    }757}758 759// Every field of a struct whose bytes are `base`, nested structs indented760// under their field. A field's bytes are cut from `base` by its offset and761// size, both from the reflect record.762kayan_print_fields: proc(type: *const reflect, base: []const u8, depth: u32) -> void = {763    for (i: u64 = 0; i < type*.count; i += 1) {764        f: option<*const reflect_field> = reflect_field_at(type, i);765        if (!f) {766            continue;767        }768        if (reflect_field_has_attr(f, "hidden")) {769            continue;770        }771        at: []const u8 = base[f*.offset..f*.offset + f*.size];772        kayan_indent(depth);773        printfmt("{}:", f*.name);774        info: option<*const reflect> = reflect_field_info(f);775        if (info && info*.kind == reflect_kind_struct) {776            printfmt("\n");777            kayan_print_fields(info, at, depth + 1);778        } else {779            printfmt(" ");780            kayan_print_builtin(f*.type, at);781            printfmt("\n");782        }783    }784}785 786kayan_inspect: proc(w: *const kayan_world, e: kayan_entity) -> void = {787    if (!kayan_alive(w, e)) {788        printfmt("{}:{} (dead)\n", e.index, e.generation);789        return;790    }791    printfmt("{}:{} ", e.index, e.generation);792    signature: u64 = kayan_signature(w, e);793    kayan_print_signature(w, signature);794    printfmt("\n");795    for (id: u32 = 0; id < w*.component_count; id += 1) {796        if ((signature & kayan_bit(id)) != 0) {797            info: *const reflect in permanent = kayan_info(w, id);798            printfmt("    {}\n", info*.name);799            bytes: []u8 = kayan_get_bytes(w, e, id);800            kayan_print_fields(info, bytes, 2);801        }802    }803}804 805// Every table: rows in use out of room, and per column its row size and its806// bytes in use out of bytes allocated. The memory a table holds and does not807// use is the cost of doubling on growth.808kayan_print_layout: proc(w: *const kayan_world) -> void = {809    for (ti: u32 = 0; ti < cast(w*.tables*.length, u32); ti += 1) {810        t: *kayan_table in level = kayan_table_at(w, ti);811        printfmt("table {} ", ti);812        kayan_print_signature(w, t*.signature);813        printfmt(": {} rows, room for {}\n", cast(t*.count, u32), cast(t*.capacity, u32));814        for (id: u32 = 0; id < w*.component_count; id += 1) {815            c: option<*kayan_column in level> = t*.columns[id];816            if (c) {817                size: u64 = c*.size;818                printfmt("    {:-9} {:2} bytes a row, {:4} of {:4} bytes in use\n", kayan_info(w, id)*.name, cast(size, u32),819                    cast(size * t*.count, u32), cast(size * t*.capacity, u32));820            }821        }822    }823}824 825// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------826// Queries827// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------828 829// The tables a system runs over: every table whose signature has all of `all`830// and none of `none`, kept by index. Tables are only ever added, at the end of831// w.tables, so the query remembers how many it has checked and, brought up to832// date, looks at the new ones only.833kayan_query: struct = {834    all: u64;835    none: u64;836    tables: *vec<u32> in level;837    checked: u64;838}839 840// The list of matched tables lives in the world's region, so a query says841// which region it is made in.842kayan_query_init: proc(r: region level, all: u64, none: u64) -> kayan_query = {843    return { .all = all, .none = none, .tables = vec<u32>make(r, 4) };844}845 846kayan_matches: proc(signature: u64, all: u64, none: u64) -> b32 = {847    return (signature & all) == all && (signature & none) == 0;848}849 850// Check the tables made since the query last looked. With none new, this is851// one comparison, so call it before every walk.852kayan_query_update: proc(w: *const kayan_world, q: *kayan_query) -> void = {853    for (ti: u64 = q*.checked; ti < w*.tables*.length; ti += 1) {854        if (kayan_matches(kayan_table_at(w, cast(ti, u32))*.signature, q*.all, q*.none)) {855            _ = vec<u32>push(q*.tables, cast(ti, u32));856        }857    }858    q*.checked = w*.tables*.length;859}860 861// The query's i-th table.862kayan_query_table: proc(w: *const kayan_world, q: *const kayan_query, i: u64) -> *kayan_table in level = {863    return kayan_table_at(w, vec<u32>at(q*.tables, i)*);864}865 866// How many entities the query matches: the rows of its tables.867kayan_query_count: proc(w: *const kayan_world, q: *kayan_query) -> u64 = {868    kayan_query_update(w, q);869    n: u64 = 0;870    for (i: u64 = 0; i < q*.tables*.length; i += 1) {871        n += kayan_query_table(w, q, i)*.count;872    }873    return n;874}875 876kayan_print_query: proc(w: *const kayan_world, name: ^const char, q: *kayan_query) -> void = {877    kayan_query_update(w, q);878    printfmt("{}: all ", name);879    kayan_print_signature(w, q*.all);880    printfmt(", none ");881    kayan_print_signature(w, q*.none);882    printfmt("; tables: {}, entities: {}\n", q*.tables*.length, kayan_query_count(w, q));883    for (i: u64 = 0; i < q*.tables*.length; i += 1) {884        kayan_print_table(w, vec<u32>at(q*.tables, i)*);885    }886}887 888// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------889// Systems890// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------891 892// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------893// Commands894// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------895 896// The frame's command buffer: the commands, and the frame arena their values897// are copied into. Made at the start of each frame, in the frame region, and898// gone with it.899kayan_commands: struct = {900    heap: *kayan_heap in frame;901    list: *vec<kayan_command> in frame;902}903 904kayan_commands_make: proc(r: region frame) -> *kayan_commands in frame = {905    return new<kayan_commands>(r, { .heap = kayan_heap_make(r), .list = vec<kayan_command>make(r, 16) });906}907 908// A spawn that has been recorded and not applied. There is no entity yet, so909// this is the spawn command's place in the list; give it components with910// kayan_pending_set.911kayan_pending: struct = {912    command: u32;913}914 915kayan_defer: proc(cmds: *kayan_commands, c: kayan_command) -> u32 = {916    index: u32 = cast(cmds*.list*.length, u32);917    _ = vec<kayan_command>push(cmds*.list, c);918    return index;919}920 921// A copy of `value`, as bytes, in the frame arena. The one trusted proc of922// the command buffer: a value's bytes are a cast.923kayan_defer_value: proc<T>(h: *kayan_heap in frame, value: T) -> []u8 in frame = {924    unsafe {925        data: ^u8 = cast(memops_arena_push(h*.arena[0]&, sizeof(T), alignof(T)), ^u8);926        memcpy(data, value&, sizeof(T));927        return cast(data[0..sizeof(T)], []u8 in frame);928    }929}930 931kayan_defer_spawn: proc(cmds: *kayan_commands, signature: u64) -> kayan_pending = {932    p: kayan_pending = {};933    p.command = kayan_defer(cmds, { .kind = kayan_command_kind.spawn, .signature = signature });934    return p;935}936 937kayan_pending_set: proc<T>(cmds: *kayan_commands, p: kayan_pending, value: T) -> void = {938    _ = kayan_defer(cmds, { .kind = kayan_command_kind.add, .spawn = p.command + 1, .id = kayan_id_of<T>(),939        .value = kayan_defer_value<T>(cmds*.heap, value) });940}941 942kayan_defer_despawn: proc(cmds: *kayan_commands, e: kayan_entity) -> void = {943    _ = kayan_defer(cmds, { .kind = kayan_command_kind.despawn, .entity = e });944}945 946kayan_defer_add: proc<T>(cmds: *kayan_commands, e: kayan_entity, value: T) -> void = {947    _ = kayan_defer(cmds, { .kind = kayan_command_kind.add, .entity = e, .id = kayan_id_of<T>(),948        .value = kayan_defer_value<T>(cmds*.heap, value) });949}950 951kayan_defer_remove: proc<T>(cmds: *kayan_commands, e: kayan_entity) -> void = {952    _ = kayan_defer(cmds, { .kind = kayan_command_kind.remove, .entity = e, .id = kayan_id_of<T>() });953}954 955// One applied command. The components given to a new entity are part of its956// spawn line, so they are not printed on their own.957kayan_print_command: proc(w: *const kayan_world, c: *const kayan_command, status: kayan_status) -> void = {958    if (c*.spawn != 0 && status == kayan_status.ok) {959        return;960    }961    printfmt("    {} ", c*.kind);962    if (c*.kind == kayan_command_kind.spawn) {963        kayan_print_signature(w, c*.signature);964        printfmt(" -> ");965    } else if (c*.kind != kayan_command_kind.despawn) {966        printfmt("{}, ", kayan_info(w, c*.id)*.name);967    }968    printfmt("{}:{}", c*.entity.index, c*.entity.generation);969    if (status != kayan_status.ok) {970        printfmt(": skipped, {}", status);971    }972    printfmt("\n");973}974 975// Apply the frame's commands in the order they were recorded. A command for976// an entity that died after it was recorded (despawned by an earlier command,977// most likely) does nothing, and is counted. Letting the commands go is the978// frame region's end, not a line here.979kayan_flush: proc(w: *kayan_world, cmds: *kayan_commands) -> void = {980    for (i: u64 = 0; i < cmds*.list*.length; i += 1) {981        c: *kayan_command = vec<kayan_command>at(cmds*.list, i);982        if (c*.spawn != 0) {983            c*.entity = vec<kayan_command>at(cmds*.list, cast(c*.spawn - 1, u64))*.entity;984        }985        status: kayan_status = kayan_status.ok;986        if (c*.kind == kayan_command_kind.spawn) {987            c*.entity = kayan_spawn(w, c*.signature);988        } else if (c*.kind == kayan_command_kind.despawn) {989            status = kayan_despawn(w, c*.entity);990        } else if (c*.kind == kayan_command_kind.add) {991            status = kayan_add_id(w, c*.entity, c*.id, c*.value);992        } else {993            status = kayan_remove_id(w, c*.entity, c*.id);994        }995        if (status == kayan_status.ok) {996            w*.applied += 1;997        } else {998            w*.skipped += 1;999        }1000        if (w*.trace) {1001            kayan_print_command(w, c, status);1002        }1003    }1004}1005 1006// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------1007// Systems1008// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------1009 1010// What a system gets for each table it runs on: the world, the table, the1011// frame's time step, the frame's command buffer, and `ctx`: whatever the1012// system needs beyond its own tables, here the game's state. It is a typed1013// pointer, not a `*void`: the checker has to know what it points at, and the1014// systems that use it test it. Every pointer names its region, so the struct1015// can be made wherever frame is open.1016kayan_iter: struct = {1017    world: *kayan_world in level;1018    table: *kayan_table in level;1019    dt: f32;1020    commands: *kayan_commands in frame;1021    ctx: option<*game in level>;1022}1023 1024kayan_system_proc: alias = *proc(it: *kayan_iter) -> void;1025 1026// A system is code: a name, and the proc run on each table its query matches.1027// A C string and a proc pointer are both pointers without a region, so a1028// struct holding them is a carrier: safe code reaches it only through a1029// pointer into a region, made by a trusted proc. Neither changes after it is1030// made, so nothing is lost.1031kayan_system: struct = {1032    name: ^const char;1033    run: kayan_system_proc;1034}1035 1036kayan_system_make: proc(r: region level, name: ^const char, run: kayan_system_proc) -> *kayan_system in level = {1037    unsafe {1038        s: *kayan_system in level = cast(memops_arena_push_zero(r, sizeof(kayan_system), alignof(kayan_system)), *kayan_system in level);1039        s*.name = name;1040        s*.run = run;1041        return s;1042    }1043}1044 1045// A system in the schedule: which system, the query that finds its tables,1046// and what it has run over so far. `tables` and `rows` count the calls.1047kayan_scheduled: struct = {1048    system: *kayan_system in level;1049    query: kayan_query;1050    ctx: option<*game in level>;1051    tables: u64;1052    rows: u64;1053}1054 1055// The schedule is a list of these, in the order the frame runs them. Each1056// entry is its own allocation so a pointer to one is a pointer into level,1057// which the checker never counts as stale.1058kayan_schedule_add: proc(r: region level, systems: *vec<*kayan_scheduled in level>, name: ^const char,1059                         all: u64, none: u64, run: kayan_system_proc, ctx: option<*game in level>) -> void = {1060    _ = vec<*kayan_scheduled in level>push(systems, new<kayan_scheduled>(r, {1061        .system = kayan_system_make(r, name, run),1062        .query = kayan_query_init(r, all, none),1063        .ctx = ctx,1064    }));1065}1066 1067kayan_scheduled_at: proc(systems: *const vec<*kayan_scheduled in level>, s: u64) -> *kayan_scheduled in level = {1068    return vec<*kayan_scheduled in level>at_const(systems, s)*;1069}1070 1071// One frame: every system in order, each over every table it matches that has1072// rows, then the commands they recorded. A system sees every value the1073// systems before it wrote this frame, and no structural change until the1074// next. The caller opens the frame region and makes the buffer in it.1075kayan_progress: proc(w: *kayan_world in level, systems: *const vec<*kayan_scheduled in level>, dt: f32,1076                     cmds: *kayan_commands in frame) -> void = {1077    for (s: u64 = 0; s < systems*.length; s += 1) {1078        sys: *kayan_scheduled in level = kayan_scheduled_at(systems, s);1079        kayan_query_update(w, sys*.query&);1080        for (i: u64 = 0; i < sys*.query.tables*.length; i += 1) {1081            it: kayan_iter = { .world = w, .table = kayan_query_table(w, sys*.query&, i), .dt = dt,1082                               .commands = cmds, .ctx = sys*.ctx };1083            if (it.table*.count > 0) {1084                sys*.tables += 1;1085                sys*.rows += it.table*.count;1086                sys*.system*.run(it&);1087            }1088        }1089    }1090    kayan_flush(w, cmds);1091}1092 1093kayan_print_schedule: proc(w: *const kayan_world, systems: *const vec<*kayan_scheduled in level>) -> void = {1094    for (s: u64 = 0; s < systems*.length; s += 1) {1095        sys: *kayan_scheduled in level = kayan_scheduled_at(systems, s);1096        kayan_print_query(w, sys*.system*.name, sys*.query&);1097    }1098}1099 1100// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------1101// The game1102// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------1103 1104// What the game's systems share: the drones, for the systems that look for1105// them, and the score. Systems get it through their ctx; it lives in level,1106// so an iterator can hold it.1107game: struct = {1108    drones: kayan_query;1109    time: f32;1110    fired: u32;1111    hits: u32;1112    fires: u32;1113    kills: u32;1114    breaches: u32;1115    came: u32;1116}1117 1118// Kernels: plain loops over plain slices, as in 3.2.1119integrate: proc[unsafe](ps: noalias []position, vs: []const velocity, dt: f32) -> void = {1120    for (i: u64 = 0; i < ps.length; i += 1) {1121        ps[i].at.x += vs[i].per_second.x * dt;1122        ps[i].at.y += vs[i].per_second.y * dt;1123    }1124}1125 1126burn: proc[unsafe](hs: noalias []health, fires: []const burning, dt: f32) -> void = {1127    for (i: u64 = 0; i < hs.length; i += 1) {1128        hs[i].points -= fires[i].per_second * dt;1129    }1130}1131 1132age: proc[unsafe](ls: noalias []lifetime, dt: f32) -> void = {1133    for (i: u64 = 0; i < ls.length; i += 1) {1134        ls[i].seconds -= dt;1135    }1136}1137 1138bullet_signature: proc() -> u64 = {1139    return kayan_mask_of<position>() | kayan_mask_of<velocity>() | kayan_mask_of<damage>() | kayan_mask_of<lifetime>();1140}1141 1142drone_signature: proc() -> u64 = {1143    return kayan_mask_of<position>() | kayan_mask_of<velocity>() | kayan_mask_of<health>();1144}1145 1146// Is there a drone in the lane at height y, ahead of x?1147drone_ahead: proc(w: *const kayan_world, g: *game, x: f32, y: f32) -> b32 = {1148    for (i: u64 = 0; i < g*.drones.tables*.length; i += 1) {1149        ps: []position = kayan_slice<position>(kayan_query_table(w, g*.drones&, i));1150        for (row: u64 = 0; row < ps.length; row += 1) {1151            dy: f32 = ps[row].at.y - y;1152            if (dy * dy < 0.25 && ps[row].at.x > x) {1153                return true;1154            }1155        }1156    }1157    return false;1158}1159 1160// A turret whose timer is up fires, if it has something to fire at.1161turret_system: proc(it: *kayan_iter) -> void = {1162    g: option<*game in level> = it*.ctx;1163    if (!g) {1164        return;1165    }1166    ps: []position = kayan_slice<position>(it*.table);1167    ts: []turret = kayan_slice<turret>(it*.table);1168    kayan_query_update(it*.world, g*.drones&);1169    for (row: u64 = 0; row < ts.length; row += 1) {1170        if (ts[row].timer <= 0.0 && drone_ahead(it*.world, g, ps[row].at.x, ps[row].at.y)) {1171            shot: kayan_pending = kayan_defer_spawn(it*.commands, bullet_signature());1172            kayan_pending_set<position>(it*.commands, shot, ps[row]);1173            kayan_pending_set<velocity>(it*.commands, shot, { .per_second = { .x = 16.0, .y = 0.0 } });1174            kayan_pending_set<damage>(it*.commands, shot, { .amount = 25.0 });1175            kayan_pending_set<lifetime>(it*.commands, shot, { .seconds = 2.0 });1176            ts[row].timer = ts[row].cooldown;1177            g*.fired += 1;1178        }1179        if (ts[row].timer > 0.0) {1180            ts[row].timer -= it*.dt;1181        }1182    }1183}1184 1185age_system: proc(it: *kayan_iter) -> void = {1186    unsafe { age(kayan_slice<lifetime>(it*.table), it*.dt); }1187}1188 1189expire_system: proc(it: *kayan_iter) -> void = {1190    ls: []lifetime = kayan_slice<lifetime>(it*.table);1191    es: []kayan_entity = kayan_entities(it*.table);1192    for (row: u64 = 0; row < es.length; row += 1) {1193        if (ls[row].seconds <= 0.0) {1194            kayan_defer_despawn(it*.commands, es[row]);1195        }1196    }1197}1198 1199move_system: proc(it: *kayan_iter) -> void = {1200    unsafe { integrate(kayan_slice<position>(it*.table), kayan_slice<velocity>(it*.table), it*.dt); }1201}1202 1203// A bullet within three quarters of a unit of a drone in its lane hits it. A1204// bullet moves a unit a frame and a drone at most a quarter, so none passes1205// through a drone between two frames without being this close in one of them.1206hit_system: proc(it: *kayan_iter) -> void = {1207    w: *kayan_world in level = it*.world;1208    g: option<*game in level> = it*.ctx;1209    if (!g) {1210        return;1211    }1212    ps: []position = kayan_slice<position>(it*.table);1213    ds: []damage = kayan_slice<damage>(it*.table);1214    es: []kayan_entity = kayan_entities(it*.table);1215    kayan_query_update(w, g*.drones&);1216    for (b: u64 = 0; b < es.length; b += 1) {1217        for (i: u64 = 0; i < g*.drones.tables*.length; i += 1) {1218            t: *kayan_table in level = kayan_query_table(w, g*.drones&, i);1219            tps: []position = kayan_slice<position>(t);1220            ths: []health = kayan_slice<health>(t);1221            for (row: u64 = 0; row < tps.length; row += 1) {1222                dx: f32 = tps[row].at.x - ps[b].at.x;1223                dy: f32 = tps[row].at.y - ps[b].at.y;1224                if (dx * dx < 0.5625 && dy * dy < 0.25) {1225                    ths[row].points -= ds[b].amount;1226                    kayan_defer_despawn(it*.commands, es[b]);1227                    g*.hits += 1;1228                }1229            }1230        }1231    }1232}1233 1234// Below half health, a drone catches fire: a component added, so a command.1235ignite_system: proc(it: *kayan_iter) -> void = {1236    g: option<*game in level> = it*.ctx;1237    if (!g) {1238        return;1239    }1240    hs: []health = kayan_slice<health>(it*.table);1241    es: []kayan_entity = kayan_entities(it*.table);1242    for (row: u64 = 0; row < es.length; row += 1) {1243        if (hs[row].points < 0.5 * hs[row].max && hs[row].points > 0.0) {1244            kayan_defer_add<burning>(it*.commands, es[row], { .per_second = 10.0 });1245            g*.fires += 1;1246        }1247    }1248}1249 1250burn_system: proc(it: *kayan_iter) -> void = {1251    unsafe { burn(kayan_slice<health>(it*.table), kayan_slice<burning>(it*.table), it*.dt); }1252}1253 1254// The entity and its values are copied out before the line is printed: a1255// print of a slice element in a loop reads as a change to the checker.1256die_system: proc(it: *kayan_iter) -> void = {1257    g: option<*game in level> = it*.ctx;1258    if (!g) {1259        return;1260    }1261    hs: []health = kayan_slice<health>(it*.table);1262    es: []kayan_entity = kayan_entities(it*.table);1263    for (row: u64 = 0; row < es.length; row += 1) {1264        e: kayan_entity = es[row];1265        points: f32 = hs[row].points;1266        if (points <= 0.0) {1267            kayan_defer_despawn(it*.commands, e);1268            g*.kills += 1;1269            printfmt("{:6.2}s  {}:{} destroyed\n", cast(g*.time, f64), e.index, e.generation);1270        }1271    }1272}1273 1274// A drone still alive at the left end has reached the base.1275breach_system: proc(it: *kayan_iter) -> void = {1276    g: option<*game in level> = it*.ctx;1277    if (!g) {1278        return;1279    }1280    ps: []position = kayan_slice<position>(it*.table);1281    hs: []health = kayan_slice<health>(it*.table);1282    es: []kayan_entity = kayan_entities(it*.table);1283    for (row: u64 = 0; row < es.length; row += 1) {1284        e: kayan_entity = es[row];1285        at: vec2 = ps[row].at;1286        points: f32 = hs[row].points;1287        if (at.x <= 0.0 && points > 0.0) {1288            kayan_defer_despawn(it*.commands, e);1289            g*.breaches += 1;1290            printfmt("{:6.2}s  {}:{} reached the base in lane {:.0}\n", cast(g*.time, f64),1291                e.index, e.generation, cast(at.y, f64));1292        }1293    }1294}1295 1296// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------1297// The level: waves, and a picture of the lanes1298// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------1299 1300lanes: u32 = 3;1301arena_end: f32 = 32.0;1302 1303spawn_turret: proc(w: *kayan_world, lane: u32) -> kayan_entity = The dojo · thirteen building blocks

The dojo

dojo/README.md

An ECS is mostly a few small building blocks put together. None of them is specific to an ECS: a renderer's texture handles are a slot map, a particle system is swap-remove over packed arrays, undo and network replication are command buffers. The course meets each block for the first time in the middle of building something bigger, which is why its chapters can feel dense. The dojo takes the blocks out and gives each one two halves:

  • a playground, to understand it: a small program that runs the block step by step and draws its insides, with one switch at the top that breaks it the way it most often breaks. Step through it in a debugger, flip the switch, watch what goes wrong.
  • a kata, to own it: you write the block yourself, and a harness checks it. Reading and stepping through code feels like learning, but writing it from a blank page, getting it wrong, and doing it again a few days later is what makes it yours.
blockwhat it isin the course
1free list and generationshandles that are safe to keep after what they name is gone1.2, 1.3
2swap-remove and the back-referencevalues packed with no holes, found by id: a sparse set1.4, 2.3, 2.6
3the slot map1 and 2 together: handles into packed values1.4, 2.4
4a type-erased columnan array of any type as bytes, viewed as a typed slice2.2, 2.3, 2.5
5a command bufferstructural changes recorded now and applied later3.3, 3.4
6bitsetsa set of components in a u64: has, all of, none of2.1, 3.1
7an arenapush, push, clear: memory for things that die togetherevery chapter
8index, not pointerlinks that stay right when their storage moves2.2, 2.4, 2.5
9interningfind or make, by key: a hash table that hands out dense ids2.4
10memoized edgesa slow lookup done once, then remembered on the edge2.6
11a reflection walkreading, writing and comparing any value through its type's record2.7
12a watermarklooking only at what was added since last time3.1
13a dispatch tablebehaviour as data: the schedule as a list of functions3.2

Do 1 to 5 in order the first time: 3 is 1 and 2 put together, and 5 applies its commands to something like 3. 6 to 13 come in the order the course meets them and stand on their own, except that 9, 10 and 12 work on 6's signatures. Any of them can come before the course, alongside it, or after it.

Each block

dojo/3.slot_map/
  README.md              the block, its invariant, the levels, the variations
  play_slot_map.rin      the playground
  harness.rin            fixed: a scenario, then a fuzz run against a model
  level1.rin ... 3.rin   where a kata starts
  solution.rin           the reference; don't peek
  kata.rin               yours: made by `start`, ignored by git

The harness doesn't know how your kata works, only what it must do. First it runs a short scenario, the playground's steps, and prints each as it passes. Then it runs 20,000 random operations from a seed against a simple model of the right answers, and checks after each one. A failure says which operation, which seed, and how to stop just before it in a debugger.

Levels, so the reps get harder:

  1. One function in an otherwise finished file: the one with the idea in it, usually the one people forget.
  2. Every function body, with the fields and signatures given. A proc that must return a real pointer or slice, a _make above all, has a body to start from, since there's nothing shorter that compiles. Some of those are finished, and some only make the vecs: read what the comment asks for.
  3. A blank page, with only a list of what the harness calls.
  4. Variations: the same harness, different insides, listed in each block's README.

Each README gives a target time for levels 1 to 3.

In the safe subset

Every kata, harness and playground here is checked by rin with its safety rules on, and so is your kata: rin compile refuses one that breaks them, and the runner prints what it said. It makes the katas look alike:

  • A kata that keeps memory lives in a region. level, which each harness opens in main and hands to the scenario and the fuzz run, is where an arena would be. Blocks 5 and 11 also use frame, a shorter region opened once per game frame or fuzz step. dojo/dojo.rin declares both.
  • **A kata is made whole by its _make proc**, handles_make(r: region level) -> *handles in level, and its vecs are fields of the form *vec<u32> in level. A vec knows its region, so a proc that pushes needs no region of its own.
  • **A proc that may find nothing returns option<*T>**, and the caller tests it, if (p), before using it.
  • A pointer or slice that comes out of the kata's storage says where it points: option<*u64 in level>, []u64 in level. Without that the checker refuses the return: the result names no region, and may point into region 'level'.
  • A pointer into a vec is good until the vec may move. Keep one across a call that can change the vec, and the checker says 'n' may be stale: 'l', which it was taken from, has been changed since; take it again. Blocks 8 and 10 are about why.
  • **What safe code can't do is in unsafe { }**, and only that: reading the command line and comparing C strings in dojo.rin, three small blocks in block 4's column, the one proc in block 13 that keeps a name and a proc pointer, and a few helpers in the harnesses of 4, 11 and 13 and the playgrounds of 4, 11 and 13. The top of each file names them.

A block's README says where this changes how its kata is solved, most of all in 4 (you write three small unsafe { } blocks, and check what they rely on), 7 (the arena hands out offsets), 11 (the walk goes through the harness's helpers) and 13 (a system is kept behind a pointer into the region).

Watching a playground

python tools/dojo.py play slot_map

A playground runs one scenario, one operation per line of main, and prints what changed after each, so it works without a debugger. In one, put a breakpoint on a line of main and step over the operations. Where the block has slots there are only a few of them, in fixed arrays, so the watch window shows the whole state. From block 6 on, a verify proc runs after every operation, checks the block's invariant, and says what broke; a breakpoint inside its failure branch stops at the first operation that breaks it.

The switch is a global b32, read each time it's used, so besides editing it and running again, you can flip it mid-run: stop where the playground's header says, set it to 0 in the watch window, and continue. rin writes C, and the global keeps its name, so in gdb:

(gdb) break handles_free
(gdb) run
(gdb) set var bump_on_free = 0
(gdb) continue

Doing reps

python tools/dojo.py                      the blocks, your reps, and what is due
python tools/dojo.py play slot_map        the playground
python tools/dojo.py start slot_map 2     a fresh kata.rin from level 2; the clock starts
python tools/dojo.py slot_map             build the harness with your kata.rin and run it

A block can be named by its number, its name or the start of its name: 3, slot_map and slot are the same. While the kata fails, fix it and run it again. When it passes, the time since start goes into dojo/log.md, and the block is due again 1, 3, 7, 14 and then 30 days after each pass. python tools/dojo.py with no arguments says what is due. Spacing reps out is what makes them stick, much more than doing many in one day.

start won't overwrite a kata.rin you've changed unless you add --force. Your log is a plain markdown table; commit it or don't.

When a kata fails, the harness says where:

FAIL at operation 64 (seed 1): row 4 holds 43's value 37043, but get(43) gives 43020
    debug it: build/dojo/swap_remove/harness --seed 1 --stop 64
    with a breakpoint on dojo_stop_here, which runs just before that operation

Run that binary under a debugger with a breakpoint on dojo_stop_here. It stops just before the failing operation, with your structure in the state that leads to the failure. If the harness crashes instead, on a vec index past the end say, the runner runs it again with --trace 1 and prints the operation that was running. --seed N reruns a different fuzz run, and --sanitize builds with AddressSanitizer and UBSan, which block 4's unsafe { } blocks are exactly what they're for.

How it's built

Every kata file is a whole program. Yours, the solution and each level import what they use, then the harness, which has main:

import "std/memops.rin"
import "std/vec.rin"
import "std/option.rin"
import "../dojo.rin"
import "harness.rin"

So any of them builds on its own, rin compile dojo/3.slot_map/solution.rin for instance, and rin check or your editor finds every name it uses. Only the harness doesn't build alone: it calls the procs the kata defines. A file imported twice is read once, so the kata and the harness both importing dojo.rin is fine. dojo/dojo.rin holds what every harness shares: the regions level and frame, dojo_handle and dojo_status, the run's settings, the random number generator, and the reporting. The runner builds kata.rin the way tools/check.py does, rin compile and then the C compiler, with the warnings for unused parameters and locals off, since a kata in progress is full of them.

python tools/check.py dojo keeps the dojo honest: every solution must build on its own, pass its harness and print its harness.expected, level 1 must fail (its gap must be a gap), level 2 must compile, and the playgrounds must print their .expected. The harnesses were also checked against broken solutions, the mistakes each block is about, and catch each one.

The same dojo exists in Rust, in rust-dod. The random number generator is the same, so a seed is the same run in both, and the playgrounds print the same thing, except where block 4's column gets its memory: a region's arena in rin, a Vec in Rust. The katas differ where the languages do: rin's are made in a region; block 7's arena hands out offsets in both, for different reasons; and in block 8 only rin can keep a pointer across a move, so only rin's switch does. Each README says how.

The dojo · block 1

Free list and generations

dojo/1.free_list/play_free_list.rin

Handles name things that come and go: entities, textures, sounds, network connections. A handle is two numbers, index:generation, and two small ideas make it safe to keep:

  • A free list. A freed index is reused before a new one is made, so the arrays an index points into stay as long as the most things ever alive at once, not the most things ever made.
  • A generation per index. Freeing bumps the index's generation, so every handle made for the old life stops matching. A reused index can't be mistaken for whatever had it before.

The invariant: a handle is alive exactly when its generation is the one its index holds now. A free index already holds its next generation, which no handle has yet, so "free" needs no flag of its own. Every index is either alive or on the free list, once. Generations start at 1, so a zeroed handle, {}, is never alive.

In the course: 1.2 builds the free list and meets its bug, 1.3 adds generations, and every later chapter keeps both.

Watch it: the playground

python tools/dojo.py play free_list

It allocates four handles, frees two, reuses one, and draws both arrays after each step:

free b, then d: their generations go up now, before anyone reuses them
    generations  0:1  1:2  2:1  3:2
    free list    [1 3]
alloc e: alloc takes from the end of the free list, so index 3, in its next life
    e 3:2

Step through it: break on handles_alloc and handles_free, and watch generations and free change. Then flip the switch at the top, bump_on_free, to 0 and run it again. The freed b is still alive, the reused index comes back with the old generation so d and e are the same handle, and freeing d again frees e and puts index 3 back on the free list while e is still using it. That's the bug from 1.2, in four lines of output.

Do reps: the kata

You write handles, an allocator of handles, made in the region level:

handles_make: proc(r: region level) -> *handles in level = {
handles_alloc: proc(h: *handles) -> dojo_handle = {
handles_free: proc(h: *handles, e: dojo_handle) -> dojo_status = {
handles_alive: proc(h: *handles, e: dojo_handle) -> b32 = {

plus handles_live (how many are alive) and handles_slots (how many indices have been handed out). dojo_handle and dojo_status are given, in dojo/dojo.rin. The arrays are *vec<u32> in level, made by handles_make; they grow in the region by themselves, so handles_alloc takes no region.

levelyou writetarget
1handles_free, in an otherwise finished file2:00
2every proc body; the fields and signatures are given8:00
3the whole file, from a blank page10:00
python tools/dojo.py start free_list 2      kata.rin from level 2, and the clock starts
python tools/dojo.py free_list              your kata.rin against the harness

The harness first runs a short scenario, the playground's steps, and prints each as it passes. Then it runs 20,000 random allocs and frees from a seed, against a model that remembers, per index, the last generation handed out and whether the index is free. It checks what your allocator does, not how: a generation is never handed out twice for an index, a freed index is reused before a new one is made, and handles_alive agrees with the model for every handle, live and dead. The seeds give the same runs as rust-dod's dojo.

Level 4, variations. The same harness, different insides:

  • Keep the free list inside the dead slots: no free vec, but a next_free field in each slot that is only meaningful while the slot is free, and a first_free in handles. What marks the end of the list?
  • 16-bit generations in the slots, stored as u16, that wrap from 65535 back to 1, never 0. What does wrapping give up?
  • Reuse in first-in, first-out order, so an index rests as long as possible before it comes back. Why might a game want that?

When it fails

FAIL at operation 266 (seed 1): after free, alive() is still true for 43:1
    debug it: build/dojo/free_list/harness --seed 1 --stop 266
    with a breakpoint on dojo_stop_here, which runs just before that operation

python tools/dojo.py free_list built that harness with your kata. If the harness crashes instead, on an index past the end of a vec say, the runner runs it again with --trace 1 and prints the operation that was running.

The dojo · block 2

Swap-remove and the back-reference

dojo/2.swap_remove/play_swap_remove.rin

Systems loop over values, so values are kept packed: one after another, no holes, nothing to skip. Removing one from the middle would leave a hole, so the last value moves into it instead. That's swap-remove: one copy, however many values there are, at the price of order.

Values move, so an id can't be the position of its value. Two arrays keep track:

  • sparse, by id: rows[id] says which row id's value is in now;
  • packed, by row: ids[row] is the id that owns the row. This is the back-reference: when the last row moves into a hole, it says whose entry in rows to fix.

The whole structure is what EnTT calls a sparse set.

The invariant: the rows are packed, and the two arrays point at each other: for every row, rows[ids[row]] names that row, and an id with no value has no row.

In the course: 1.4 packs entities into rows this way, 2.3 does it for every column of a table, and 2.6 does it when an entity moves between tables.

Watch it: the playground

python tools/dojo.py play swap_remove

It inserts four values, removes one from the middle, and draws both sides after each step:

remove 7, in row 1: the last row, 5's, moves into the hole
    row         0    1    2
    ids         3    5    1
    values     30   50   10
    rows    1->2  3->0  5->1  (id -> row)

Step through it: break on sparse_set_remove, and watch ids and rows as the last row moves. Then flip the switch at the top, fix_back_reference, to 0 and run it again. Id 5's row still says 3, past the end, so get 5 finds nothing. Then insert 9 puts 9's value in row 3, and get 5 returns 90, another id's value, with nothing to say it's wrong. That's the bug every packed array invites, and the reason the back-reference exists.

Do reps: the kata

You write sparse_set, made in the region level, with values, ids and rows each a *vec<...> in level. The heart of it is sparse_set_remove:

sparse_set_remove: proc(s: *sparse_set, id: u32) -> option<u64> = {
    if (sparse_set_get(s, id) == null) {
        return option<u64>none();
    }
    entry: *u32 = vec<u32>at(s*.rows, cast(id, u64));
    row: u64 = cast(entry* - 1, u64);
    entry* = 0;
    value: u64 = vec<u64>at(s*.values, row)*;
    last_value: u64 = vec<u64>pop(s*.values);
    last_id: u32 = vec<u32>pop(s*.ids);
    if (row < s*.values*.length) {
        vec<u64>at(s*.values, row)* = last_value;
        vec<u32>at(s*.ids, row)* = last_id;
        vec<u32>at(s*.rows, cast(last_id, u64))* = cast(row, u32) + 1;
    }
    return option<u64>some(value);
}

That's the reference, so don't read it before level 1 if you'd rather not know. vec has no swap-remove of its own: the last element is popped, and written over the hole unless the hole was the last row. The full API:

sparse_set_insert: proc(s: *sparse_set, id: u32, value: u64) -> option<u64> = {
sparse_set_get: proc(s: *sparse_set, id: u32) -> option<*u64 in level> = {

plus sparse_set_make(r), sparse_set_len, sparse_set_values (the packed values, in row order, a []u64 in level) and sparse_set_ids (ids[row] owns values[row], a []u32 in level).

The harness runs the playground's steps as a scenario, then 20,000 random inserts and removes over a small range of ids, so the same ids come and go many times, against a plain array from id to value. Every 64 operations it checks the packed rows themselves: as many as the model has, and each row's owner holding exactly that row's value. The seeds give the same runs as rust-dod's dojo.

rin notes. Where Rust's kata returns Option<T> and has get_mut, this one uses std's option<u64> for what insert and remove give back (the old value, or none), and one sparse_set_get that returns an option<*u64 in level>, a pointer to the value, null for none, to read or to change, the way kayan_get<T> does in the course. The caller tests it, if (current), before using it. The in level is there, on sparse_set_values and sparse_set_ids too, because the pointer comes out of a vec in level, and the checker refuses a result that doesn't say so. rows[id] holds the row plus one, so a new entry, 0, means "no row", and growing rows is appending zeros.

Level 4, variations. The same harness, different insides:

  • Pages: rows split into pages of 64 ids, each page made only when an id in it gets a value. A big id no longer means a big rows. This is what EnTT does, with a pointer per page, null for a page not made yet. Here sparse_set_insert has no region to make a page in, and a struct can't keep one, so a page is a struct holding [64]u32 in a vec of pages, and a vec<u32> by page number holds one more than its place there, 0 for a page not made yet.
  • A sentinel: rows[id] holds the row itself, with 0xFFFFFFFF for "no row". What does growing rows cost now?
  • A flag: a second vec<b32>, has_row, beside rows. Compare the memory with the plus-one encoding.

And one that fails on purpose: a remove that keeps order, shifting every later row down and fixing each one's back-reference. The scenario stops it at the first ids line. Why does the harness insist on swap-remove's order, and what does keeping order cost?

When it fails

A forgotten back-reference often shows up as a crash in a sparse_set_get that is right, not in the sparse_set_remove that is wrong: get follows the stale row past the end, and vec<u64>at stops the program.

rin runtime: vec index out of bounds
the harness crashed in the scenario, after the last step printed above

The last step printed is the last that passed, so the bug is in what ran after it. In the fuzz run, the runner runs the harness again with --trace 1 and prints the operation that was running when it crashed. A failed check gives the operation and the seed:

FAIL at operation 64 (seed 1): row 4 holds 43's value 37043, but get(43) gives 43020
    debug it: build/dojo/swap_remove/harness --seed 1 --stop 64
    with a breakpoint on dojo_stop_here, which runs just before that operation

Run the harness under your debugger with those arguments and a breakpoint on dojo_stop_here (gdb --args build/dojo/swap_remove/harness --seed 1 --stop 64, then break dojo_stop_here, run). It stops just before the operation that fails; step out and into your code.

The dojo · block 3

The slot map

dojo/3.slot_map/play_slot_map.rin

Dojos 1 and 2, put together. Values live packed in rows, so a loop over them has no holes (dojo 2). The rest of the program keeps handles, which survive rows moving and say when their value is gone (dojo 1). In between is a slot per index:

handle 1:2  ->  slots[1] { generation 2, row 0 }  ->  values[0]

A lookup is two steps: the handle's generation must be the slot's, and the slot says the row. A remove is both dojos' work: bump the generation and free the index, then swap-remove the row and fix the slot of whoever moved. Game engines keep textures, meshes and sounds this way, and it is the ECS's entity index.

The invariant: dojo 1's and dojo 2's together. A handle is alive exactly when its generation is its slot's; the rows are packed; and for every row, the slot of the row's handle points back at that row.

In the course: 1.4 is a slot map with an entity's components as its value, and every chapter after keeps it, with a table number added to the slot in 2.4.

Watch it: the playground

python tools/dojo.py play slot_map

It keeps three textures, removes one, reuses its index, and draws the slots and the rows after each step:

remove stone: free index 1 in its next life, and water moves into row 1
    slots    0: generation 1, row 0 | 1: generation 2, free | 2: generation 1, row 1
    rows     0:1 grass | 2:1 water

Step through it: break on slot_map_remove, and watch the slot, the free list and the rows change in that order. Then flip the switch at the top, check_generation, to 0 and run it again. The removed stone still finds slot 1, and reads whatever is in slot 1's row now: water, then lava. In a game, that's a sound that plays the wrong sample, or a mesh drawn with another mesh's texture.

Do reps: the kata

You write slot_map, made in the region level, with its four arrays each a *vec<...> in level. Its two-step lookup:

slot_map_get: proc(m: *slot_map, h: dojo_handle) -> option<*u64 in level> = {
    if (!slot_map_contains(m, h)) {
        return null;
    }
    row: u32 = vec<slot_map_slot>at(m*.slots, cast(h.index, u64))*.row;
    return vec<u64>at(m*.values, cast(row, u64));
}

and the API around it:

slot_map_insert: proc(m: *slot_map, value: u64) -> dojo_handle = {
slot_map_remove: proc(m: *slot_map, h: dojo_handle) -> option<u64> = {

plus slot_map_make(r), slot_map_contains, slot_map_len, slot_map_values (the packed values, in row order, a []u64 in level) and slot_map_handles (handles[row] owns values[row], a []dojo_handle in level). dojo_handle comes from dojo/dojo.rin, as in dojo 1.

Level 3 is the one to come back to. Once you can write a slot map from a blank page in fifteen minutes, dojos 1 and 2 are in your hands too.

The harness runs the playground's steps as a scenario, then 20,000 random inserts, removes, reads and writes against a model that keeps, per index, the last generation handed out, whether the index is free, and its value. It checks dojo 1's rules for the handles (a generation never handed out twice for an index, a freed index reused before a new one is made, a removed handle never alive again) and dojo 2's for the rows (packed, each row's handle holding that row's value). The seeds give the same runs as rust-dod's dojo.

rin notes. As in dojo 2, slot_map_remove gives back std's option<u64> and slot_map_get returns an option<*u64 in level>, a pointer that is null for a dead handle and tested before use, to read or to change the value; Rust's kata has get and get_mut. The in level is there, and on the two slices, because the checker refuses a result that comes out of a vec in level and doesn't say so. A zeroed handle, {}, is never alive, since generations start at 1, and the scenario checks that too.

Level 4, variations. The same harness, different insides:

  • Free list inside the slots: a next_free: u32 in each slot, only meaningful while the slot is free, and a first_free in slot_map. No free vec. What marks the end of the list?
  • One look at the slot: slot_map_remove without slot_map_contains: fetch the slot once, check its generation, and use it. How many times does the reference look the slot up?
  • **slot_map_retain(m, keep)**, with keep a *proc(h: dojo_handle, value: u64) -> b32: remove every value it rejects, in one pass, keeping the rows packed. Which way should the loop walk? (Not checked by the harness; write your own test.)

When it fails

FAIL at operation 233 (seed 1): remove(33:1) returned 214, the model says 210
    debug it: build/dojo/slot_map/harness --seed 1 --stop 233
    with a breakpoint on dojo_stop_here, which runs just before that operation

The wrong value usually means a slot pointing at the wrong row: an earlier remove moved a row and didn't fix its slot. Run the harness under your debugger with those arguments and a breakpoint on dojo_stop_here, which runs just before that operation, then look at the slot of the handle being removed.

If the harness crashes instead, on a row past the end of values say, the runner runs it again with --trace 1 and prints the operation that was running, or says the crash came in the scenario, after the last step printed.

A removed handle21// still finds a slot, and reads whatever value is in that slot's row now. The dojo · block 4

A type-erased column

dojo/4.column/play_column.rin

A column is one component's rows, kept as bytes. It doesn't know the type it holds, only how many bytes make a row and how they must be aligned. That is enough to grow, to zero a new row, and to move the last row into a hole, which is everything a table does to its columns. The type comes back only at the edge: a typed view turns the bytes into a []T, for a T of the column's size and alignment.

Two things make it work:

  • Aligned storage. The bytes come from the region aligned to the column's alignment, so every row of the type lands where that type may live.
  • Growing by a factor. A full column doubles, so the copies that growing costs add up to about one per push, however many rows there are.

The invariant: the column holds count rows of size bytes each, packed from the start of a block aligned to align, with room for capacity rows. A typed view is only handed out for a plain-data T of exactly size bytes, aligned to exactly align, and only when the rows fit in the bytes. Plain data means a struct of numbers with no pointers in it, since a column copies rows as bytes.

In the course: 2.2 builds the column, 2.3 puts columns in a table, and 2.5 is about what happens to a pointer into a column that grows.

Watch it: the playground

python tools/dojo.py play column

It fills a column of vec2s and draws each row's bytes next to the value they are:

push 3 zeroed rows, and write each through the typed view
    capacity 4, 3 rows in use, 32 bytes of storage
    row 0  00 00 80 3f 00 00 00 40   as a vec2 (1, 2)
    row 1  00 00 40 40 00 00 80 40   as a vec2 (3, 4)

Then it grows the column, swap-removes from it, and asks for the rows as two wrong types. Step through it: break on column_grow and watch the rows move to the new block. The old block stays in the region, unused, so a slice taken before the grow still points somewhere valid, and anything written through it is lost without a word.

The switch at the top, grow_by_doubling, picks how a full column grows. Set it to 0, so the column grows by one row, and run it again. The last line is the point: the same 1000 pushes copy 1,020 rows when the column doubles, and 499,494 when it grows by one.

1000 pushes into a u32 column, growing by doubling
    9 grows, 1020 rows copied to make room

Do reps: the kata

You write column. Its bytes are a slice, data: []u8 in level, so even type erasure is mostly checked code: slice<u8>copy and slice<u8>zero do the work, and a row past the end stops the program like any index. Three things need unsafe { }, a few lines each, and their signatures are the promise safe code relies on:

  • column_make keeps the region's arena, since a region can't be stored: a field arena: ^memops_arena, and c*.arena = r.
  • column_grow takes a block from that arena, because new_slice<u8> can't ask for an alignment, and makes it a slice.
  • column_slice tests the address and casts the bytes to T.

Keep each block that small: put your checks outside it, where the checker can see them.

A full column's new bytes come from the arena, aligned to the column's alignment:

        raw: ^u8 = cast(memops_arena_push_zero(c*.arena[0]&, c*.size * capacity, c*.align), ^u8);
        bytes: []u8 in level = cast(raw[0..c*.size * capacity], []u8 in level);

and the rows go across with slice<u8>copy(bytes[0..kept], c*.data[0..kept]). Slicing checks both ends, so the copy can't run off either block. The typed view is a generic proc that checks everything it relies on before it casts:

column_slice: proc<T>(c: *const column) -> []T in level = {

plus column_make(r, size, align), column_len, column_capacity, column_push_zeroed (a zeroed row at the end, and its row number), column_swap_remove(c, row), and column_row(c, row), a row's bytes as a []u8 in level. The kata has no vec to lean on: it is the thing a vec would be built from.

**What an unsafe block may believe.** rin has no private fields. Any checked code holding a *column can write c*.count = 1000, so an unsafe block must not trust a field or an argument unless the value carries its own bound, as a slice does. That decides what column_slice tests:

  • The type's size and alignment, against the column's. The column can't know the type, but it can refuse every type that can't be the one it was made for.
  • That the type is plain data, reflect_is_plain(T<>&). Any bytes are then a valid T, so a wrong type of the right shape gives wrong numbers, never a bad pointer: a vec3 column read as a struct of three u32s gives 1065353216, 1073741824 and 1077936128, the bits of 1.0, 2.0 and 3.0. A T with a pointer in it would turn bytes into an address, so it stops the program. T<> needs a struct or an enum, so a row is always one: the four-byte row here is word: struct = { value: u32; }, and column_slice<u32> doesn't compile.
  • That the rows fit: c*.count against c*.data.length / size. count is a field, and can say anything; length belongs to the slice, and can't be wrong about it.
  • The address itself: cast(c*.data.data, usize) % align, the bytes as they are, not what c*.align says about them.

The checked procs get this for nothing: a column_row with a lying count or size stops at the slice, range 6000..6012 out of bounds (length 48). The one field still believed is arena: a raw pointer carries no bound. rin seals a struct holding one to the file that declares it, so the harness and anything else importing this file cannot write its fields. Inside the file that is on you: only column_make writes arena, and every unsafe author owes that much.

levelyou writetarget
1column_slice, the typed view, in an otherwise finished file3:00
2every proc body, and a column_grow of your own; the fields and the other signatures are given15:00
3the whole file, from a blank page20:00
python tools/dojo.py start column 2         kata.rin from level 2, and the clock starts
python tools/dojo.py column                 your kata.rin against the harness
python tools/dojo.py column --sanitize      the same with AddressSanitizer and UBSan

The harness first runs a short scenario: three vec3s written through column_slice and read back as bytes, a swap-remove, a column aligned to 16, and a column of tags, zero-byte rows. Then it runs 20,000 random pushes, writes and swap-removes, shared between four row types: 3 bytes aligned to 1, a word holding a u32, a 12-byte vec3, and a 16-byte vec4 aligned to 16. Each is checked against a vec of that type, through column_slice and through column_row, along with the alignment of every view, and that a full column grows by at least half. The harness has two trusted helpers of its own, bytes_of and slice_address, to look at a value's bytes and a slice's address. The seeds give the same runs as rust-dod's dojo.

--sanitize is worth the wait here. A slice made from a raw pointer, raw[0..n], has whatever length you say, so a block asked for too small often works on your machine. AddressSanitizer and UBSan don't let it happen by luck. (They need the C compiler's sanitizer runtime; with clang that may be missing, so try CC=gcc.)

What the harness can't check is a refusal: a column read as the wrong type should stop the program with a message, and so should a row past the rows in use, and a harness that stops can't go on to the next step. It never lies to your column either, so a column_slice that tests only the type passes it. Try them by hand in a scratch program: a copy of your kata with level: region; where its import "harness.rin" was, and a main that opens the region, level: region = { ... }, makes c: *column in level = column_make(level, sizeof(vec3), alignof(vec3)); in it, and pushes two rows. Then, one at a time:

  • read it as a word (the wrong size), then as a struct of twelve u8s (the right size, aligned to 1);
  • ask for column_row(c, 2);
  • write c*.count = 1000;, then read it as a vec3;
  • write c*.data = c*.data[1..25];, then read it as a vec3;
  • make a column of a struct with an option<*u32 in level> in it, by its own sizeof and alignof, and read it as that struct.

Each should stop with a message that says what was wrong. Then read the vec3s you wrote as a struct of three u32s, which should not stop, and print what comes back. rust-dod's harness checks the first refusals, because Rust can catch a panic.

Level 4, variations. The same harness, different insides:

  • Grow by 1.5 instead of 2. Count the grows and the rows copied for 1000 pushes. Why do some allocators prefer it?
  • Allocate with **memops_arena_realloc_**, on c*.arena[0]& and inside column_grow's unsafe { }, instead of a new block and a slice<u8>copy. Hand it the old block by c*.data.data and c*.data.length, the slice's own bound, not by c*.capacity. When does it move the rows, and when can it extend the block in place?
  • Shrink: when a swap-remove leaves the column less than a quarter full, move the rows to a block of half the capacity. Why a quarter and not a half? (Push and remove one row, over and over, at the boundary.) In a region, what does shrinking actually give back?

When it fails

FAIL at operation 11 (seed 1): the column was full at 4 rows and grew to 5; it should grow by at least half
    debug it: build/dojo/column/harness --seed 1 --stop 11
    with a breakpoint on dojo_stop_here, which runs just before that operation

python tools/dojo.py column built that harness with your kata. Run it under your debugger with those arguments and a breakpoint on dojo_stop_here (gdb --args build/dojo/column/harness --seed 1 --stop 11, then break dojo_stop_here, run). It stops just before the operation that fails; step out and into your code.

If the harness crashes instead, on a slice range past the end say, the runner runs it again with --trace 1 and prints the operation that was running.

The playground. The kata's harness is dojo/4.column/harness.rin, and the levels start from dojo/4.column/level1.rin to level3.rin.

The dojo · block 5

A command buffer

dojo/5.commands/play_commands.rin

Systems walk tables, and while they walk, they decide to change which things exist: a bullet's time is up, a turret fires, a drone catches fire. Doing it on the spot breaks the walk. A despawn swap-removes, so the last row moves into the hole, behind the loop, and is never looked at. So a system records the change instead, as a command, and the frame applies every command, in order, once nothing is walking anything.

Three details make it work:

  • Pending spawns. A spawn has no handle until it is applied, so recording one hands back a pending number, and later commands in the same buffer can name the spawn by it.
  • Skipping the dead. Two systems may both despawn the same thing, or set a value on something an earlier command removed. Applied in order, the second finds a dead handle and is skipped. Generations make that one comparison.
  • Room that stays. After the buffer is applied its vecs are cleared, and keep their room, so once a game has run a few frames, recording a command allocates nothing.

The invariant: recording changes nothing but the buffer. Applying it has exactly the effect of running every command straight away, in the order it was recorded, with each pending number meaning the handle its spawn made.

In the course: 3.3 builds the buffer and shows the bug it fixes, and 3.4's game runs on it. The Advanced lesson 6 has one too.

Watch it: the playground

python tools/dojo.py play commands

A packed world of five things, and one frame of three systems. The expire system records a despawn for each thing whose life is up, the spawner records a replacement and sets its life through its pending number, and a second system despawns something the first already did. Then the buffer is applied:

apply the buffer, in the order it was recorded
    despawn 0:1: ok, 4:1 moves into 0:1's row
    despawn 2:1: ok, 3:1 moves into 2:1's row
    despawn 3:1: ok, it was the last row
    spawn with life 1: pending 0 is 3:2
    set pending 0 life 5: ok, 3:2 has life 5
    despawn 2:1: skipped, 2:1 is dead

Step through it: break on commands_apply and walk the list. Then flip the switch at the top, defer, to 0, so every system changes the world on the spot, and run it again. The expire system despawns 0:1, 4:1 moves into its row behind the loop, and when the loop ends, 3:1 is still there with no life:

things left with no life: none

becomes things left with no life: 3:1, moved behind the loop and never looked at. That's 3.3's bug.

Do reps: the kata

You write commands. A command names its target either way, a handle or a spawn of this buffer:

target: struct = {
    is_pending: b32;
    handle: dojo_handle;
    spawn: pending;
}

made by target_entity(h) or target_pending(p), so commands_set and commands_despawn take either:

commands_set: proc(c: *commands, t: target, value: u32) -> void = {
commands_apply: proc(c: *commands, w: *world) -> applied = {

plus commands_make(r), which makes the buffer and its two vecs in the region level, commands_spawn(c, value), which returns a pending, commands_despawn(c, t), and commands_len, the commands waiting. The world is given, in the harness: a generational store of numbers with world_spawn, world_despawn and world_set, where the last two return dojo_status.dead for a dead handle. commands_apply returns applied, the count of commands that changed something and of those that were skipped.

python tools/dojo.py start commands 2       kata.rin from level 2, and the clock starts
python tools/dojo.py commands               your kata.rin against the harness

The harness first runs a short scenario: a set, a despawn, a spawn that reuses the despawned index, a set through the spawn's pending number, and two commands that find their target dead. Then a fuzz run, frame after frame: random commands recorded against live handles, dead handles and the frame's own pending spawns, then applied. A model runs the same commands straight away on a copy of the world from before the frame, and the harness checks the two worlds match, the applied and skipped counts match, and the buffer is empty afterwards. Each frame of the run opens the region frame for its lists and its model, gone when the frame ends. The two copies of the world hold pointers typed in level, so they are made in level and stay until the run ends. The seeds give the same runs as rust-dod's dojo.

Level 4, variations. The same harness, different insides:

  • Keep the spawned handles in the command list itself, as 3.3 does: a spawn command holds the handle commands_apply gives it, and a pending number finds its spawn through it. No spawned vec.
  • Record the whole buffer as **one vec<u8>**: a kind byte, then the command's fields as bytes. One allocation for any mix of commands, read back in order. Safe code can't see a struct as bytes, so a u32 goes in a byte at a time, with shifts and cast(..., u8), and comes back the same way.
  • Keep the buffer in **the region frame**, opened once per game frame, as 3.3 and lesson 6 do: commands_make(r: region frame) -> *commands in frame, its vecs in frame, and nothing to clear, since the end of the region lets them all go. The harness makes one buffer in level for the whole run, so this one needs a test of your own. What must not live in that region? Keep a pointer into it in a world that lives in level, and the checker tells you: this points into region 'frame', which may end before the memory in region 'level' that holds it.

When it fails

FAIL at operation 28 (seed 1): commands_apply returned applied 7, skipped 4, the model says applied 9, skipped 2
    debug it: build/dojo/commands/harness --seed 1 --stop 28
    with a breakpoint on dojo_stop_here, which runs just before that operation

python tools/dojo.py commands built that harness with your kata. Run it under your debugger with those arguments and a breakpoint on dojo_stop_here (gdb --args build/dojo/commands/harness --seed 1 --stop 28, then break dojo_stop_here, run). It stops just before the operation that fails; step out and into your code.

If the harness crashes instead, on a pending number past the spawns applied so far say, the runner runs it again with --trace 1 and prints the operation that was running.

The playground. The kata's harness is dojo/5.commands/harness.rin, and the levels start from dojo/5.commands/level1.rin to level3.rin.
