The dojo · block 6

Bitsets

dojo/6.bitset/play_bitset.rin

A set of small numbers, 0 to 63, fits in one u64: bit id is set when id is in the set. An ECS keeps what each kind of entity is made of this way, a signature with a bit per component, and a query as two sets: the ids a table must have, and the ids it must not. The questions an ECS asks all day are then one or two instructions each, however many components there are:

with(set, id)            set | (1 shl id)
without(set, id)         set & ~(1 shl id)
has(set, id)             (set & (1 shl id)) != 0
contains_all(set, all)   (set & all) == all
intersects(set, none)    (set & none) != 0

The same trick is a file's permissions, which of 64 workers are idle, and which chunks of a map are loaded.

The invariant: bit id is set exactly when id is in the set. Everything else follows from it: one set contains all of another when masking it with the other leaves the other whole, and two sets share an id when their AND isn't zero.

In the course: 2.1 gives each component a bit and each kind of entity a signature, 2.4 finds a table by its signature, 2.6 moves an entity by setting or clearing one bit, and 3.1 matches queries against tables with contains_all and intersects.

Watch it: the playground

python tools/dojo.py play bitset

It gives five kinds of thing a signature each, draws them as rows of bits, highest id first, and runs queries over them:

query move: all {position velocity}, none {frozen}
    all     00000011
    none    01000000
    player  00011111  matches
    drone   00001111  matches
    turret  00101101  no
    rock    00001001  no
    ghost   01001011  no

Read it by columns: a kind matches when it has a 1 under every 1 of all, and a 0 under every 1 of none. Then the drone is frozen and the ghost thaws, one bit each, and the same query gives a different answer. Each kind keeps its ids twice, as a signature and as a b32 per id, and verify checks the fast answer against the slow one after every step. A kind is named by its place in kind_names, as a component is by its place in names, because a struct holding a C string is not a value safe code may write to.

Step through it: break on matches, and watch set & wanted in the watch window, in binary. Then flip the switch at the top, all_not_any, to 0 and run it again. contains_all now asks whether the signature has any of the ids. The turret and the rock have a position, so both match the movement query, and the turret and the ghost each have half of what the think query wants:

    verify: turret matches, but it has no velocity

It's the most common bitset bug, and it compiles: the compiler has no idea which question you meant.

Do reps: the kata

You write procs over a u64. Bitsets are plain values, so there's no region and no _make in this kata, and nothing for the checker to object to. The one with the idea in it:

bitset_contains_all: proc(set: u64, wanted: u64) -> b32 = {
    return (set & wanted) == wanted;
}

and a query, built from it:

bitset_matches: proc(set: u64, all: u64, none: u64) -> b32 = {
    return bitset_contains_all(set, all) && !bitset_intersects(set, none);
}

plus bitset_bit (the set of id alone), bitset_with, bitset_without, bitset_has, bitset_intersects, bitset_count and bitset_ids, which writes the ids, smallest first, into a slice with room for 64 and returns how many. Ids are u32s, 0 to 63.

levelyou writetarget
1bitset_contains_all, in an otherwise finished file1:00
2every proc body; the signatures are given5:00
3the whole file, from a blank page6:00
python tools/dojo.py start bitset 2
python tools/dojo.py bitset

The harness runs the playground's kinds and queries as a scenario, then 20,000 random operations on a set: adding and taking away ids, and asking has, contains_all, intersects, matches, count and ids, against a model that keeps a b32 per id and answers one id at a time. The sets it asks about are mostly made from the set itself: part of it, part of it plus one more id, or ids it doesn't have, so the answers aren't nearly always false. Ids go up to 63, so a shift done in 32 bits shows. The seeds give the same runs as rust-dod's dojo.

rin notes. rin binds & tighter than ==, as Rust does, so set & wanted == wanted means what it says; in C it would be set & (wanted == wanted). The reference keeps the parentheses anyway, for anyone reading it with C eyes. And a bare 1 is an i32, which rin won't turn into a u64 for you: return 1 shl id; is refused, implicit conversion from 'i32' to 'u64' changes sign, so the reference writes 1'u64 shl cast(id, u64). The 32-bit bug needs a u32 on the left, one: u32 = 1; cast(one shl id, u64). rin masks a shift's amount to the width of what it shifts, so nothing there is undefined and --sanitize has nothing to report: id 63 lands on bit 31, and the harness is what catches it.

Level 4, variations. The same harness, different insides:

  • Count without a loop over 64: set & (set - 1) clears the lowest set bit. Loop until the set is empty, one step per id rather than per bit.
  • **bitset_ids the same way**: low = set & (0 - set) is the lowest set bit alone, its id is the number of bits below it, bitset_count(low - 1), and clearing it moves on.
  • More than 64 components: a struct of two u64s, with id i at bit i % 64 of word i / 64, and the same procs. What does contains_all become? (Not checked by the harness; write your own test.)

    debug it: build/dojo/bitset/harness --seed 1 --stop 2
    with a breakpoint on dojo_stop_here, which runs just before that operation

That one is set ^ bitset_bit(id): an XOR flips the bit, so taking away an id the set doesn't have puts it in. Sets print as their ids, smallest first. Run the harness under your debugger with those arguments and a breakpoint on dojo_stop_here, which runs just before that operation.

The playground. The kata's harness is dojo/6.bitset/harness.rin, and the levels start from dojo/6.bitset/level1.rin to level3.rin.

1// Dojo 6, the playground: bitsets.2//3// A set of component ids fits in a u64: bit `id` is set when `id` is in the4// set. In an ECS that set is a signature, what a kind of entity is made of,5// and a query is two sets: the ids an entity must have, and the ids it must6// not. A query against a signature is then two ANDs and two compares,7// however many components there are:8//9//   (signature & all) == all  &&  (signature & none) == 010//11// This program gives five kinds of thing a signature each, draws them as rows12// of bits, runs queries over them, and changes two of them. Each kind keeps13// its ids twice: the fast way, a signature, and the slow way, a b32 per id.14// After every step, verify checks the fast way against the slow way and says15// what disagrees; break inside its `if`s to stop on the first.16//17// The switch: set all_not_any to 0 and run it again. contains_all then asks18// whether the signature has any of the ids, not all of them, and the turret,19// which can't move, matches the movement query. It's a global, read each time20// it's used, so a debugger can flip it mid-run too: stop on the first `query`21// in main, set it to 0 in the watch window, and continue.22//23// A kind is named by its place in `kind_names`, as a component24// is by its place in `names`, because a struct holding a C string is not a25// value safe code may write to.26 27import "std/print.rin"28 29all_not_any: b32 = 1;30 31names: [8]^const char = { "position", "velocity", "health", "sprite", "player", "turret", "frozen", "loot" };32kind_names: [8]^const char = { "player", "drone", "turret", "rock", "ghost", "", "", "" };33position: u32 = 0;34velocity: u32 = 1;35health: u32 = 2;36sprite: u32 = 3;37player: u32 = 4;38turret: u32 = 5;39frozen: u32 = 6;40 41bit: proc(id: u32) -> u64 = {42    return 1'u64 shl cast(id, u64);43}44 45with: proc(set: u64, id: u32) -> u64 = {46    return set | bit(id);47}48 49without: proc(set: u64, id: u32) -> u64 = {50    return set & ~bit(id);51}52 53has: proc(set: u64, id: u32) -> b32 = {54    return (set & bit(id)) != 0;55}56 57contains_all: proc(set: u64, wanted: u64) -> b32 = {58    if (all_not_any) {59        return (set & wanted) == wanted;60    }61    return (set & wanted) != 0;62}63 64matches: proc(set: u64, all: u64, none: u64) -> b32 = {65    return contains_all(set, all) && (set & none) == 0;66}67 68// Eight bits, highest id first, the way a number is written.69print_bits: proc(set: u64) -> void = {70    for (id: u32 = 8; The dojo · block 7

An arena

dojo/7.arena/play_arena.rin

Most of what a frame allocates dies with the frame: commands, scratch lists, text for the screen. An arena hands all of it out of one buffer and keeps one number, how much of the buffer is used. A push rounds that number up to the alignment asked for, hands out the offset there, and moves the number past the new bytes. Nothing is freed on its own. A mark remembers the number, a rewind puts it back, and a clear sets it to 0: everything pushed since goes at once, in one store, with no list of what to free.

push(4, 4) with 1 used:   round 1 up to 4, hand out offset 4, used is now 8

For an align that is a power of two, rounding up is (used + align - 1) & ~(align - 1): adding align - 1 reaches the next multiple unless used is one already, and the mask drops what's past it.

The invariant: every push not yet let go of starts at a multiple of its alignment, ends at or before used, and stops before the next push starts; used never passes the end of the buffer.

In the course: everywhere. A region is a memops_arena the checker can see. Every lesson from 2.2's columns on allocates from the region level, and never frees anything on its own. 3.3 adds a second, frame: region in level;, for one frame's commands, let go when it ends, and kayan does the same in 6. This block is the arena inside a region, small enough to write in a few minutes.

Watch it: the playground

python tools/dojo.py play arena

It pushes things of different sizes and alignments into a 64-byte buffer, rewinds, fills it to the last byte, and clears it. After each step it draws the buffer, 16 bytes to a group: a letter for each byte of a push, - for padding, . for free.

push b: a u32 count, 4 bytes, align 4
    offset 4, used 8 of 64: 3 bytes of padding first
    a---bbbb........|................|................|................
...
rewind to the mark: e and f are gone at once
    a---bbbbcccccccc|dddddddddddddddd|................|................

Each push is filled with its letter, written through b*.bytes[offset], and verify checks after every step that each push is aligned, inside used, clear of the next, and still holds its letter. Step through it: break on bump_push and watch used. The playground keeps its 64 bytes inside the struct.

Then flip the switch at the top, align_offsets, to 0 and run it again. Pushes are handed out at used as it is, packed with no padding, and the u32, the u64 and the 16-byte vector land at offsets 1, 5 and 13:

    verify: b is at offset 1, not a multiple of 4: a 4-byte thing can't be read from there

The playground only ever writes bytes, so nothing breaks yet, and safe code can't do anything else: reading a u32 out of bytes is a cast to a pointer, which takes unsafe { }. (Block 11 copies the bytes into a local with memcpy instead, which has no alignment to get wrong.) Do the cast from there, though, and it's undefined behaviour in C, so in rin: on x86 it usually works, slower when it straddles two cache lines; an aligned SIMD load faults; and the optimiser is allowed to assume it never happens. --sanitize reports it, as UBSan's "misaligned address".

Do reps: the kata

You write bump, an arena over bytes it gets from the region level. It isn't called arena, since the one every lesson uses already has that name: memops_arena.

bump: struct = {
    bytes: []u8 in level;
    // Bytes before `used` are handed out; bytes after it are free.
    used: u64;
}

Its one proc with an idea in it:

bump_push: proc(b: *bump, size: u64, align: u64) -> option<u64> = {

the offset of size bytes, a multiple of align, or none, changing nothing, when they would end past the last byte. It can't be an address: a ^u8 has no region, so safe code can't hand one out. The caller writes and reads through bump_bytes(b)[offset], a slice the checker bounds-checks. Plus bump_make(r, capacity), which gets its bytes with new_slice<u8>(r, capacity), bump_bytes, which returns a []u8 in level, bump_used, bump_capacity, bump_mark, bump_rewind(b, mark) and bump_clear.

levelyou writetarget
1bump_push, in an otherwise finished file2:00
2every proc body; the fields and signatures are given6:00
3the whole file, from a blank page8:00
python tools/dojo.py start arena 2
python tools/dojo.py arena
python tools/dojo.py arena --sanitize     the same with AddressSanitizer and UBSan

The harness runs the playground's steps as a scenario, then 20,000 random pushes, marks, rewinds and clears on a 256-byte buffer, against a model that keeps the used count and every push not yet let go of. Pushes are 1 to 24 bytes at alignments 1 to 16, with some sized to end exactly at the last byte and some one byte past it. Each push is filled with a pattern at the offset it gave, and read back later, so a push that lands on another shows. The seeds give the same runs as rust-dod's dojo.

rin notes. memops_arena_push hands out an address, and safe code never calls it: it is what a region is built on, behind new<T> and new_slice<T>. rust-dod's kata hands out an offset too, for its own reason: a slice from push would borrow the whole arena for as long as it was kept, and the arena couldn't push again until it was gone. An offset can still be kept past a rewind, which is the arena's one way to go wrong: an offset from before a rewind or a clear names bytes the next push will hand out again. In safe code that gets you the wrong bytes, and never memory outside the slice.

Level 4, variations. The same harness, different insides:

  • Align the address, not the offset, which fails on purpose: round the address of byte used up, and subtract the address of byte 0 again. That takes a small unsafe { }, cast(b*.bytes[0]&, usize), since safe code can't turn a pointer into a number. memops_arena does it this way. new_slice<u8> aligns its bytes only as a u8 needs, so unless they happen to start on a multiple of 16, the harness soon finds an offset that isn't a multiple of its alignment. Which one is right, and what would bump_make have to do for both to agree?
  • **bump_push_zero**: the same, with the bytes zeroed. Rewind, push again, and read the bytes before zeroing: what's there? (Not checked by the harness; write your own test.)
  • Temporary scopes: bump_temp_begin(b) returns a record of the mark and bump_temp_end(t) rewinds to it, like memops_arena_temp_begin and _end. The record keeps b, so bump_temp_begin takes a *bump in level, and the field is one too. What goes wrong if two scopes end out of order? (Not checked by the harness; write your own test.)

When it fails

FAIL in the scenario: push 4 bytes, align 4: 3 bytes of padding first gave 1, it should give 4

No rounding up at all: the offset is used as it is. The fuzz run is what finds the rest:

FAIL at operation 29 (seed 1): push(12, 2) gave offset 59, which isn't a multiple of 2
    debug it: build/dojo/arena/harness --seed 1 --stop 29
    with a breakpoint on dojo_stop_here, which runs just before that operation

That one rounds every alignment but 2, which the scenario never asks for. Run the harness under your debugger with those arguments and a breakpoint on dojo_stop_here, which runs just before that operation, and step into bump_push.

If the harness crashes instead, on an index past the end of the bytes say, index 257 out of bounds (length 256), the runner runs it again with --trace 1 and prints the operation that was running.

The playground. The kata's harness is dojo/7.arena/harness.rin, and the levels start from dojo/7.arena/level1.rin to level3.rin.

The dojo · block 8

Index, not pointer

dojo/8.index/play_index.rin

A linked list whose nodes live side by side in one vec, and link to each other by index: node 1's next is 0, a position in the vec, not an address. When the vec is full and grows, it moves: the nodes are copied to a bigger place, and the old one is let go. Every index is still right after the move, because an index says where a node is in the vec, wherever the vec is. A pointer says where the node is in memory, so it still points at the old place, and nothing tells you.

That's the whole idea, and it's everywhere in data-oriented code: an ECS keeps an entity's row by number because a growing column moves its rows, a mesh keeps triangles as three vertex indices, a scene graph keeps a parent index. A freed node goes on a free list and is used again before the vec grows, as in dojo 1.

The invariant: walking next from the head visits every live node once and ends at the tail; each node's prev is the node before it; and a node's index names it from the moment it's made until it's removed, however many times the vec moves in between.

In the course: 2.4 keeps an entity's table and row as numbers in its slot. It's why a pointer into 2.2's columns goes stale when a column grows, and why 2.5 says to keep handles and borrow pointers only to use them. The tables themselves are level pointers in a vec, so the vec can grow without moving a table: the other way out, for a thing that never has to move.

Watch it: the playground

python tools/dojo.py play index

Memory in the playground is an array of 16 cells, small enough to see whole in a debugger, and the list takes 2 cells of it, then 4, then 8. It keeps node b two ways: by its index, and by a *node to its cell. Then the list fills up and moves, and the program writes to b:

push_back 30 as c: the list is full
    the list moves from cells 0..2 to cells 2..6
    c is node 2
...
write 21 into b through its index, 1: cell 3 now
    nodes    0: 10, prev -, next 1 | 1: 21, prev 0, next 2 | 2: 30, prev 1, next -
    list     10 21 30
    memory   0..2 old copy: 10 20 | 2..6 the list: 10 21 30 .

After every step verify walks the links and checks that every node holds what the program last wrote to it. Put a breakpoint on broken, which it calls when something is wrong.

Then break on the line that writes 21 into b, set use_index to 0 in the watch window, and continue. The write goes through the kept pointer, into the old copy, and the list never sees it:

write 21 into b through what was kept, cell 1: where b was before the move
    ...
    memory   0..2 old copy: 10 21 | 2..6 the list: 10 20 30 .
    verify: node 1 holds 20, but the program last wrote 21 to it

Nothing crashes, and AddressSanitizer stays quiet too: the old copy is still memory the program owns, as a region's old blocks are until the region ends. The write is simply lost. The checker lets the playground keep that pointer because its cells are a fixed array inside the list, so to it nothing has moved. In the kata the nodes are in a vec, and it won't.

Do reps: the kata

You write list, made in the region level, with nodes and free each a *vec<...> in level. The idea is in list_remove: the two neighbours link to each other, past the node, and the node's index goes on the free list. The node's fields are read first, and it is marked free, before the calls that touch other nodes, since each of those ends what n may be used for:

list_remove: proc(l: *list, node: u32) -> option<u64> = {
    n: option<*list_node> = list_live(l, node);
    if (!n) {
        return option<u64>none();
    }
    prev: u32 = n*.prev;
    next: u32 = n*.next;
    value: u64 = n*.value;
    n*.alive = 0;
    if (prev != list_none) {
        list_at(l, prev)*.next = next;
    } else {
        l*.head = next;
    }
    if (next != list_none) {
        list_at(l, next)*.prev = prev;
    } else {
        l*.tail = prev;
    }

and the playground's lesson is one the checker holds you to, in list_insert_after:

// A new node between `node` and the one after it; list_none if `node` isn't
// in the list. Every pointer into the nodes is taken after list_take, which
// can move them.
list_insert_after: proc(l: *list, node: u32, value: u64) -> u32 = {

plus list_make(r), which sets head and tail to list_none, list_push_back, list_push_front, list_get, list_len, and the links to walk the list by: list_head, list_tail, list_next and list_prev. A link past either end is list_none, the largest u32, which no node ever gets.

python tools/dojo.py start index 2
python tools/dojo.py index

The harness runs the playground's steps as a scenario, then 20,000 random pushes, inserts, removes, reads and writes against a model that keeps the live nodes in list order. After every operation it walks your list both ways, list_head to the end by list_next, and list_tail back by list_prev, so a link left wrong is caught by the operation that left it. The list grows to about a thousand nodes, moving many times, and every node is checked by the index it was given. A freed index must be handed out again before a new one is made. The seeds give the same runs as rust-dod's dojo.

rin notes. Rust's kata has Option<u32> links; here a link is a u32, and list_none stands for none, as UINT32_MAX would in C. list_get returns an option<*u64 in level>, a pointer that is null for a node not in the list and tested before use, to read or to change the value; Rust's kata has get and get_mut. Helpers that hand out a node say the same, list_at a *list_node in level and list_live an option<*list_node in level>. The checker refuses a result that comes out of a vec in level and doesn't say so.

Level 4, variations. The same harness, different insides:

  • The free list through the nodes: a freed node's next is the next free node, and the list keeps first_free: u32. No free vec.
  • **A pointer kept across list_take**, which fails on purpose, twice: in list_insert_after, take list_live(l, node) once, before list_take, and write through it after. The checker stops it first: 'n' may be stale: 'l', which it was taken from, has been changed since; take it again. Now declare it n: option<*list_node in level>, a pointer good for as long as the region, which is true: the old block is still there. It builds. Which operation does the harness stop at, and where did the write go? Then put it back.
  • A list walker: list_each(l, visit), with visit a *proc(node: u32, value: u64) -> void, called head to tail. Read the next link before you call it: the checker counts a call through a proc pointer as one that may change the list. (Not checked by the harness; write your own test.)

When it fails

FAIL at operation 17 (seed 1): walking head to tail, list_next(3) gives 2, but 3 is the last of 3 nodes
    debug it: build/dojo/index/harness --seed 1 --stop 17
    with a breakpoint on dojo_stop_here, which runs just before that operation

A link pointing somewhere it shouldn't is usually a node from the free list that kept its old links, or a neighbour that wasn't told about a change: an insert at the tail that didn't move the tail, a remove that fixed next but not prev, or a write through a pointer kept in level past a move. Run the harness under your debugger with those arguments and a breakpoint on dojo_stop_here, which runs just before that operation, and look at the nodes the message names.

If the harness crashes instead, on a node past the end of the vec say, the runner runs it again with --trace 1 and prints the operation that was running, or says the crash came in the scenario, after the last step printed.

An index alone can't tell a removed node from the new node that took its place: a is node 0, and so is e after it. That's dojo 1's problem, and its answer, a generation beside the index, works here unchanged.

The playground. The kata's harness is dojo/8.index/harness.rin, and the levels start from dojo/8.index/level1.rin to level3.rin.

The dojo · block 9

Interning

dojo/9.interning/play_interning.rin

An interner gives each distinct key a small number, an id: the next one, 0, 1, 2, the first time it sees the key, and the same one every time after. Find it, or make it. The ids are dense, so they index plain vecs: the key of id 3 is keys[3], and whatever else belongs to that key can live at index 3 of its own vec.

Behind it is a hash table, written here by hand: a row of slots, each empty or holding an id. A key's hash says which slot to look in first. If that one holds another key, look in the next one, and the next, wrapping round at the end, until the key or an empty slot turns up. This is linear probing. A full table would make those runs long, and an absent key's run endless, so the table doubles before it's more than 3/4 full, and every id is put back where its key's hash says in the bigger table: a different slot, since the hash now picks from twice as many.

The invariant: every id is in exactly one slot, and a walk from its key's hash reaches that slot before it reaches an empty one; the table is never more than 3/4 full; and ids are 0 to len - 1, in the order their keys first came.

In the course: 2.4's kayan_table_for is an interner. Its keys are signatures and its ids are table indices, with std's hashmap doing the lookup, and std's hashmap is this same design: linear probing, a power of two, grown before 3/4. Here you write it. 2.6 then makes the lookup rare, by remembering where each add and remove leads, and dojo 10 practises that.

Watch it: the playground

python tools/dojo.py play interning

It interns the signatures of a few kinds of thing in a game, in a table of 8 slots that grows to 16, and prints every slot it looks at:

intern rock, signature 7
    slots looked at: 4 5 6; new: id 3, in slot 6
    table    1:turret 4:drone 5:player 6:rock, 4 of 8 slots used
...
intern bird, signature 15
    slots looked at: 1 2; not there
    7 ids would fill more than 3/4 of 8 slots: the table grows to 16, and every id
    goes where its key's hash says now
    slots looked at: 9 10; new: id 6, in slot 10
    table    4:rock 5:player 7:chest 8:tank 9:turret 10:bird 12:drone, 7 of 16 slots used

After every step verify checks the invariant; put a breakpoint on broken, which it calls when something is wrong.

Then break on the first interner_intern, set mix_hash to 0 in the watch window, and continue. The hash is now the key itself, so the first slot is the key's lowest bits. Those are the components nearly every kind has, position, sprite and health, since they were made first, so every kind starts at the same slot and the runs pile up:

intern chest, signature 135
    slots looked at: 7 0 1 2 3; new: id 4, in slot 3
...
slots looked at, in all: 41

against 17 with the hash. Nothing is wrong, only slow, so verify stays quiet. Flip it later instead, with ids already in the table, and verify complains straight away: the ids are where the old hash put them, and the new hash looks somewhere else. A table's hash can't change under it.

Do reps: the kata

You write interner, its table included, made in the region level, with slots and keys each a *vec<...> in level. The idea is in interner_intern:

interner_intern: proc(t: *interner, key: u64) -> u32 = {
    at: u64 = interner_slot_of(t, key);
    if (vec<u32>at(t*.slots, at)* != 0) {
        return vec<u32>at(t*.slots, at)* - 1;
    }
    if ((t*.keys*.length + 1) * 4 > t*.slots*.length * 3) {
        interner_grow(t);
        at = interner_slot_of(t, key);
    }

and the API around it:

interner_find: proc(t: *interner, key: u64) -> option<u32> = {
interner_key: proc(t: *interner, id: u32) -> u64 = {

plus interner_make(r) and interner_len. A slot holds id + 1, so that 0 can mean empty and key 0 is a key like any other. interner_make has 8 empty slots to push, which level 2's version leaves to you. Growing doesn't need a new vec, or a region: interner_grow clears slots, pushes twice as many zeros, and puts every id back.

The harness runs the playground's steps as a scenario, then 20,000 random interns and finds against a model, std's hashmap and a vec of the keys in order. The keys are the kinds an ECS's tables meet: small numbers, 0 among them; signatures with a few bits set; keys that differ only in their high bits; and any u64 at all. Ids must be dense, in the order keys were first interned, and never change; interner_find must agree with interner_intern; and interner_key must give the key back. It checks what the interner does, not how fast: an interner with no mixing in its hash passes, and the playground shows what it costs. The seeds give the same runs as rust-dod's dojo.

Level 4, variations. The same harness, different insides:

  • The hash beside the id: two u32s a slot, the id and the low bits of its key's hash, so a run compares hashes and reads keys only when they match, and interner_grow never hashes a key again.
  • Robin Hood: on the way along a run, an id that is closer to its home slot than the new one gives its slot up and moves on instead. The longest run gets much shorter. How does interner_find stop early on an absent key?
  • Grow at 1/2: what happens to the slots looked at in the playground, and to the memory?

When it fails

FAIL in the scenario: find turret gave none, it should give 2

A key that was interned and can't be found usually means interner_grow copied the slots across instead of putting each id back by its key's hash: in a table twice the size, a key's run starts somewhere else. A run that steps off the end without wrapping stops the program with rin runtime: vec index out of bounds, and the runner runs it again with --trace 1 to show the operation that was running. If the run stops and never ends, the table filled up: a lookup for a key that isn't there walks round and round, never meeting an empty slot to stop at. Break into it in your debugger and look at slots.

In the fuzz run, a failure says which operation and seed, as in the other blocks; run the harness under your debugger with the --seed and --stop it gives, and a breakpoint on dojo_stop_here.

The dojo · block 10

Memoized edges

dojo/10.edges/play_edges.rin

In an archetype ECS, an entity that gains a component moves to the table whose signature has one more bit. Finding that table by its signature is a search. But a game moves entities between the same few tables over and over: a drone catches fire, the fire goes out, it catches fire again. So each table remembers where each component leads, once a move has found it:

node 3 {position velocity health}  --+burning-->  node 4
node 4 {position velocity health burning}  --burning-->  node 3

The first move from 3 with burning searches, and writes the answer on both nodes: an add edge one way and a remove edge back. Every move after that, in either direction, follows an edge. Remembering the answer to a slow question is memoizing, and the nodes and their edges are the archetype graph that flecs is built around.

The invariant: every known edge leads to the node one component away, and that node has the edge back. Each move that changes a signature searches at most once; after that, both directions are edges.

In the course: 2.6 adds add_edges and remove_edges to each table, and moves entities along them.

Watch it: the playground

python tools/dojo.py play edges

A drone gains and loses components, eight nodes at most. Each move says where it went and how, and the graph is drawn twice:

catches fire: node 3 -> 4 {position velocity health burning}, by a lookup
the fire goes out: node 4 -> 3 {position velocity health}, by an edge
catches fire again: node 3 -> 4 {position velocity health burning}, by an edge
...
    node 3 {position velocity health}: +burning 4, -velocity 5, -health 2
...
moves that looked up a node by signature: 7; that followed an edge: 4

Step through it: break on with and watch the two edges get written after find_or_make. verify runs after every move and prints any edge that leads to the wrong node or has no edge back. Then flip the switch at the top, memo, to 0 and run it again. The drone goes to the same nodes, but nothing is remembered: eleven moves, eleven lookups, and every node drawn with no edges known. With a few hundred tables and a game moving thousands of entities a frame, that's the difference.

Do reps: the kata

You write graph, made in the region level, with nodes a *vec<graph_node> in level. The move that adds a component:

graph_with: proc(g: *graph, node: u32, id: u32) -> u32 = {
    signature: u64 = graph_signature(g, node);
    if ((signature & graph_bit(id)) != 0) {
        return node;
    }
    edge: u32 = vec<graph_node>at(g*.nodes, cast(node, u64))*.add[id];
    if (edge != 0) {
        g*.hits += 1;
        return edge - 1;
    }
    to: u32 = graph_find_or_make(g, signature | graph_bit(id));
    // graph_find_or_make can make a node, and the vec can move them all to
    // grow, so both pointers are taken after it.
    vec<graph_node>at(g*.nodes, cast(node, u64))*.add[id] = to + 1;
    vec<graph_node>at(g*.nodes, cast(to, u64))*.remove[id] = node + 1;
    return to;
}

and its mirror, graph_without, plus graph_make(r) (node 0 is the empty signature, and level 2's version leaves that node to you), graph_signature, graph_len, graph_lookups (moves that searched) and graph_hits (moves that followed an edge). The edges are stored as one more than the node, so a zeroed node knows none, 64 each way:

graph_node: struct = {
    signature: u64;
    // add[id] is one more than the node with component id added, once a move
    // has looked it up, so 0 means not known yet; remove[id] is the same, with
    // it removed.
    add: [64]u32;
    remove: [64]u32;
}

The harness runs the playground's moves as a scenario, then 20,000 random moves from random nodes, with ids up to 63, against a model that knows each node's signature and which edges a graph that writes both directions knows by now. After every move it checks the node, its signature, and both counters: a known edge is a hit, any other move that changes the signature is one lookup, and a move that changes nothing (adding what the node has) is neither. The seeds give the same runs as rust-dod's dojo.

rin notes. The comment in graph_with is the one to remember: a pointer into nodes taken before graph_find_or_make can point at memory the vec has moved out of, so the edges are written through fresh pointers after it. Here the checker holds you to it: keep one across that call, and it says 'n' may be stale: 'g.nodes', which it was taken from, has been changed since; take it again. That's dojo 8's lesson, and 2.6 has the same comment over its slots.

Level 4, variations. The same harness, different insides:

  • One hash map of edges, a *hashmap<u64, u32> in level from hashmap<u64, u32>make(r), keyed by node * 128 + id * 2 + adding, instead of two 64-wide arrays per node. Which takes less memory with 300 tables, and which is faster to follow?
  • A hash map for the slow path: graph_find_or_make searches every node. Keep a hashmap<u64, u32> from signature to node, as 2.4 does, or build one in dojo 9.
  • Removing a node. An ECS that deletes empty tables must forget every edge into them. Which nodes have edges into node n? (Not checked by the harness; write your own test.)

When it fails

FAIL in the scenario: lookups and hits gave 5 1, it should give 4 2

Five lookups where the model counts four: the fire going out searched, instead of following the edge back that catching fire should have written. The edge back is the one people forget, or write on the wrong node: the move from 3 to 4 sets node 3's add edge and node 4's remove edge.

The scenario's ids stop at 3. The fuzz run's go up to 63, and a failure there says which operation and seed:

FAIL at operation 9 (seed 1): with(3, 63) gave node 6, which is {2 3 31}; from {2 3} it should be {2 3 63}
    debug it: build/dojo/edges/harness --seed 1 --stop 9
    with a breakpoint on dojo_stop_here, which runs just before that operation

That's a bit made in 32 bits, 1 shl id on a u32: bit 63 lands on bit 31. rin masks a shift's amount to the width of what it shifts, so nothing is undefined and --sanitize stays quiet. Run the harness under your debugger with those arguments and a breakpoint on dojo_stop_here, and step into the move.

But a game moves entities between the same few tables over and6// over, so each table remembers where each component leads: an add edge per7// component, and a remove edge back. The tables and their edges form a graph,8// the archetype graph of the course's 2.6.9//10// Here the nodes are bare signatures, eight at most, over four components. A11// drone gains and loses components, and each move prints the node it went to12// and whether it took a lookup or followed an edge. verify runs after every13// move: every known edge must lead to the node with that one component added14// (or removed) and have its edge back, and the drone's node must have the15// components the drone has. Put a breakpoint inside its failure branch to stop16// where the graph goes wrong.17//18// The switch: set memo to 0 and run it again. Nothing is remembered: the19// drone goes to the same nodes, but every move is a lookup. It's a global,20// read on every move, so a debugger can flip it mid-run too: stop on the21// first `lose` in main, set it to 0 in the watch window, and continue.22 23import "std/print.rin"24 25memo: b32 = 1;26 27names: [4]^const char = { "position", "velocity", "health", "burning" };28position: const u32 = 0;29velocity: const u32 = 1;30health: const u32 = 2;31burning: const u32 = 3;32 33bit: proc(id: u32) -> u64 = {34    return 1'u64 shl cast(id, u64);35}36 37node: struct = {38    signature: u64;39    // add[id] is one more than the node with component id added, once a move40    // has found it, so 0 means not known yet; remove[id] the same, with it41    // removed.42    add: [4]u32;43    remove: [4]u32;44}45 46graph: struct = {47    nodes: [8]node;48    count: u32;49    lookups: u32;50    edges: u32;51}52 53// The slow path: search every node for the signature, and make one if none54// has it.55find_or_make: proc(g: *graph, signature: u64) -> u32 = {56    g*.lookups += 1;57    for (i: u32 = 0; i < g*.count; i += 1) {58        if (g*.nodes[i].signature == signature) {59            return i;60        }61    }62    g*.nodes[g*.count] = { .signature = signature };63    g*.count += 1;64    return g*.count - 1;65}66 67with: proc(g: *graph, from: u32, id: u32) -> u32 = {68    if (memo && g*.nodes[from].add[id] != 0) {69        g*.edges += 1;70        return g*.nodes[from].add[id] - 1;71    }72    to: u32 = find_or_make(g, g*.nodes[from].signature | bit(id));73    if (memo) {74        g*.nodes[from].add[id] = to + 1;75        g*.nodes[to].remove[id] = from + 1;76    }77    return to;78}79 80without: proc(g: *graph, from: u32, id: u32) -> u32 = {81    if (memo && g*.nodes[from].remove[id] != 0) {82        g*.edges += 1;83        return g*.nodes[from].remove[id] - 1;84    }85    to: u32 = find_or_make(g, g*.nodes[from].signature & ~bit(id));86    if (memo) {87        g*.nodes[from].remove[id] = to + 1;88        g*.nodes[to].add[id] = from + 1;89    }90    return to;91}92 93print_names: proc(signature: u64) -> void = {94    printfmt("{");95    first: b32 = 1;96    for (id: u32 = 0; id < 4; id += 1) {97        if ((signature & bit(id)) != 0) {98            if (!first) {99                printfmt(" ");100            }101            printfmt("{}", names[id]);102            first = 0;103        }104    }105    printfmt("}");106}107 108drone: struct = {109    node: u32;110    // What the drone has, kept apart from the graph: verify checks the two111    // agree.112    has: u64;113}114 115// Every edge leads to the node one component away, and comes back; and the116// drone's node is the one with its components.117verify: proc(g: *graph, d: *drone) -> void = {118    for (n: u32 = 0; n < g*.count; n += 1) {119        here: *node = g*.nodes[n]&;120        for (id: u32 = 0; id < 4; id += 1) {121            if (here*.add[id] != 0) {122                there: *node = g*.nodes[here*.add[id] - 1]&;123                if (there*.signature != (here*.signature | bit(id)) || there*.remove[id] != n + 1) {124                    printfmt("verify: node {}'s +{} edge leads to node {} ", n, names[id], here*.add[id] - 1);125                    print_names(there*.signature);126                    printfmt("\n");127                }128            }129            if (here*.remove[id] != 0) {130                there: *node = g*.nodes[here*.remove[id] - 1]&;131                if (there*.signature != (here*.signature & ~bit(id)) || there*.add[id] != n + 1) {132                    printfmt("verify: node {}'s -{} edge leads to node {} ", n, names[id], here*.remove[id] - 1);133                    print_names(there*.signature);134                    printfmt("\n");135                }136            }137        }138    }139    if (g*.nodes[d*.node].signature != d*.has) {140        printfmt("verify: the drone has ");141        print_names(d*.has);142        printfmt(", but its node {} is ", d*.node);143        print_names(g*.nodes[d*.node].signature);144        printfmt("\n");145    }146}147 148report: proc(g: *graph, d: *drone, what: ^const char, from: u32, lookups: u32) -> void = {149    printfmt("{}: node {} -> {} ", what, from, d*.node);150    print_names(g*.nodes[d*.node].signature);151    if (g*.lookups > lookups) {152        printfmt(", by a lookup\n");153    } else {154        printfmt(", by an edge\n");155    }156    verify(g, d);157}158 159gain: proc(g: *graph, d: *drone, id: u32, what: ^const char) -> void = {160    from: u32 = d*.node;161    lookups: u32 = g*.lookups;162    d*.node = with(g, d*.node, id);163    d*.has = d*.has | bit(id);164    report(g, d, what, from, lookups);165}166 167lose: proc(g: *graph, d: *drone, id: u32, what: ^const char) -> void = {168    from: u32 = d*.node;169    lookups: u32 = g*.lookups;170    d*.node = without(g, d*.node, id);171    d*.has = d*.has & ~bit(id);172    report(g, d, what, from, lookups);173}174 175draw: proc(g: *graph) -> void = {176    for (n: u32 = 0; n < g*.count; n += 1) {177        here: *node = g*.nodes[n]&;178        printfmt("    node {} ", n);179        print_names(here*.signature);180        printfmt(":");181        known: u32 = 0;182        for (id: u32 = 0; id < 4; id += 1) {183            if (here*.add[id] != 0) {184                printfmt("{} +{} {}", known > 0 ? "," : "", names[id], here*.add[id] - 1);185                known += 1;186            }187        }188        for (id: u32 = 0; id < 4; id += 1) {189            if (here*.remove[id] != 0) {190                printfmt("{} -{} {}", known > 0 ? "," : "", names[id], here*.remove[id] - 1);191                known += 1;192            }193        }194        if (known == 0) {195            printfmt(" no edges known");196        }197        printfmt("\n");198    }199}200 201main: proc() -> i32 = {202    g: graph = {};203    g.count = 1;204    d: drone = {};205    printfmt("the drone starts at node 0 {}\n", "{}");206    gain(g&, d&, position, "gains position");207    gain(g&, d&, velocity, "gains velocity");208    gain(g&, d&, health, "gains health");209    gain(g&, d&, burning, "catches fire");210    lose(g&, d&, burning, "the fire goes out");211    gain(g&, d&, burning, "catches fire again");212    lose(g&, d&, burning, "the fire goes out");213    printfmt("the graph so far:\n");214    draw(g&);215    lose(g&, d&, velocity, "stops");216    gain(g&, d&, burning, "catches fire");217    gain(g&, d&, velocity, "moves again");218    lose(g&, d&, burning, "the fire goes out");219    printfmt("the graph:\n");220    draw(g&);221    printfmt("moves that looked up a node by signature: {}; that followed an edge: {}\n", g.lookups, g.edges);222    return 0;223}

The dojo · block 11

A reflection walk

dojo/11.reflect/play_reflect.rin

A reflect record lists a struct's fields: each one's name, where its bytes start in the struct, how many there are, and its type, with the type's own record when it's a struct too. rin's compiler writes one for every struct: lamp<> is lamp's. With records, one piece of code can list, read, write and compare the fields of any type it's handed, by name: an inspector, an editor, a save file, a network diff. It never names the type. It walks the bytes by the record:

"at.y" in a lamp:  lamp's field at, offset 8  ->  vec2's field y, offset 4  ->  bytes 12..16

Each offset counts from the start of the field's own struct, so a path adds them up as it goes down. And an offset is the record's to say, not something to work out from the sizes before it: a u8 followed by an f32 leaves 3 bytes of padding, and the f32 starts at 4.

The invariant: the walk reads and writes exactly the bytes the compiler gave each field. Read by path, every field is what the struct holds.

In the course: 2.7 prints any entity field by field from records. The Advanced lesson 5 builds an inspector, and an editor's write by name.

Watch it: the playground

python tools/dojo.py play reflect

It prints a lamp's record, walks the lamp by it, changes fields by path, and diffs the lamp with how it was:

a lamp's record: 20 bytes
    on: offset 0, size 1, u8
    power: offset 4, size 4, f32
    at: offset 8, size 8, a struct
    flicker: offset 16, size 4, f32, hidden
...
set at.x to 5.00: true
diff with the lamp before: power at.x
set flicker to 0.50: true
diff with the lamp before: power at.x

The walk reads the lamp through its bytes, with a few trusted procs at the top of the file for what safe code can't do, read four bytes as an f32, index a C string, see a struct as bytes. Step through it: break on find and watch offset add up. verify runs after every step and checks every f32 the walk reads against the field read directly, l.power and so on. Then flip the switch at the top, use_record_offsets, to 0 and run it again. The walk adds up the sizes before each field instead, as if nothing had padding: power is read from offset 1, three padding bytes and one byte of the real power, and writing at.x lands on power. The record printed above it still says 4.

Do reps: the kata

You write the walk, over the compiler's records, reflect and reflect_field from std/reflect.rin. Safe code cannot index a C string or read four bytes as an f32, so the kata itself stays checked and gets those from outside. The harness gives it four trusted helpers, each a few lines: walk_cstr_at(s, i), walk_cstr_append(dst, at, src), walk_read_f32(bytes, at) and walk_write_f32(bytes, at, value). And it asks the record for field i with std's reflect_field_at(type, i), which says when it is past the end, instead of indexing reflect_fields(type), and compares type names with reflect_cstr_equal.

First, every field a tool shows, by path, walking into the ones that are structs. The path so far is a slice of the leaf's own text:

walk_leaves: proc(type: *const reflect, prefix: []const c8, base: u64, out: *vec<walk_leaf>) -> void = {
    for (i: u64 = 0; i < reflect_field_count(type); i += 1) {
        f: option<*const reflect_field> = reflect_field_at(type, i);
        if (!f) {
            continue;
        }
        if (reflect_field_has_attr(f, "hidden")) {
            continue;
        }
        leaf: walk_leaf = { .offset = base + f*.offset, .size = f*.size };
        for (k: u64 = 0; k < prefix.length; k += 1) {
            leaf.path.text[k] = prefix[k];
        }
        end: u64 = walk_cstr_append(leaf.path.text[0..48], prefix.length, f*.name);
        if (reflect_is_struct(f*.info)) {
            leaf.path.text[end] = '.';
            walk_leaves(unwrap(f*.info), leaf.path.text[0..end + 1], leaf.offset, out);
        } else {
            _ = vec<walk_leaf>push(out, leaf);
        }
    }
}

and on it and on a walk down one path, walk_find, the procs the harness calls. The two that make a list make it in a region the caller names, r: region R:

walk_paths: proc(r: region R, type: *const reflect) -> *vec<walk_path> in R = {
walk_diff: proc(r: region R, type: *const reflect, a: []const u8, b: []const u8) -> *vec<walk_path> in R = {
walk_get_f32: proc(type: *const reflect, bytes: []const u8, path: ^const char) -> option<f32> = {
walk_set_f32: proc(type: *const reflect, bytes: []u8, path: ^const char, value: f32) -> b32 = {

A path is a walk_path, 48 characters at most, ending in a zero. A hidden field is left out of walk_paths and walk_diff, with everything inside it, but a path still reaches it: hiding is for tools that list, not for code that asks by name. walk_get_f32 and walk_set_f32 refuse a path that names a struct, a u8, or nothing.

levelyou writetarget
1walk_leaves, the walk, in an otherwise finished file4:00
2every proc body; the types and signatures are given15:00
3the whole file, from a blank page18:00
python tools/dojo.py start reflect 2
python tools/dojo.py reflect

The harness's test types have the traps in them: lamp has padding after on: u8, room has a lamp inside it (paths three deep, offsets added twice), and a hidden draft: vec2. It runs the playground's steps as a scenario, then 20,000 random reads, writes and diffs of a room by path, each checked against the same fields reached directly, r.light.at.x and so on. The paths include ones that name a struct, a u8, or nothing: light.atx.x, corner.x.y, light.. The seeds give the same runs as rust-dod's dojo.

rin notes. rin's compiler writes the records; Rust's kata gets them from a macro in its harness, the way 2.7 makes them, and has paths return Vec<String> where this one fills a *vec<walk_path> in R in the caller's region. The harness opens the region frame once per fuzz operation for it, so what a walk allocates is gone after it. walk_read_f32 and walk_write_f32 cut a field's bytes out with a slice, bytes[at..at + 4], so a wrong offset past the end stops the program instead of reading past the value, and copy them through a local f32 with memcpy, so a field at any offset can be read without casting to a pointer that may be misaligned.

Level 4, variations. The same harness, different insides:

  • **walk_find by recursion**: find the field the first name names, and recurse into its record with the rest of the path. Safe code can't move a ^const char along, so the rest of the path is an index, a start passed to a helper.
  • Paths without a vec of leaves: one walk that does both jobs, with out, and a and b for a diff, passed down to each leaf: walk_paths keeps every leaf, and walk_diff the ones whose bytes differ. A callback looks like the way to do it, and it costs the harness its build. The checker can't see through a proc pointer, so it says of what the harness hands walk_diff: this was taken from 'before', and 'walk_diff' can move it through a global: take it after the call.
  • A tiny text format: write a value as path = value lines and read it back. That's a save file and a network message. (Not checked by the harness; write your own test.)

When it fails

FAIL at operation 4 (seed 1): set_f32("light.", -50.25) returns true, it should return false
    debug it: build/dojo/reflect/harness --seed 1 --stop 4
    with a breakpoint on dojo_stop_here, which runs just before that operation

The name after the dot is empty, and it matched a field anyway: a name compare that stops at the end of the shorter of the two finds range for nothing, and at for atx. Run the harness under your debugger with those arguments and a breakpoint on dojo_stop_here, then step through walk_find, watching each name and offset. If it crashes instead, the runner runs it again with --trace 1 and prints the operation that was running.

The playground. The kata's harness is dojo/11.reflect/harness.rin, and the levels start from dojo/11.reflect/level1.rin to level3.rin.

The dojo · block 12

A watermark

dojo/12.watermark/play_watermark.rin

A query keeps the list of tables it matches, so a system doesn't search for them every frame. Tables are only ever added, at the end, and never removed. So the query remembers how many tables it has looked at, its watermark, and an update looks only at the tables past it:

tables   0 P   1 PV   2 PVH  |  3 PVHB   4 H
                             ^ movers has checked 3: an update looks at 3 and 4

A frame with no new tables costs one comparison, and each query looks at each table once, ever. It works for anything that only grows at the end: a log read by several readers, a list of events, the lines of a file being written.

The invariant: a query lists exactly the tables below its watermark that match, each once, in order, and it has looked at each of them once.

In the course: 3.1 builds the query and its checked count, and 3.2 updates every system's query at the start of every frame, which is what makes the watermark matter.

Watch it: the playground

python tools/dojo.py play watermark

It makes tables a few at a time, and updates two queries: movers, all {Position Velocity}, and healthy, all {Health}, none {Burning}. After each step it draws the tables, and under them what each query has looked at, with a | at its watermark:

update movers: it looks at tables 3 and 4 only
    table     0    1    2    3    4
    has       P    PV   PVH  PVHB H
    movers    -    yes  yes  yes  -    |    checked 5, scanned 5, tables 1 2 3
    healthy   |                             checked 0, scanned 0, tables none

scanned counts every table an update has looked at. With the watermark it always equals checked. Then verify checks both queries against the tables and prints what's wrong; break inside its if to stop when it fires.

Step through it: break on query_update and watch from, checked and found. Then flip the switch at the top, use_watermark, to 0, and run it again. Every update starts from table 0, and the second update of movers, with nothing new, finds tables 1 and 2 again:

movers    -    yes  yes  |    checked 3, scanned 6, tables 1 2 1 2
verify: movers lists tables 1 2 1 2; it should list 1 2
verify: movers has looked at 6 tables to check 3; each should be looked at once

A system walking that list would run twice over the same entities, and the work grows with every frame. The switch is a global, read on every update, so a debugger can flip it mid-run too: stop on query_update, set it to 0 in the watch window, and continue.

Do reps: the kata

You write query:

query: struct = {
    all: u64;
    none: u64;
    // The tables that match, by index, in the order they were found.
    tables: *vec<u32> in level;
    // The watermark: tables 0 to checked - 1 have been looked at.
    checked: u64;
    // How many tables query_update has looked at, ever. With the watermark,
    // each table once.
    scanned: u64;
}

and its update, which is given the world's tables as their signatures, a []const u64, since it only reads them:

query_update: proc(q: *query, signatures: []const u64) -> void = {

plus query_make(r, all, none), which makes the query and its list of tables in the region level, query_tables (the matching tables, in increasing order, a []u32 in level), query_checked and query_scanned. A table matches when its signature has every bit of all and no bit of none.

levelyou writetarget
1query_update, in an otherwise finished file2:00
2every proc body; the fields and signatures are given5:00
3the whole file, from a blank page7:00
python tools/dojo.py start watermark 2
python tools/dojo.py watermark

The harness runs the playground's steps as a scenario, then 20,000 random operations: tables made with random signatures, four queries with random masks updated at random, and now and then one replaced by a new query, which must start from nothing. The new one is made in the region, and the old one stays in level until the run ends, which is what an arena does. A model keeps, for each query, the tables that match among the ones it has been updated over. After every update the query must have checked the whole list, list exactly the model's tables, and have scanned each table once. Some none masks have two bits, so "none of these" and "not all of these" give different answers. The seeds give the same runs as rust-dod's dojo.

Level 4, variations. The same harness, different insides:

  • **A while loop, and scanned added once**: scanned grows by the number of new tables, which is known before the loop starts.
  • Push, don't poll: flecs does the reverse. When the world makes a table, it tells every query, and query_update has nothing left to do. What does the world have to keep, and what happens to a query made after the table? (Not checked by the harness; write your own test.)
  • A table that can go away: the list keeps a tombstone where a removed table was, a signature no query matches. What must a query do with a table it already lists? (Not checked by the harness.)

When it fails

The scenario catches the common mistakes first:

FAIL in the scenario: make tables 3 and 4, update movers: tables gave 1 2 0, it should give 1 2 3

That's a count of the new tables pushed as if it were the table's index: a loop that counts from 0 over the tables past the watermark has to add checked back. A failure in the fuzz run says where:

FAIL at operation 27 (seed 1): after query_update, query 1 (all {0 5}, none {0 6}): it lists 1, the model 0; the first difference is at position 0: table 1, where the model has nothing
    debug it: build/dojo/watermark/harness --seed 1 --stop 27
    with a breakpoint on dojo_stop_here, which runs just before that operation

That one tested none the way it tested all, (signature & none) != none, which is "not every bit of none" rather than "no bit of it". It only differs when none has more than one bit. Run the harness under your debugger with those arguments and a breakpoint on dojo_stop_here, then step into query_update and look at the table it lists.

The playground. The kata's harness is dojo/12.watermark/harness.rin, and the levels start from dojo/12.watermark/level1.rin to level3.rin.

The dojo · block 13

A dispatch table

dojo/13.dispatch/play_dispatch.rin

A frame is a list of systems run in order, and the list is data: a name and a pointer to a proc for each, in an array the program changes as it runs. Adding, removing, reordering or switching off a system is an edit to the array, not to the code that calls them:

schedule  0 move   1 shoot   2 damage   3 die
a frame   for each enabled system, in order: entry.run(world)

The order is a statement about data: a system that reads what another writes runs after it. damage writes health and die reads it, so damage goes before die, and a drone dies in the frame its health runs out. The same table drives an interpreter's opcodes, a menu's actions, a network protocol's message handlers: a number or a name picks a proc.

The invariant: a run calls every enabled system once, in the list's order, and nothing else. Edits keep the order of everything they don't touch.

In the course: 3.2 makes a system a name, a query and a proc pointer, and runs a schedule of them each frame, and 3.4's game has nine, each placed after what it reads.

Watch it: the playground

python tools/dojo.py play dispatch

A drone flies at a turret. Four systems, move, shoot, damage and die, run frame by frame, and between frames the program edits the schedule: shoot is switched off while the turret reloads, back on, and removed at the end. Each system is made in the region level, and the schedule's array holds pointers to them, for the reason the kata explains below. After each step it prints the schedule or the world:

frame 2
    ran       move shoot damage die
    drone     4 from the turret, health 60, alive
switch shoot off: the turret is reloading
    schedule  move (shoot off) damage die
frame 3
    ran       move damage die

Then verify checks that the drone is dead exactly when its health has run out; break inside its if to stop when it fires. Step through it: break on schedule_run and step into each call, through the pointer, into the system.

Then flip the switch at the top, in_order, to 0, and run it again. damage is added at the end of the schedule instead of before die, so die reads the health from before this frame's damage:

frame 5
    ran       move shoot die damage
    drone     0 from the turret, health -20, alive
    verify: the drone has health -20 and is still alive

and it dies in frame 6, a frame late. A frame late is a drone that fires once more after it should be dead, or a death sound one frame after the explosion. The switch is a global, read when damage is added, so a debugger can flip it too: stop on the first line of main, set it to 0 in the watch window, and continue.

Do reps: the kata

You write schedule. A system is a plain pointer to a proc, which takes the harness's ctx. Here the safe subset changes the design: a C string and a proc pointer are both pointers without a region, so a struct holding them is one safe code cannot write, hold by value or make with new. So the name and the proc you are given go behind a pointer into the region level, made by the kata's one trusted proc, and never change:

system_proc: alias = *proc(c: *ctx) -> void;

// A system as it was given: its name and its proc. Made in the region by
// schedule_system_make, the kata's one trusted proc.
schedule_system: struct = {
    name: ^const char;
    run: system_proc;
}

schedule_system_make: proc(r: region level, name: ^const char, run: system_proc) -> *schedule_system in level = {
    unsafe {
        s: *schedule_system in level = cast(memops_arena_push_zero(r, sizeof(schedule_system), alignof(schedule_system)),
            *schedule_system in level);
        s*.name = name;
        s*.run = run;
        return s;
    }
}

What does change, enabled and calls, sits beside that pointer in an entry, and the schedule is a vec of entries, in the order they run:

// A system in the schedule: which, whether it runs, and how many times
// schedule_run has called it.
schedule_entry: struct = {
    system: *schedule_system in level;
    enabled: b32;
    calls: u32;
}

schedule: struct = {
    // In the order they run.
    systems: *vec<schedule_entry> in level;
}

A proc that makes a system takes the region, since a struct can't keep it:

schedule_insert_before: proc(s: *schedule, r: region level, before: ^const char, name: ^const char,
                             run: system_proc) -> b32 = {
schedule_run: proc(s: *schedule, c: *ctx) -> void = {

plus schedule_make(r), schedule_add(s, r, name, run) (at the end), schedule_remove(s, name), schedule_set_enabled(s, name, on), schedule_len and schedule_name(s, i) (every name, enabled or not, in order), and schedule_calls(s, name). schedule_insert_before, schedule_remove and schedule_set_enabled return 0, and change nothing, when there's no system by that name. Names are C strings, compared with dojo_cstr_equal, since strcmp is C's and safe code can't call it.

The harness has twelve systems, input to save, and each one writes its number in the ctx's log when it's called, so after a run the log says what ran, in what order, and through which proc. It runs a short scenario, then 20,000 random adds, inserts, removes, enables, disables and runs against a model that keeps the schedule as a plain list. After every operation the order and every count must match the model, and every run must log exactly the enabled systems, in order. The seeds give the same runs as rust-dod's dojo.

rin notes. Rust's kata has order(), which returns the names as a Vec; here schedule_len and schedule_name give them one at a time, so nothing is allocated to read them.

Level 4, variations. The same harness, different insides:

  • A fixed array: [16]schedule_entry and a count instead of a vec, as the playground has. An array starts as zeros, so the entry's system has to be an option<*schedule_system in level>, tested before use. What happens on the seventeenth add?
  • Struct of arrays: the system pointers, the flags and the counts in three vecs, one place per system. The names and procs stay together behind their pointer, since a vec<^const char> is refused: a raw pointer lasts only for a call. schedule_insert_before and schedule_remove must move all three the same way.
  • Reads and writes: each system declares bitmasks of what it reads and writes, and schedule_insert_before refuses a place where a system would read something a later one writes. Then: which neighbours could run at the same time, on two threads? (Not checked by the harness; write your own test.)

A system with data of its own is one more pointer beside the proc pointer, handed back on every call: 3.4's kayan_system has a ctx: option<*game in level> for that, typed so the checker knows what it points at, which is what a closure is, written out.

When it fails

The scenario catches the common mistakes first:

FAIL in the scenario: run: what ran gave move, it should give move damage die

That run stopped at the first disabled system, collide: a break where a skip was meant. A failure in the fuzz run says where:

FAIL at operation 110 (seed 1): after schedule_remove(die), schedule_calls(damage) is 0; the model counts 2 since it was added
    debug it: build/dojo/dispatch/harness --seed 1 --stop 110
    with a breakpoint on dojo_stop_here, which runs just before that operation

That kata kept the counts in a vec of their own, the struct of arrays above, and schedule_remove popped the last count rather than the removed system's, so the counts after it shifted one place. Run the harness under your debugger with those arguments and a breakpoint on dojo_stop_here, then step into schedule_remove and watch both vecs.

If the harness crashes instead, on a proc pointer that was never set, say, the runner runs it again with --trace 1 and prints the operation that was running, or says the crash came in the scenario, after the last step printed.

The playground. The kata's harness is dojo/13.dispatch/harness.rin, and the levels start from dojo/13.dispatch/level1.rin to level3.rin.
