Advanced · seven lessons

Layout and SIMD

docs/README.md

Seven lessons for after Build an ECS. The course builds the ECS. These go underneath it, to the memory and the machine code:

  • Lesson 1, aos vs soa. The same particles in three layouts: what a loop fetches per cache line, what noalias promises the compiler, which loops it vectorizes, what the bounds checks cost, and how to check that in the assembly.
  • Lessons 2 to 6 build an archetype ECS again, compressed into five steps, and end with a small game. They came first and move fast. After the course, read them as a recap, or as a second take on the same design. Lesson 4 builds the world in includes/kayan.rin, and lessons 5 and 6 import it unchanged.
  • Lesson 7, layout follows access. Four layouts under streams and under random lookups, timed, and how an ECS decides where each component lives.
  • Lesson 0, from kayan, reviews the C kayan these lessons started from: what they kept from it, what they changed, and why.
lessonabout
0from kayanwhat was kept from the C kayan, what changed, and why
1aos vs soathe same particles in three layouts, what a loop fetches, and what SIMD needs
2archetype tableone table: columns, rows, spawn, swap-remove, systems over slices
3many archetypesone table type for every archetype: ids, signatures, queries
4entity handlesgenerational handles, slots, moving between archetypes
5inspectorprinting and editing any entity from reflection records
6kayana small game, and deferring structural changes to a command buffer
7access patternsfour layouts under streams and lookups, and how an ECS decides

How to read them

Read each lesson's .rin file from the top. It opens with the problem it solves, and the code follows in the order it runs. Then run it and read the output against the code: every lesson prints what it does, step by step. The guides here give the background that doesn't fit in a file header, and end with exercises.

Every lesson is in rin's safe subset. The memory they share lives in a region, level, that main opens; the checker follows every pointer into it. Two things it cannot follow stay in code marked for it: unsafe { } blocks over raw bytes, and proc[unsafe] kernels that make a noalias promise, which are called from inside unsafe { }.

Timings only mean something in a Release build. Debug does not optimize, and every slice index is a function call. Release keeps the bounds checks: they run in every build, because the safety rules rest on them. Lesson 1's guide shows how to build one, what the checks cost, and what to look for in the disassembly.

Advanced · lesson 0 · review

From kayan

docs/0_from_kayan.md

kayan is a sketch of an archetype entity component system in C, about 200 lines in src/kayan.h, with haikal generating its containers. These lessons start from its idea and rebuild the rest. This page says what was kept, what was changed, and why, so the lessons can be read as a review of it as much as a rewrite.

What kayan does

Components are bits in an enum, positions = 1 << 0, velocities = 1 << 1 and so on. Each archetype is a C struct written by hand (A, B, C, D) that starts with an ArchetypeHeader and then holds one haikal Array_T per component. The header has a u64 signature and a Map_u64 from column name to the column's byte offset in the struct.

A query walks an array of void * pointing at the archetypes, reads each header, and tests (signature & want) == want. For a match it looks up "positions" and "velocities" in the offset map, adds the offsets to the struct's address, and runs the loop over the two columns.

Kept

  • An archetype is a struct of arrays. Each component is a contiguous column and every entity in the table has every column. That is the whole point, and kayan had it right from the start.
  • A signature is a u64 of component bits, and a query is the test (signature & all) == all. Lesson 3 adds a none mask beside it.
  • Arenas for all of it. Nothing in these lessons is freed one at a time. In safe rin an arena is a region: level: region; names it, main opens it, and the whole of it ends at one closing brace.

Changed

  • One table type for every archetype (lesson 3). kayan needs a new C struct, a new signature line and new offset-map lines for every archetype. Here an archetype is data: a signature, and the world makes its table the first time something needs it (lesson 4).
  • Columns by component id, not by name (lesson 3). kayan hashes the strings "positions" and "velocities" on every query. Here a table's columns are an array indexed by component id, so finding one is an index. Names are kept for tools, through reflection (lesson 5).
  • The signature comes from the columns (lesson 3). In kayan they are written separately and can disagree. In D they do: it has positions and velocities columns, but its signature is health | damage | alive, so the movement query never visits it.
  • A row is added and removed in one place (lesson 2). kayan appends to each column at the call site, and keeps entity_count apart from the columns. For B and D it increments a's count instead of their own (kayan.h lines 142, 145, 168, 174), so A reports seven entities and the others report none. Nothing breaks only because the query loop happens to use the column's own length.
  • Entities have handles (lesson 4). kayan's entity id is the value of an archetype's entity_count before it is bumped: meant per table, in practice A's, as above. Nothing records where an entity lives, so there is no way to refer to one entity from elsewhere, to remove it, or to move it to another archetype. The lessons use an {index, generation} handle and a slot list that tracks each entity's table and row.
  • Entities move between archetypes (lesson 4). Adding or removing a component moves the entity to the matching table, copying the components both tables share.
  • Structural changes wait for the end of the frame (lesson 6), through a command buffer in a frame region. kayan never changes structure while a query runs, but only because it never changes structure at all.
  • Reflection replaces hand-written tables (lessons 3 to 5). A component's size and alignment come from T<>, and so do the names a tool prints. The offset map goes away entirely.
  • The compiler checks the memory. kayan's query reads through void * and adds byte offsets it trusts. Here the void * is gone: a pointer says which region it points into, a lookup that can miss returns option<*T>, and a slice is bounds checked. A type-erased column is still bytes, because that is what lets one table type hold every archetype, but it is a []u8 that knows its length. Reading it as a []T is one small unsafe { } block that checks what it is given (lesson 3), and everything above it is checked.

Not carried over

  • **vec4s for positions.** kayan pads 3D vectors to 16 bytes, which suits SIMD loads. The lessons use vec2 and vec3 and plain loops, and leave vectorizing to the C compiler. noalias on the kernels' parameters, in lessons 1, 2, 3, 6 and 7, lets it do that without run-time overlap checks. Lesson 1 adds a third layout, one f32 array per coordinate, which is the one SIMD runs cleanly over, and its exercises come back to vec4. Lesson 7 weighs that layout against lookups, which it is bad at.
  • cglm and the haikal containers. rin's generics and std (vec<T>, hashmap<K, V>, slices) cover what they did.

Small things in kayan.h

  • The query's inner loop declares i32 i, shadowing the outer i (line 201).
  • Each lookup on lines 199 and 200 hashes and compares a string, once per column per archetype per query. That is cheap next to a large loop, but it is work that an array index does for nothing.

Advanced · lesson 1

AoS vs SoA

src/1.aos_vs_soa/aos_vs_soa.rin

src/1.aos_vs_soa/aos_vs_soa.rin

The same 262,144 particles, stored three times: as an array of 68-byte particle structs (AoS), as seven arrays, one per field (SoA), and with position and velocity split one step further into six arrays of f32, one per coordinate (split). Sixty steps of movement run over each, and the program checks that all three end with the same positions.

Where the particles live

All three layouts are in one region. A region is an arena the compiler can see:

level: region;

Each array is a slice, and a slice kept in memory says which region holds its elements:

particles: struct = {
    positions: []vec3 in level;
    velocities: []vec3 in level;
    ...
}

main opens the region, and new_slice is an arena push that keeps the length:

level: region = {
aos: []particle in level = new_slice<particle>(level, particle_count);
soa: *particles in level = new<particles>(level, {
    .positions = new_slice<vec3>(level, particle_count),
    ...
});

Everything lives exactly as long as that block. Nothing is freed one at a time, and the checker will not let a pointer into level outlive the closing brace. The movement procs take plain slices and know nothing about any of this.

What the loop fetches

Memory reaches the CPU in 64-byte cache lines. A loop that reads 24 bytes of each 68-byte particle still pulls every byte of every line those particles sit in, so about two thirds of what movement fetches in the AoS loop is tint, age, lifetime, size and name. In the SoA loop the two arrays it reads are the only thing it fetches, and the hardware prefetcher sees two simple streams. The split loop fetches the same 24 bytes per particle as SoA, as six streams.

The program prints that arithmetic:

bytes fetched per step: 17825792     (AoS: 68 bytes x 262144)
bytes fetched per step: 6291456      (SoA: 24 bytes x 262144)
bytes fetched per step: 6291456      (split: 6 x 4 bytes x 262144)

What the CPU does with each layout

SSE registers hold four floats, AVX registers eight. One instruction adds four (or eight) pairs of floats at once, but only if they arrive side by side. Here is what clang-cl /O2 makes of each loop for Windows x64, read from the object file:

loopparticles per passinstructions per passper particleshuffles
move_aos116161
move_soa477about 1930
move_split42050
move_split, /arch:AVX2814under 20
  • AoS goes one particle at a time: each particle's fields are 68 bytes from the next particle's, so there is nothing to load four of.
  • SoA is vectorized, four particles per pass, but each vec3 keeps x, y and z side by side. To get four x's into one register the compiler loads them one float at a time and stitches them together, then takes them apart again to store. About a tenth of the loop is arithmetic, and per particle it costs about what AoS does.
  • Split is what SIMD wants. Each line of move_split becomes one load of four consecutive floats, one multiply, one add, one store:
  movups (%r10,%rsi,4), %xmm4     four vx
  movups (%r8,%rsi,4), %xmm5      four px
  mulps  %xmm1, %xmm4             vx * dt
  addps  %xmm5, %xmm4             px + vx * dt
  movups %xmm4, (%r8,%rsi,4)      four px back

A layout is right for SIMD when its vector loop is mostly full-width loads, math and stores. When it is mostly movss, unpcklps and shufps, the data is fighting the registers.

Split is right for this loop, which runs over every particle in order. It is wrong for a loop that reaches particles by index, where x, y and z in three arrays are three trips to memory instead of one. Lesson 7 measures both kinds of loop over four layouts.

The bounds checks

Every positions[i] is bounds checked, in every build, Release included. The safety rules rest on it, so it does not hang on NDEBUG. A check is a compare and a branch to a call that never returns, in the middle of a loop that wants to do four particles at once, so you would expect it to cost the vector loop.

On clang it does not. The table above is with the checks on, and the passes are the same with them off. The compiler sees that the loop runs i up to px.length, works out before the loop how many full passes fit inside every column's length, runs the vector loop for those with no checks in it, and leaves the rest to a one-at-a-time loop that does check. A column shorter than px stops the program there, with a message. What the checks add to move_split is around the loop: 257 instructions in the whole proc instead of 79, and 27 in the one-at-a-time loop instead of 17.

gcc does not do this for move_soa or move_split. With the checks on, -fopt-info-vec reports no vector loop over either, and split, the layout that needs one most, is its slowest. -DRIN_NO_BOUNDS_CHECKS removes the checks and brings the vector loop back, as the timings below show. A program built that way has given up rin's guarantee. Try 8 is the other way, which keeps it.

Timings

--time prints how long each layout took. Release builds on one core, best of five runs, on a Ryzen 9 9950X3D: 1 MB of L2 a core and 96 MB of L3. clang-cl 22 on Windows, gcc 16 under WSL on the same machine. Each run did ten times the work and is divided by ten, because clock() on Windows ticks in milliseconds. ms for sixty steps:

buildAoSSoAsplit
clang-cl /O212.210.86.7
clang-cl /O2 /arch:AVX29.87.25.5
gcc -O331.411.626.5
gcc -O212.511.227.5
gcc -O3 -DRIN_NO_BOUNDS_CHECKS55.49.04.8
gcc -O2 -DRIN_NO_BOUNDS_CHECKS9.98.54.4

The clang-cl rows do not change with -DRIN_NO_BOUNDS_CHECKS, beyond the noise, and clang -O3 is the same as -O2.

The same loops with 8,192 particles, so everything stays in L2, and 1,920 steps so the work is the same:

buildAoSSoAsplit
clang-cl /O211.89.94.5
clang-cl /O2 /arch:AVX29.25.73.9
gcc -O330.711.610.6
gcc -O3 -DRIN_NO_BOUNDS_CHECKS53.48.92.7

And with 2,097,152 particles and 7.5 steps' worth, so the work is the same again. AoS, at 143 MB, no longer fits in L3:

buildAoSSoAsplit
clang-cl /O227.910.87.9
clang-cl /O2 /arch:AVX228.08.26.0
  • In cache, split is the only layout SSE helps much. SoA and AoS come out about even in L2 on clang-cl, as the instruction counts say they should. AVX2's eight-float registers help SoA too.
  • Out of cache, the bytes show. At 262,144 particles all three sit in this machine's 96 MB of L3, and AoS fetching three times the bytes costs little. At 2,097,152, AoS has left L3 and takes more than twice as long, while SoA and split, at 50 MB, are where they were. How much the layout matters here depends on the size of the cache you run on.
  • **gcc's AoS at -O3 is the odd one.** Two and a half to five times its -O2, and it is the loop vectorizer: -fno-tree-loop-vectorize brings it back to about 12 ms. It vectorizes the loop with 8-byte vectors, and I have not explained why that is so slow on this machine.

The machine was busy; expect about 20 percent noise between runs, more for AoS, which came out up to twice as slow in unlucky runs. Debug numbers are not worth comparing: nothing is optimized there, and every check is a function call.

For a Release build, set build_type to "Release" in build.rin and run rin build again. Release optimizes and defines NDEBUG, and the checks stay. To take them out, add "RIN_NO_BOUNDS_CHECKS" to build_defines, or compile the C that tools/check.py leaves in build/check/aos_vs_soa/ with -O2 -DRIN_NO_BOUNDS_CHECKS.

The parameter list is the data

move_aos(ps: noalias []particle, ...) says it needs particles. move_soa(positions: noalias []vec3, velocities: noalias []vec3, ...) and move_split(px, py, pz, vx, vy, vz, ...) say exactly which data they read and write. In lessons 2 and 3 every system is written that way. In lesson 6 each system runs its own query, then works only on the columns it named.

Naming the columns is what lets a scheduler see that two systems touch different data, and it is what makes a system easy to test: hand it two small arrays.

noalias

As far as the C compiler can tell, two []vec3 slices could overlap. So before it works on several particles at once, it checks at run time that the two are apart, and keeps a one-at-a-time copy of the loop for when they are not, or it does not vectorize at all. noalias on a parameter promises that, for the call, nothing else reaches the memory behind it. The check and the second copy go away.

It is a promise the checker cannot keep, so it lives in code marked for it. A proc with a noalias parameter is proc[unsafe]:

move_soa: proc[unsafe](positions: noalias []vec3, velocities: noalias []vec3, dt: f32) -> void = {

and a call to it sits in unsafe { }:

unsafe { move_soa(soa*.positions, soa*.velocities, dt); }

Take the [unsafe] off and rin stops:

noalias is a promise to the C optimiser that the checker cannot keep: it belongs on a 'proc[unsafe]'

So the three movement kernels are outside what the checker vouches for. That is the trade, and it is yours to make per kernel: take off both noalias and [unsafe], and the same loop is checked like everything else, at the cost below.

The SoA loop without and with it, Release, ms:

buildwithout noaliaswith noalias
clang-cl /O223.210.8
clang-cl /O2 -DRIN_NO_BOUNDS_CHECKS10.810.8
clang -O2, Linux9.911.0
gcc -O311.811.6
gcc -O3 -DRIN_NO_BOUNDS_CHECKS9.19.0
  • clang-cl is where it shows. Without the promise it does not vectorize move_soa at all, and with the checks on it reads both slices from memory on every pass: one particle, 47 instructions. Without the checks it is 26 instructions and costs what the vector loop does, since four vec3s gain little from SSE anyway.
  • clang on Linux vectorized the loop either way. Without the promise it checks once per call, so removing the check saves nothing that shows here.
  • gcc puts the loop behind a run-time check only when the bounds checks are gone and it vectorizes at all: "loop versioned for vectorization because of possible aliasing". The promise removes the check, and it does not show here either.

On Windows, one slice needs it too. move_aos has a single slice, which cannot overlap another, and it still takes noalias. Windows passes a slice to a proc by reference, as a pointer to a copy, and clang-cl does not use C's type rules to decide what can overlap (it matches MSVC). So, without the promise, a float written through ps might be the slice's own pointer or length, and the loop reads both again after every particle:

movq   (%rcx), %r8                         ps.data, every particle
...
cmpq   0x8(%rcx), %rdx                     ps.length, every particle

With noalias the compiler gets the pointer and the length once, in registers, and the loop is 16 instructions instead of 18.

**And gravity is a const.** rin computes a constant and hands C the number, so the loops say -(9.8f) and there is no variable for a write to change:

gravity: static const f32 = -9.8;

A plain global is different. gravity: f32 = -9.8; is something other files could reach, and to gcc that is something a write through a slice might change, even through a noalias one, so gcc -O3 without the bounds checks puts a run-time check in front of move_split's vector loop. static f32 keeps it to this file, nothing takes its address, and the check goes away. Passing it as a parameter would do the same, which is what dt does.

The promise is checked at run time, in every build. Pass soa*.positions as both arguments to move_soa and the program stops before the loop runs:

aos_vs_soa.rin:153: noalias parameters 'positions' and 'velocities' overlap

That is one check per call, not per particle. Only -DRIN_NO_BOUNDS_CHECKS turns it off. That build runs on, and the lesson prints same result: no.

Fused multiply-add

With -mfma, -march=native or clang-cl's /arch:AVX2, clang fuses p + v * dt into one instruction that rounds once instead of twice. All three layouts are fused the same way and still agree, but the checksum's last digits move, from 38572460.505 to 38572460.519, and the byte-for-byte check against aos_vs_soa.expected fails. tools/check.py builds without those flags.

When AoS is right

When the code that touches a record touches most of its fields, AoS fetches nothing wasted, and keeping a record together is simpler. Data-oriented design does not mean SoA everywhere. It means choosing the layout from the loops that run over it. An entity component system is the case where many small loops each touch a few fields.

Try

  1. Run with --time in Release. Then remove tint, age, lifetime and name from particle and run again. The AoS loop should close most of the gap, because the struct shrinks toward what the loop reads.
  2. Add /arch:AVX2 to build_c_flags and compare --time. Then read move_split in the disassembly: eight floats per register, and vfmadd.
  3. kayan stored positions as 16-byte vec4s. Change vec3 to four floats and see what it does to the bytes-per-step line, to move_soa's disassembly and to the timing.
  4. Store the split columns in blocks of eight, { x: [8]f32; y: [8]f32; ... }, and write the loop over blocks. Each block is a whole AVX register per coordinate, and a particle's coordinates stay near each other.
  5. Remove noalias from move_soa and build Release with gcc -O3 -DRIN_NO_BOUNDS_CHECKS. Compare --time, then compile with -fopt-info-vec and find "loop versioned for vectorization because of possible aliasing". Then take off [unsafe] and the unsafe { } around its call, and read what clang-cl makes of a kernel the checker can vouch for.
  6. Change gravity to a plain gravity: f32 = -9.8;, build with gcc -O3 -DRIN_NO_BOUNDS_CHECKS -fopt-info-vec, and find the same message for move_split. Then make it static f32.
  7. Pass soa*.positions as both arguments to move_soa. Run it in Debug, in Release, then with -DRIN_NO_BOUNDS_CHECKS.
  8. Get gcc's vector loop back with the checks on. At the top of move_split, cut every column to one length, ys: []f32 = py[0..px.length]; and so on, and loop over those. gcc can now see that one bound covers them all, and it vectorizes, behind an overlap check, since the cuts carry no noalias. Split goes from 26.5 ms to about 8 on gcc -O3, a column that is too short stops the program at the cut, before the first particle, and nothing has been given up.

Advanced · lesson 2

One archetype table

src/2.archetype_table/archetype_table.rin

src/2.archetype_table/archetype_table.rin

In the dojo: 2. swap-remove and the back-reference, 4. a type-erased column, each on its own, to watch and to practise.

Eight sparks in one table with three component columns, positions, velocities and lives, plus a numbers column that exists only so the output can say which spark is which. Each frame they move, they age, and the ones that ran out are removed.

Two rules

Columns never disagree. spark_spawn and spark_despawn are the only places rows come and go, and each touches every column. A new component means a new column, one line in each of those two procs, and one more argument to spark_spawn. A call site cannot add a row to some columns and forget the others.

Rows are packed. Systems loop over 0..count and never test whether a row is alive. Removing a row moves the last row into the hole:

spark 0 in row 0 expired; spark 7 moved from row 7 into it

That one copy per column is the whole cost of a despawn, whatever the table's size. The price is that a row number is not a name for a spark. After that line, "row 0" means spark 7. Lesson 4 adds names that do not move.

The table lives in a region

The table and its columns come from the region level, and their types say so:

spark_table_create: proc(r: region level, capacity: u64) -> *spark_table in level = {
    return new<spark_table>(r, {
        .capacity = capacity,
        .numbers = new_slice<u32>(r, capacity),
        .positions = new_slice<vec2>(r, capacity),
        .velocities = new_slice<vec2>(r, capacity),
        .lives = new_slice<f32>(r, capacity),
    });
}

main opens level and holds the result as *spark_table in level, so the checker will not let it be kept past the region's end. Every column here is typed, so no byte is ever reinterpreted, and the only unsafe in the file is for noalias, below.

Removing while iterating

expire_system walks the rows backwards. When it removes row i, the row that moves in comes from the end, and the end has already been tested. A forward loop would have to stay on i after a removal, and it is easy to get wrong. Lesson 6 removes the question entirely by not removing anything during a loop.

Systems take slices

move_system(positions: noalias []vec2, velocities: []const vec2, dt) gets the rows in use, sparks*.positions[0..sparks*.count], and knows nothing about tables. []const says it only reads velocities. Each positions[i] is bounds checked, in every build, against the count rather than the capacity, so a system that runs past the live rows stops with a message instead of reading stale data.

noalias says that for the call, nothing else reaches the memory positions covers. Only the column the system writes needs it: a promise on the written column already rules out a write landing in the column being read. Without it, clang -O2 on Linux vectorized this loop behind a run-time check that the two columns are apart, and so did gcc -O3 with the bounds checks compiled out. With it, neither checks. A build with the bounds checks in checks the promise instead, once per call.

The promise is one the checker cannot keep, so the two kernels are proc[unsafe], and main calls each from inside unsafe { }:

unsafe { move_system(sparks*.positions[0..sparks*.count], sparks*.velocities[0..sparks*.count], dt); }

age_system(lives: noalias []f32, dt) has one slice, and still takes it. Windows passes a slice by reference, as a pointer to a copy, and clang-cl does not use C's type rules to decide what can overlap. So without the promise, a float written through lives might be the slice's own pointer or length. clang-cl then reads both again after every element and does one float at a time. With it, the loop is eight floats per pass:

movups (%rcx,%r8,4), %xmm2         four lives
movups 0x10(%rcx,%r8,4), %xmm3     four more
subps  %xmm0, %xmm2                minus dt
subps  %xmm0, %xmm3
movups %xmm2, (%rcx,%r8,4)
movups %xmm3, 0x10(%rcx,%r8,4)

The bounds check does not cost this loop anything: lives.length is already the loop's bound, so the compiler drops it. move_system, with two lengths to check, keeps its vector loop on clang too, as lesson 1 explains; clang-cl does not vectorize it at all without noalias, and gcc -O3 does not with the checks in.

The rule that holds on every compiler: noalias on every slice a loop writes, even when it is the only one.

lives is a plain run of floats. positions and velocities are vec2, x and y side by side, but both get the same math, so the compiler keeps the pairs together and move_system's vector loop needs no shuffles at all: four vec2s a pass in two registers. A vec3, which does not divide into a register, is another matter. Lesson 1 measures what that costs.

Status codes

spark_spawn returns spawn_status, an enum[must_use]: calling it and ignoring the result is a compile error. That is rin's convention for a proc that can fail: a status, with the result through an out-parameter. The ninth spark shows the full case.

Try

  1. Rewrite expire_system to walk forwards with a plain for. The output does not change, because no frame here expires a spark together with the one in the last row. Change two lives so that one does, and find the spark that outlives its life by a frame. Then fix the loop.
  2. Delete the line in spark_despawn that copies lives. What does the output show, and how long did it take to notice?
  3. Call spark_spawn without using its result and read the compiler's error. Then discard it on purpose with _ = spark_spawn(...).
  4. Make the table grow instead of reporting full: spark_spawn now needs the region, r: region level, to new_slice double the capacity, and a plain loop copies every column across. It is all checked, since the columns are typed. Lesson 4's kayan_table_grow is the same idea over columns of bytes.
1// 2. One archetype table2//3// An archetype is one combination of components. Its table holds every entity4// that has exactly that combination: one column per component, one row per5// entity. It is lesson 1's struct of arrays with two rules added.6//7// Every column has the same length, always. Spawn appends to every column in8// one place and despawn removes from every column in one place. kayan appended9// to each column at the call site, and three appends that must happen together10// are three chances to forget one.11//12// Rows are packed. Despawn moves the last row into the hole it leaves (a13// swap-remove), so a system loops over 0..count with no gaps and no "alive"14// flag to test. The price is that a row is not a stable name for an entity: the15// last entity changes rows every time something before it dies. Lesson 4 deals16// with that.17//18// The sparks here have a position, a velocity and a life in seconds. Each frame19// they move, they age, and the ones whose life ran out are removed. Removal20// walks the rows backwards, so the row swapped into a hole has already been21// looked at this frame.22//23// The arena is the region `level`; the table is made in it and24// its columns are slices that name it. The two kernels are `proc[unsafe]`, because25// `noalias` is a promise the checker cannot check: each call says `unsafe`, and the26// checker sees every other line of this lesson.27 28import "std/print.rin"29 30level: region;31 32vec2: struct = {33    x: f32;34    y: f32;35}36 37// The table for the archetype {position, velocity, life}. Each column is sized38// to the capacity once; count says how many rows are in use. `numbers` is not a39// component: it only lets the output say which spark sits in which row.40spark_table: struct = {41    count: u64;42    capacity: u64;43    numbers: []u32 in level;44    positions: []vec2 in level;45    velocities: []vec2 in level;46    lives: []f32 in level;47}48 49spawn_status: enum[must_use] = {50    ok,51    full,52}53 54// The table and its columns come from the region: the pointer says so, and55// the checker will not let it be kept past the region's end.56spark_table_create: proc(r: region level, capacity: u64) -> *spark_table in level = {57    return new<spark_table>(r, {58        .capacity = capacity,59        .numbers = new_slice<u32>(r, capacity),60        .positions = new_slice<vec2>(r, capacity),61        .velocities = new_slice<vec2>(r, capacity),62        .lives = new_slice<f32>(r, capacity),63    });64}65 66// The only place a row is added: every column gets its value here.67spark_spawn: proc(t: *spark_table, number: u32, position: vec2, velocity: vec2, life: f32,68                  row: *u64) -> spawn_status = {69    if (t*.count == t*.capacity) {70        return spawn_status.full;71    }72    r: u64 = t*.count;73    t*.numbers[r] = number;74    t*.positions[r] = position;75    t*.velocities[r] = velocity;76    t*.lives[r] = life;77    t*.count += 1;78    row* = r;79    return spawn_status.ok;80}81 82// The only place a row is removed. The last row moves into `row`, in every83// column, and the table shrinks by one. Returns the row that moved, which is84// `row` itself when the removed row was the last one.85spark_despawn: proc(t: *spark_table, row: u64) -> u64 = {86    last: u64 = t*.count - 1;87    t*.numbers[row] = t*.numbers[last];88    t*.positions[row] = t*.positions[last];89    t*.velocities[row] = t*.velocities[last];90    t*.lives[row] = t*.lives[last];91    t*.count = last;92    return last;93}94 95// Systems. Each takes the columns it reads and writes, cut to the rows in use.96// noalias on the column a system writes promises nothing else reaches it, so97// the loop can be vectorized without runtime overlap checks.98move_system: proc[unsafe](positions: noalias []vec2, velocities: []const vec2, dt: f32) -> void = {99    for (i: u64 = 0; i < positions.length; i += 1) {100        positions[i].x += velocities[i].x * dt;101        positions[i].y += velocities[i].y * dt;102    }103}104 105// One slice, and still noalias: on Windows the slice arrives by reference, and106// without the promise a float written through lives might be its own pointer107// or length, so clang-cl reads both again after every element.108age_system: proc[unsafe](lives: noalias []f32, dt: f32) -> void = {109    for (i: u64 = 0; i < lives.length; i += 1) {110        lives[i] -= dt;111    }112}113 114// Structural change: rows leave the table. Backwards, so the row a swap-remove115// pulls in has already been tested.116expire_system: proc(t: *spark_table) -> void = {117    i: u64 = t*.count;118    while (i > 0) {119        i -= 1;120        if (t*.lives[i] <= 0.0) {121            number: u32 = t*.numbers[i];122            moved: u64 = spark_despawn(t, i);123            if (moved != i) {124                printfmt("    spark {} in row {} expired; spark {} moved from row {} into it\n",125                    number, i, t*.numbers[i], moved);126            } else {127                printfmt("    spark {} in row {} expired; it was the last row\n", number, i);128            }129        }130    }131}132 133print_table: proc(t: *spark_table) -> void = {134    for (i: u64 = 0; i < t*.count; i += 1) {135        printfmt("    row {}  spark {}  position ({:6.2}, {:6.2})  life {:.2}\n",136            cast(i, i32), cast(t*.numbers[i], i32),137            cast(t*.positions[i].x, f64), cast(t*.positions[i].y, f64), cast(t*.lives[i], f64));138    }139}140 141main: proc() -> i32 = {142    level: region = {143    sparks: *spark_table in level = spark_table_create(level, 8);144    printfmt("a table with room for {} sparks, {} bytes of components a row\n", sparks*.capacity,145        sizeof(vec2) * 2 + sizeof(f32));146 147    // Eight sparks with lives of 0.5s to 4s, plus one more than fits.148    for (i: u64 = 0; i < 9; i += 1) {149        f: f32 = cast(i, f32);150        row: u64 = 0;151        life: f32 = 0.5 + cast((i * 5) % 8, f32) * 0.5;152        status: spawn_status = spark_spawn(sparks, cast(i, u32), { .x = f, .y = 0.0 }, { .x = 1.0, .y = f },153            life, row&);154        if (status == spawn_status.full) {155            printfmt("spark {} did not fit: the table is full\n", i);156        }157    }158    print_table(sparks);159 160    dt: f32 = 0.5;161    for (frame: i32 = 1; frame <= 4; frame += 1) {162        printfmt("frame {}\n", frame);163        unsafe { move_system(sparks*.positions[0..sparks*.count], sparks*.velocities[0..sparks*.count], dt); }164        unsafe { age_system(sparks*.lives[0..sparks*.count], dt); }165        expire_system(sparks);166        print_table(sparks);167    }168    printfmt("{} sparks left\n", sparks*.count);169    }170    return 0;171}

Advanced · lesson 3

Many archetypes

src/3.many_archetypes/many_archetypes.rin

src/3.many_archetypes/many_archetypes.rin

In the dojo: 4. a type-erased column, 6. bitsets, each on its own, to watch and to practise.

Four archetypes (rock, ship, bullet, turret) and four components (position, velocity, health, damage). One table type holds all four archetypes, and two queries decide which tables each system visits.

A table without a type

Lesson 2's table had one typed field per column. That cannot work for every archetype at once, so the columns become bytes:

table: struct = {
    name: ^const c8;
    signature: u64;
    count: u64;
    capacity: u64;
    columns: [component<>.count][]u8 in level;
}

columns[id] is empty when the table has no such component, and table_has reads that from the signature. Its element size is component_info[id]*.size, where component_info holds each component's reflect record, position<>& and so on. table_add_row and lesson 4's moves work only from sizes, so they never need to know a component's type. A column is a slice of bytes, so all of that is checked: a row past the end stops the program like any index.

slice<u8>zero(t*.columns[c][row * size..(row + 1) * size]);

Types come back at the edges. column<T>(t) asks component_of<T>() for T's id, views that column's bytes as T, and returns a []T of the rows in use. component_of is one specialisation per component, one line each. Systems take []position, []velocity and so on, exactly as in lesson 2.

What the checker cannot see

Two things are unsafe { } here. table_create allocates columns with a component's alignment, which only the arena can promise. column<T> turns bytes into a type, which no checker can vouch for:

column: proc<T>(t: *const table) -> []T in level = {
    c: component = component_of<T>();
    if (!table_has(t, c)) {
        printfmt("table {} has no {} column\n", t*.name, component_info[c]*.name);
        exit(1);
    }
    if (!reflect_is_plain(T<>&)) {
        printfmt("a column holds plain data, and {} is not\n", T<>.name);
        exit(1);
    }
    bytes: []u8 in level = t*.columns[c];
    if (t*.count > bytes.length / sizeof(T)) {
        printfmt("table {} has {} rows and room for {}\n", t*.name, t*.count, bytes.length / sizeof(T));
        exit(1);
    }
    unsafe {
        if (cast(bytes.data, usize) % alignof(T) != 0) {
            printfmt("table {}: a column that is not aligned for {}\n", t*.name, T<>.name);
            exit(1);
        }
        raw: ^T = cast(bytes.data, ^T);
        return cast(raw[0..t*.count], []T in level);
    }
}

Most of that is checks, and each one is there for a reason.

rin has no private fields. Any checked proc can write t*.count, so an unsafe block must not trust a field or an argument unless the value carries its own bound, as a slice does. Here the bytes know their length, and count is measured against them. Write tables[1]*.count = 1000; in main and the program stops rather than hand out a slice past the column:

table ship has 1000 rows and room for 16

Set a bit in a signature by hand and it stops the same way, since the column behind that bit is empty.

A plain-data T means any bytes are a valid T. reflect_is_plain accepts numbers, enums, and arrays and structs of them, and refuses a pointer. So reading the wrong type gives wrong numbers, never a bad pointer. Make component_of<health> return component.position and the program runs to the end, with ships at ( 62.0, 100.0). That is a bug, and it is one the output shows. It is not a memory error.

What comes back is []T in level, and it is a borrow of the table, good until a row is added or removed. Everything above those two procs is checked, and works in slices and *table. A struct holding a raw pointer, here the table's name, is only ever made by a proc that vouches for it, so main holds the tables by pointer, in the region:

tables: [4]*table in level = {
    table_create(level, "rock", rock_components, 16),
    table_create(level, "ship", ship_components, 16),
    table_create(level, "bullet", bullet_components, 16),
    table_create(level, "turret", turret_components, 16),
};

Sized by reflection

component has no count member at the end. component<>.count is the number of members, from the enum's reflect record, and it sizes both columns and component_info. With a hand-added count member the reflected count is one more than the number of components. That is how the bounds check found a bug while this lesson was being written.

component_info is a global, and globals live in permanent, the region of the whole program, so its type says that of the records it holds:

component_info: [component<>.count]*const reflect in permanent = {

components_check compares each enum member's name with the name in component_info. Swap two entries in component_info and the program stops before anything runs:

component 2 is health in the enum but damage in component_info

Different types, fewer checks

move_system takes noalias []position, as lesson 2's takes noalias []vec2, and for the same reason, so it is proc[unsafe] too. regen_system takes noalias []health, its only slice, for the reason lesson 2 gives for age_system.

One difference shows without noalias: clang on Linux vectorizes this move_system without a run-time overlap check, and lesson 2's only with one. Here the two columns are different struct types, position and velocity, and clang reads C's type rules as saying they cannot share memory; built with -fno-strict-aliasing, it checks here too. In lesson 2 both are vec2. gcc checks in both, once it vectorizes at all (lesson 1). clang-cl, rin's default compiler, does not use those rules, to match MSVC, so on Windows neither lesson vectorizes without it. noalias makes the answer the same everywhere, whatever the column types are.

Queries

moving: query = { .all = bit(component.position) | bit(component.velocity) };
healing: query = { .all = bit(component.health), .none = bit(component.damage) };

A table matches when it has every bit in all and none in none. moving visits ships and bullets. healing visits ships but not turrets, which have health but also deal damage. The output prints each visit.

The signature cannot lie

table_create builds the signature from the component list it allocates columns for. kayan wrote them separately, and archetype D's signature left out two of its columns (see 0_from_kayan.md).

Try

  1. Add an armor component, give it to turrets, and make a query that visits only tables with both health and armor.
  2. Ask a rock for column<velocity>. Read the message, then find where it comes from.
  3. Change columns to [4][]u8 in level. Then add a fifth component, give it to a table, and see what happens, and where.
  4. Write table_remove_row with the swap-remove from lesson 2, working only from component_info sizes and slice<u8>copy. It needs no unsafe, since both ends of each copy are slices.
  5. Give damage a field that holds a pointer, owner: option<*position in level>, and read what column<damage> says. Then take out that check, and the check of count against the bytes, and work out what a stray write to count could now reach.

Turrets stand5// still, can be hurt and hurt back. Advanced · lesson 4

Entity handles

src/4.entity_handles/entity_handles.rin

src/4.entity_handles/entity_handles.rin, includes/kayan.rin

In the dojo: 1. free list and generations, 3. the slot map, 9. interning, each on its own, to watch and to practise.

The world: tables made on demand, entity handles that survive row moves, despawning with index reuse, and moving an entity between archetypes when a component is added or removed. The code is includes/kayan.rin. The lesson program calls each part and prints what happened.

Handles, slots, rows

kayan_entity: struct = { index: u32; generation: u32; }
kayan_slot:   struct = { generation: u32; table: u32; row: u32; }

A handle is what the rest of a program keeps. Its index picks a slot, and the slot says where the entity lives now. Rows move all the time: every despawn and every archetype change swap-removes. When one does, the table's entities column says which entity owned the moved row, and that entity's slot gets the new row number. Handles never change.

generation is what makes a handle safe to keep after its entity dies. Despawning bumps the slot's generation and frees the index, and the next spawn reuses the index with the new generation:

spawn d: it reuses a's index with the next generation
    d = 0:2 in table 0 row 2 {position velocity} at (4.0, 0.0)
    a = 0:1 is dead

kayan_alive is one comparison: the handle's generation against the slot's. A free slot already holds its next generation, which no handle carries yet, so no separate "alive" flag is needed. a cannot reach d's data, kayan_get returns null for it, and despawning it again returns kayan_status.dead and changes nothing.

Generations start at 1. A zeroed handle, {}, is 0:0, which never matches a slot, so it can stand for "no entity" without a separate flag.

A handle to keep, a pointer to borrow

kayan_get can miss, and its type says so. It returns option<*T>, which the checker will not let you read until you have tested it:

p: option<*position> = kayan_get<position>(w, e);
if (p) {
    printfmt(" at ({:.1}, {:.1})", cast(p*.at.x, f64), cast(p*.at.y, f64));
}

The pointer is a borrow of the world, good until the next spawn, despawn, add or remove, which can move what it points at. The checker holds you to that: use one after a call that can change the world and rin says

'kept' may be stale: 'world', which it was taken from, has been changed since; take it again

So a pointer is for now, and the handle is for later. That was already this lesson's advice; now it is checked.

The world in a region

world: *kayan_world in level = kayan_world_make(level);

kayan_world_make makes the world whole, inside the region, and every list it holds says where it lives:

tables: *vec<kayan_table> in level;
by_signature: *hashmap<u64, u32> in level;
slots: *vec<kayan_slot> in level;
free: *vec<u32> in level;

A table holds lesson 3's columns of bytes, and its entities, as slices:

kayan_table: struct = {
    signature: u64;
    count: u64;
    capacity: u64;
    entities: []kayan_entity in level;
    columns: [64][]u8 in level;
}

Each slice knows its own length, so nothing here depends on a count being right. Almost all of includes/kayan.rin is checked because of that: spawning, despawning, moving, growing a table, adding and removing a row are plain indexing and slice<u8>copy, and a row past the end stops the program. Only three procs need unsafe { }. kayan_world_make keeps the region's arena, a raw pointer, so columns can grow without being handed the region on each call. kayan_bytes takes a block from that arena with a component's alignment. kayan_view<T> is the one place bytes become a type:

kayan_view: proc<T>(bytes: []u8 in level, count: u64) -> []T in level = {
    if (!reflect_is_plain(T<>&)) {
        printfmt("kayan: a column holds plain data, and {} is not\n", T<>.name);
        exit(1);
    }
    if (count > bytes.length / sizeof(T)) {
        printfmt("kayan: a view of {} {} on {} bytes\n", count, T<>.name, bytes.length);
        exit(1);
    }
    unsafe {
        if (cast(bytes.data, usize) % alignof(T) != 0) {
            printfmt("kayan: bytes that are not aligned for {}\n", T<>.name);
            exit(1);
        }
        raw: ^T = cast(bytes.data, ^T);
        return cast(raw[0..count], []T in level);
    }
}

It takes nothing on trust, for the reasons lesson 3 gives. rin has no private fields: a program can write kayan_table_at(world, 0)*.count = 1000;, and an unsafe block must not trust a field or an argument unless the value carries its own bound, as a slice does. That write stops at the next view:

kayan: a view of 1000 position on 128 bytes

And a component must be plain data, so any bytes are a valid T: reading the wrong type gives wrong numbers, never a bad pointer. Everything else, kayan_column and kayan_get included, is written in terms of this. The lesson program itself has no unsafe at all.

Statuses

kayan_despawn, kayan_add, kayan_remove and kayan_move return kayan_status, an enum[must_use]: ok, or dead when the handle no longer names a live entity. Ignoring one is a compile error. The lesson discards them on purpose with _ = kayan_add<health>(...) where the handle is known to be alive.

Tables on demand

kayan_table_for(w, signature) looks the signature up in a hashmap<u64, u32> and makes the table if it is new. Nobody declares archetypes; they appear when an entity first needs that combination. Tables live in a vec<kayan_table> and are referred to by index, because adding one can move the whole list.

Tables start with room for 16 rows and double when full. The old columns stay in the region unused, which is a waste these lessons accept. The last part of the program spawns 40 entities so the first table grows twice, despawns every other one, and checks the result two ways.

Checking the world

Reading back each survivor's position is a weak check. Swap-remove copies rows, so a stale row often still holds the right numbers. kayan_verify checks the invariant instead: every row of every table belongs to a live entity whose slot points back at that table and row, and the rows add up to the live count. It prints each problem it finds and returns how many there were. The lesson prints kayan_verify: 0 problems and fails if that is not so.

kayan_get also checks the slot's row against the rows in use, in every build, so a slot that points past the end of its table stops the program at the first lookup.

Moving between archetypes

give b health: b moves to a new table and keeps its position

kayan_add<health> computes signature | bit(health), finds or makes that table, appends a row, copies every component the two tables share, then swap-removes the old row. kayan_remove is the same move with the bit cleared. A move costs two row copies, one into the new table and one to fill the hole in the old, so components that come and go every frame are better as a field than as a component. A burning flag in health, say, instead of a burning component.

Try

  1. Despawn b and keep using its handle. Which calls notice, and which would not if kayan_alive did not check the generation?
  2. Remove the line in kayan_table_remove_row that updates the moved entity's slot. The program stops at the first kayan_get through a stale row, with index 2 out of bounds (length 2), in Debug and in Release. Print kayan_verify(world) right after the first despawn, and it names the slot: 2:1 is in table 0 row 0, its slot says table 0 row 2. Now build it with -DRIN_NO_BOUNDS_CHECKS, without that print. c reads back (3.0, 0.0) from a row nobody owns, the right numbers from the wrong place, and the program runs on until kayan_table_remove_row's own check stops it: kayan: row 30 is past the 28 rows in use.
  3. At the end of the lesson, table 0 has 22 rows and room for 64. Hold a []position from kayan_column, spawn at least 43 more so the table grows, then write through the old slice. rin refuses, with the same message. Compile it with rin compile --unsafe, which turns the rules off, and read the position back through kayan_get. The write is lost, and nothing reports it. That stale slice is why lesson 6 defers spawns. Now do what the message says, and take the slice again after the spawns.
  4. Add kayan_has<T>(w, e) -> b32 without moving anything.
  5. Make component_of<velocity> return component.position. Both are 8 bytes, so nothing stops it: position and velocity now share a column, every position reads (0.0, 1.0), and the lesson's own position check fails, with no crash anywhere. Then make component_of<health> return component.velocity, which is a different size, and read what kayan_view says.

Advanced · lesson 5

The inspector

src/5.inspector/inspector.rin

src/5.inspector/inspector.rin

In the dojo: 11. a reflection walk, on its own, to watch and to practise.

A soldier and a crate, printed field by field by code that names no component type, then edited by component and field name, then a table layout report. Everything comes from the reflect records the world already holds for sizes.

What a reflect record has

T<> is a reflect record: name, size, align, kind, count, and for a struct, count fields. Each field has its name, offset, size, type ("f32" for a builtin, "array_16_c8" for a [16]c8), elem_type and array_count for arrays, and info, the record of the field's own type when it has one. A nested struct or an enum field has info; a builtin like f32 does not.

The walk asks for these through procs that return option<*const>, because a record can run out of fields and a builtin has no record of its own:

f: option<*const reflect_field> = reflect_field_at(type, i);
...
info: option<*const reflect> = reflect_field_info(f);

print_fields walks that. It takes the component's bytes as a []const u8, from kayan_get_bytes, and cuts each field's bytes out of it by offset and size, so a record that disagreed with the data would stop the program in any build. Struct fields recurse through info, enum fields print their member name through reflect_name_from_value_or, a [16]c8 prints as text, and builtins print by type name. Because components are structs, even a single float like health.points has a name to print.

Bytes as a value

The walk is checked. The last step is not: a field's bytes may sit at any address, so they cannot simply be cast to a *f32. They go through a local, which is aligned, with memcpy, and memcpy is C's, so that is unsafe. These are the lesson's small unsafe procs, one a type, each checking the length it is given:

bytes_as_f32: proc(at: []const u8) -> f32 = {
    unsafe {
        if (at.length < sizeof(f32)) { printfmt("inspector: too few bytes for an f32\n"); exit(1); }
        value: f32 = 0.0;
        memcpy(value&, at.data, sizeof(f32));
        return value;
    }
}

bytes_as_u32, bytes_as_i32 and bytes_set_f32 are the same, print_text prints a [N]c8, and cstr_into copies a C string into one. The bytes come from kayan_get_bytes, which is checked: a []u8 cut from the column.

Tags

health: struct = { points: f32; max: f32; regen_timer: f32 @ "hidden"; }

@ "hidden" is a string attached to the field, read with reflect_field_has_attr. The inspector skips it. The component decides what a tool shows, and the tool does not need to know the component.

Names belong in tools

set_f32_by_name(world, soldier, "health", "points", 55.0) finds the component by name, the field by name, checks the field is an f32, and writes it. It refuses weapon.ammo, a u32, and the crate's health, which it does not have. That is the flexibility an editor or a console needs. It is also the string comparison kayan did in every query, once per archetype. Here it runs once per edit, and systems keep using ids.

Layout

print_layout lists each table's columns with size and alignment, and each column's bytes in use out of the bytes allocated for the table's capacity. It is the kind of report that shows when a component has grown padding, when a table has far more room than rows, or when a table carries a column most of its systems never read.

Try

  1. Add a bool-like b32 field to weapon and teach print_builtin to print it as yes or no. It needs a reader beside bytes_as_u32, through a local in the same way.
  2. Give position a @ "readonly" tag and make set_f32_by_name refuse fields that carry it.
  3. Write set_by_name for u32 and i32 as well, picking the write from f*.type. Each new write is another small unsafe proc, like bytes_set_f32.
  4. Print a whole table as rows and columns: one line per entity, one column per field.

Advanced · lesson 6

kayan

src/6.kayan/kayan.rin

src/6.kayan/kayan.rin

In the dojo: 5. a command buffer, 7. an arena, each on its own, to watch and to practise.

A turret at the centre, five wings of three drones, 140 frames. Seven systems run each frame, and every structural change they want goes through a command buffer applied at the end of the frame.

The frame

spawner    wings of drones enter                    records spawns
turret     shoot at the nearest drone               records spawns
movement   position += velocity * dt                writes
lifetime   bullets expire                           records despawns
collision  live bullets against drones              writes health, records despawn and add
burning    burning drones lose health               writes
outcome    destroy dead drones, catch leaks         records despawns
  blast    a destroyed drone hurts its neighbours   writes health, records adds
apply      every recorded change, in order

Writes to components happen in place, during queries. Changes to which table an entity is in are recorded, and applied once nothing is iterating.

Lifetime runs before collision, and collision skips bullets whose lifetime is used up. Those bullets are only still in their table because nothing structural happens until the end of the frame. Without the skip, a bullet that hit on its last frame would be despawned twice and counted as both a hit and a miss.

The frame is a region inside level, declared frame: region in level; and opened once per frame, around the systems and the apply:

frame: region = {
    c: *commands in frame = commands_make(frame);
    spawner_system(g, c);
    turret_system(g, c, dt);
    movement_system(g*.world, dt);
    lifetime_system(g, c, dt);
    collision_system(g, c);
    burning_system(g*.world, dt);
    outcome_system(g, c);
    result: apply_result = commands_apply(c, g*.world);
    skipped += result.skipped;
}

The world outlives every frame, so it is in level. The buffer belongs to one frame, so it is made inside the block and passed to the systems beside the game.

Systems and kernels

movement_system and burning_system are each a query and a kernel:

integrate: proc[unsafe](ps: noalias []position, vs: []const velocity, dt: f32) -> void
burn: proc[unsafe](hs: noalias []health, bs: []const burning, dt: f32) -> void

The system walks the tables and calls the kernel once for each table that matches:

unsafe { integrate(kayan_column<position>(t), kayan_column<velocity>(t), dt); }

The kernel sees two columns, so the compiler sees a straight loop over two arrays. noalias qualifies parameters, so the loop needs a proc of its own to carry it, and since noalias is a promise the checker cannot keep, that proc is proc[unsafe]. The split is what keeps the promise small: the query around it stays checked. The output does not change.

With the bounds checks compiled out, gcc -O3 vectorized both loops behind a run-time check that the columns were apart before the split, and without the check after it. With the checks in, it vectorizes neither here, as lesson 1 says of gcc. clang on Linux had no check either way, for the reason lesson 3 gives: the columns are different types. clang-cl, which does not use C's type rules, needs noalias here too.

burn is the cleanest loop in the game. health and burning are each one f32, so their columns are plain runs of floats, and the kernel is eight floats per pass with nothing to rearrange: loads, mulps, subps, stores. integrate works on vec2s, both coordinates get the same math, and it is just as clean at four vec2s per pass; lesson 1 shows what a vec3 does to that, and what the fully split layout looks like.

integrate and burn are streams: every row of every matching table, in order. collision_system and blast_system are closer to lookups: for each bullet or each blast, they visit drones that could be anywhere. Lesson 7 measures what each layout costs for both kinds of loop, and why the components here stay small structs.

lifetime_system stays one proc. Its loop records a despawn for each expired bullet, and a loop that calls something per row is not vectorized whatever its parameters say. The other systems branch, search or record in their loops too.

Why not change tables during a query

Each of these would be a real bug with the world from lesson 4:

  • Despawn. The swap-remove moves the last row into the hole, behind the loop, so that entity is not processed this frame. Meanwhile the slice the system cut before the despawn still reaches the old last row, a stale copy, and anything written to it is lost.
  • Spawn. A table that is full grows, and its columns move to new memory. A system holding a []position from before the spawn keeps writing to the old copy. Nothing crashes; the writes are just lost.
  • Add or remove. The entity moves to another table, which the same query may reach later. That entity is processed twice this frame.

The checker catches the stale slices, the first two. It reads the body of a checked proc to see what the proc can move. kayan_spawn and kayan_despawn can grow or shrink what the world holds, so a column held across one is an error at compile time. Put a kayan_spawn or a kayan_despawn in lifetime_system's loop and rin says:

'ls' may be stale: 'g.world.tables', which it was taken from, has been changed since; take it again

blast_system and nearest_drone take the game or the world, but nothing in them can move a table, so a column stays good across them. turret_system and outcome_system take their columns again at the top of every pass all the same, which is more than the checker asks today.

It does not catch the rest. Take the columns again as it says, and the loop compiles, and you are back to visiting an entity twice or not at all, or to a bounds check stopping the program: a wrong answer or a stop, not a memory error. The checker rules out the lost write. The design rule, that nothing changes structure during a query, is still yours.

The buffer

command: struct = { kind; entity; pending; signature; id; payload; }

Spawned entities have no handle until the buffer runs, so commands_spawn returns a pending number, and commands_set_spawned<T> writes a component into "the entity that pending spawn will create". T has to be in the spawn's signature, and applying the buffer stops the program with a message if it is not. Payloads are copies of the component value, kept as []u8 in frame next to the commands, and the commands themselves are *vec<command> in frame. commands_apply runs everything in order. Nothing clears anything: the frame region ends at its closing brace in main, and every command and payload go with it.

So a command cannot outlive its frame, by construction. Try to keep the buffer in the game, in a field that says level, and rin refuses:

this points into region 'frame', which may end before the memory in region 'level' that holds it

Copying a component into bytes is the one unsafe act here, in commands_payload. commands_make keeps the region's arena, and commands_spawned takes a block from it. Everything else is checked. write_component copies a payload out with slice<u8>copy, so both ends are slices and the copy cannot run off either. The systems are checked too, but for their kernels' noalias.

Skipped commands

Frame 113 is the interesting one. A bullet destroys one drone, and its blast takes two burning neighbours below zero in the same loop. Each of them is destroyed in turn, and each blast reaches back to drones already recorded as destroyed:

bullet 8:9 hits drone 6:1, health -13.2
drone 6:1 is destroyed
drone 7:1 is caught in the blast, health -14.4
drone 4:2 is caught in the blast, health -4.8
drone 7:1 is destroyed
drone 6:1 is caught in the blast, health -54.0
...

The blast cannot know 6:1 is doomed: its despawn is only recorded, and it is still in its table. So it records an add<burning> against it. When the buffer is applied the despawn comes first, and kayan_move reports kayan_status.dead for the add, so the command is skipped. The summary counts three.

Try

  1. Call kayan_despawn directly in outcome_system instead of recording it. It compiles, because that loop takes its columns again each pass. Then the program stops at frame 56 with index 1 out of bounds (length 1). Explain why, from the swap-remove and drones_here, the count the loop took before it started.
  2. Make blast_system skip neighbours whose health is already at or below zero. The skip count drops to zero. Is the buffer's check still needed?
  3. Give the turret a health component and let leaking drones damage it. When it reaches zero, despawn it through the buffer and end the game.
  4. Print the buffer before applying it, as a log of every structural change the frame made.
  5. Inline integrate back into movement_system, build with gcc -O3 -fopt-info-vec, and find the loop it now versions for aliasing. It needs no unsafe now: without noalias, the checker can vouch for all of it.
  6. Hold a column across a kayan_spawn that grows its table, and read the message. Then let it through with RIN_UNSAFE=1 python tools/check.py kayan --sanitize, which turns the rules off. AddressSanitizer says nothing, because the old memory is still valid memory in the region. That is why this is a rule in the checker: no sanitizer would have found it.

Returns 0 if e has no such component.190// Both ends are slices, so the copy cannot run off either.191write_component: proc(w: *kayan_world, e: kayan_entity, id: u32, payload: []const u8) -> b32 = {192    target: []u8 = kayan_get_bytes(w, e, id);193    if (target.length == 0) {194        return 0;195    }196    if (payload.length < target.length) {197        printfmt("write_component: payload of {} bytes for a component of {}\n", payload.length, target.length);198        exit(1);199    }200    slice<u8>copy(target, payload[0..target.length]);201    return 1;202}203 204// Every command, in the order it was recorded. {};208    spawned: []kayan_entity in frame = commands_spawned(c);209    list: []command = vec<command>items(c*.list);210    for (i: u64 = 0; i < list.length; i += 1) {211        cmd: command = list[i];212        switch (cmd.kind) {213            case command_kind.spawn: {214                spawned[cmd.pending] = kayan_spawn(w, cmd.signature);215                result.applied += 1;216 Advanced · lesson 7

Layout follows access

src/7.access_patterns/access_patterns.rin

src/7.access_patterns/access_patterns.rin

Lesson 1 found the layout SIMD wants: one array per float. This lesson asks what that layout costs everywhere else. 1,048,576 bodies are stored four ways, and two kinds of loop run over each, and the program checks that all four end with the same positions.

Two kinds of loop

Stream: every body, in order, the same math. Integration is the example:

for (i: u64 = 0; i < px.length; i += 1) {
    px[i] += vx[i] * dt;
    ...
}

The next body is always right after the last one, so the hardware prefetcher has it ready, and SIMD can take four or eight at once if they sit side by side.

Lookup: bodies picked by index, two at a time, in no particular order. Contacts are the example, the way collision and constraints reach bodies:

a: u64 = cast(cs[c].a, u64);
b: u64 = cast(cs[c].b, u64);
dx: f32 = px[b] - px[a];
...

Each body is somewhere else in memory. What matters is how many cache lines one body's data sits in, because each one is a separate trip to memory. SIMD does not help: there are no four neighbours to load at once.

Four layouts

aos      [ x y z vx vy vz m r ][ x y z vx vy vz m r ] ...      32 bytes a body
columns  positions  [ x y z ][ x y z ][ x y z ] ...
         velocities [ vx vy vz ][ vx vy vz ] ...                 24 bytes a body
split    px [ x x x x ... ]   py [ y y y y ... ]   pz ...  vx ...  vy ...  vz ...
blocks   [ x0..x7 | y0..y7 | z0..z7 | vx0..vx7 | vy0..vy7 | vz0..vz7 ][ x8..x15 ...
  • aos keeps everything about a body together, two fields neither loop uses included.
  • columns is one array per component, each component a small struct. This is what an ECS table stores, and what lessons 2 to 6 use.
  • split is one array per float, lesson 1's move_split.
  • blocks is eight bodies at a time, each coordinate a run of eight floats. It is split cut into pieces of eight, with the pieces of one body kept near each other. The usual name is AoSoA, an array of structs of arrays.

As in lesson 1, the arena is the region level, every array is a slice that names it, and each loop is a proc[unsafe] kernel so that it can take noalias, called from inside unsafe { }.

The program prints how many 64-byte cache lines one body's position sits in:

cache lines one lookup touches: aos 1.000, columns 1.125, split 3.000, blocks 2.000

A 12-byte vec3 crosses a line boundary 2 times in 16, hence 1.125. In split, x, y and z are in three different arrays. In a block, x and y share a line and z is in the next.

The program works that out from byte offsets within an array, as if each array began on a line. new_slice aligns to the element, not to the line, so nothing promises that. In this build most arrays do start on a line, positions and velocities start 32 bytes into one, and the counts from the real addresses come out the same. A promise would take an arena push with an alignment of 64, which is unsafe.

Measured

Release, clang on Windows (clang -O2 and clang-cl /O2, which make the same loops) on one core, best of at least three runs, on a Ryzen 9 9950X3D: 1 MB of L2 a core and 96 MB of L3. The body count, the contact count and the steps were changed in the source for the first and last columns. At 16,384 bodies each layout fits in L2; at the lesson's 1,048,576 each is 24 to 32 MB and sits in L3; at 8,388,608 each is 192 to 256 MB and comes mostly from RAM.

Stream, ns per body:

layout16,3841,048,5768,388,608
aos0.480.571.26
columns0.670.620.93
split0.330.430.76
blocks0.140.290.88

Lookup, ns per contact:

layout16,3841,048,5768,388,608
aos1.051.7610.20
columns1.051.727.25
split1.672.7211.01
blocks1.622.6714.00

clang-cl with /arch:AVX2 agrees on the main points: split streams fastest from RAM, and columns look up fastest. So does gcc -O3 on the lookups. On the stream it does not, with the checks on: it leaves split unvectorized, as in lesson 1, and split streams slowest from RAM, at 1.86 ns. With -DRIN_NO_BOUNDS_CHECKS it is fastest again, at 0.80. Where two numbers are within about 20 percent, the order changes from build to build. The machine was busy, and everything on it shares that L3: lookups at a million bodies came out up to three times slower in unlucky runs.

What it says:

  • Split wins the stream from RAM and loses the lookup. There it streams 1.2 times faster than columns, and looks up 1.5 times slower: three lines a body instead of one.
  • Columns win the lookup once the data leaves the cache, and tie with AoS before that, since both have about one line a body. From RAM, columns' positions are 100 MB, about all of L3, while AoS spreads the same lookups over 256 MB. In the stream they are slowest in cache: lesson 1 showed why a vec3 fights the registers.
  • Blocks are the compromise, mostly in the stream. In cache they streamed fastest of all, more than twice split's speed in L2. From RAM they fall a little behind split. They look up no better than split: two lines a body instead of three did not show here.
  • Out of cache, a lookup costs about ten times a streamed body. From RAM, 7 to 14 ns a contact against about 1 ns a body. Turning lookups into something closer to a stream, by sorting contacts or walking space in order, usually saves more than any layout choice.

What the compiler makes of it

clang-cl /O2, Windows x64, from the object file:

loopbodies a passinstructions a passshuffles
integrate_aos1161
integrate_columns47730
integrate_split4200
integrate_blocks8370
integrate_split, /arch:AVX28140
integrate_blocks, /arch:AVX28140
contacts_columns1 contact290
contacts_split1 contact440

Blocks vectorize as cleanly as split: the inner loop over eight lanes is a fixed-size loop over consecutive floats, which compilers turn into whole registers. The contact loops are one contact a pass in every layout.

Bounds checks are on in all of these, and the stream loops are as they would be without them, as lesson 1 explains. The contact loops are where the checks stay. A contact's two indexes come out of data, so nothing can prove them in range, and each index stays a compare and a branch per use: contacts_columns would be 25 instructions without them, contacts_split 32. It hardly shows in the time, since the trip to memory is most of a lookup. With -DRIN_NO_BOUNDS_CHECKS the lookup table moves by about 10 percent from RAM and not at all in cache.

In between

Engines that have both kinds of loop do one of these:

  • Blocks, as above. One layout, decent at both.
  • Gather, work, scatter. Storage stays in columns or AoS, good for lookups. The hot loop copies a batch of bodies into a wide layout, x's in one register and y's in another, does its math, and copies them back. The copy pays off when the same batch is worked on many times, as a constraint solver does over several iterations. Box2D v3 solves contacts this way, four or eight at a time.
  • Two layouts for two jobs. A particle system that only ever streams stores split. The bodies that collision looks up stay in columns.

How an ECS decides

An ECS does not decide where each float goes. The component is the unit it stores together, and the programmer decides what a component is.

  • Tables. kayan, Unity's entities, Bevy and flecs keep one table per archetype, with one column per component. That is this lesson's columns layout: an array per component, and each component's fields side by side inside it. Unity cuts its tables into 16 KB chunks, each holding every component array for as many entities as fit, which is close to blocks at the level of components.
  • Sparse sets. EnTT stores each component in its own dense array with a lookup table from entity to index, and can keep several components in the same order ("groups") so a system over them streams. Bevy lets each component choose: table storage, or a sparse set for components added and removed often.
  • Systems are streams. A system is a query and a kernel, as in lesson 6: the ECS finds the tables that match, and hands the kernel each table's columns. That stream over columns is the fast path every ECS is built for. Systems that say which columns they read and which they write are what lets a scheduler run them in parallel.
  • Lookups go through the handle. Reaching one entity is handle, slot, table and row, then the column: kayan_get in lesson 4. That is this lesson's lookup loop with an extra hop in front. ECS code keeps lookups for the places that need them, such as relationships between entities and collision, and finds the rest by query.

So the decisions that are yours:

  1. Keep components small, to what one stream system reads. A component a system reads half of is AoS's wasted bytes again.
  2. Leave components as small structs, position { x, y, z }, unless a profiler shows a stream over them is the bottleneck. They are the best layout for lookups and good enough for most streams.
  3. For a hot stream over huge counts, particles above all, store split or blocks, or gather into them for the hot loop.
  4. Make lookups rarer and less random before tuning their layout.

Try

  1. Sort cs by a before the timing loops and run --time again. Which lookup numbers change, and by how much?
  2. Set body_count and contact_count to 8388608 and run --time in Release. Compare with the tables above.
  3. Make the contacts push velocities too, vx, vy and vz of both bodies. How many lines does a lookup touch in each layout now?
  4. Add /arch:AVX2 to build_c_flags and compare the stream column.
  5. Write contacts_gather: for every eight contacts, copy the sixteen bodies' positions into [8]f32 arrays, do the arithmetic over the arrays, and copy back. Contacts that share a body in the same eight break it; find the case and decide what to do about it.
  6. Make body 64 bytes with fields neither loop uses, and watch aos in both tables.

1// kayan: archetype tables, entity handles, and moving entities between tables.2//3// This is the world lesson 4 builds, kept as a library so lessons 5 and 6 can4// use it as it is. Read it with lesson 4: the lesson explains the why, this5// file is the how.6//7// What a program using it provides:8//9//   * its components, as structs, and an enum with one member per component;10//   * `component_of: proc<T>() -> <its enum>` for each component type, which11//     the generic procs here call to find a type's id;12//   * a call to `kayan_register` for each component, with its reflect record.13//14// Ids are u32 here, so the library does not need to know the program's enum.15// Up to 64 components, because a signature is a u64.16//17// Not here, on purpose: threads, change tracking, chunked storage, relations.18// Each is worth a lesson of its own and none is needed to see the idea.19//20// A table's columns are bytes addressed by a component's size and alignment, and21// almost all of this is checked anyway: the bytes are a `[]u8`, so a row past the22// end stops the program like any index. Three procs need unsafe { }: making the23// world, which keeps the region's arena; taking an aligned block from it; and24// viewing bytes as T. What a lesson can hold is said in the types: `option<*T>`25// where null is possible, `*const` where nothing is written, a `[]T` cut to the26// rows in use.27//28// The world lives in the region `level`, declared here for every program that29// imports this file; lesson 6 also uses `frame`, one region per game frame.30 31import "std/print.rin"32import "std/memops.rin"33import "std/vec.rin"34import "std/hashmap.rin"35import "std/slice.rin"36import "std/reflect.rin"37 38level: region;39frame: region in level;40 41// A handle. `index` picks a slot in the world's slot list and `generation` says42// which life of that slot the handle was made for. Generations start at 1, so a zeroed handle, `{}`, never45// names a live entity and can stand for "none".46kayan_entity: struct = {47    index: u32;48    generation: u32;49}50 51// Where an entity lives now: which table, which row. Rows move (swap-remove,52// lesson 2), so this is updated whenever one does. Handles never move. A free53// slot already holds its next generation, which no handle has yet, so the54// generation check alone says whether a handle is alive.55kayan_slot: struct = {56    generation: u32;57    table: u32;58    row: u32;59}60 61// One archetype. `entities[row]` is the handle of the entity in that row, which62// is how a swap-remove finds the slot to fix. `columns[id]` holds `capacity` rows63// of component `id` when the signature has bit `id`, and is empty otherwise.
